units.title: Memory through the OS’s eyes
units.blurb: What the operating system sees when .NET asks for memory: virtual addresses and pages, reserve and commit, why a process has several "memory used" numbers, the stack limit and CPU caches.

lessons.title: Virtual memory
lessons.sub: Addresses, pages, the MMU and page faults

cards.title: An address in your program is not an address in RAM
cards.body:
When C# code reads an object’s field, the CPU gets an address like 0x7FF6_1234_5678. That’s a virtual address: it says nothing about which memory chip actually holds the bytes.

Every process has its own address space, a huge map of addresses that is almost entirely empty. On every access the CPU translates the virtual address into a physical one. The translation is done by a unit inside the CPU, the MMU, and the OS keeps the translation rules in the process’s page table.
cards.deep: Why bother: processes are isolated from each other, you can hand out more addresses than there is RAM, rarely used data can be moved out to disk, and a file can be mapped into memory as if it were an array. The OS’s own code lives in the same map, but in the half that user code cannot touch.

cards.title: Pages
cards.body:
Translating every byte separately would be far too expensive, so memory is split into pages, usually 4 KB (4096 bytes) each. Translation works in whole pages.

An address splits into two parts: the high bits are the page number, the low 12 bits are the offset inside the page (212 = 4096). For 0x7FF6_1234_5678 the offset is 0x678 and the page number is everything else.

A page table entry holds the physical page number plus flags: is the page in memory, is it writable, can code run from it, can user code access it.
cards.deep: On x86-64 the page table is a four-level tree, 9 address bits per level, plus 12 bits of offset: 48 bits in total. Walking the tree on every read would be slow, so finished translations are cached in the TLB, a small buffer inside the CPU. A TLB miss costs a table walk. There are also large pages: 2 MB and 1 GB on x86-64. The normal page size depends on the platform: 4 KB on x86-64, 16 KB on Macs with Apple Silicon, and on ARM64 Linux the kernel is built with 4, 16 or 64 KB pages. From .NET you can read it with Environment.SystemPageSize.

cards.q: How many low bits of an address hold the offset inside a 4 KB page?
cards.explain: 4096 is 2 to the power of 12, so an offset from 0 to 4095 fits in exactly 12 bits. The remaining bits are the page number.

cards.title: Page faults
cards.body:
What if the page table entry says "this page is not in memory"? The CPU stops the instruction and calls an OS handler: that’s a page fault. The OS works out what happened:

  • Soft (minor) fault: the data is already in RAM, or all it takes is a zeroed page. The OS fills in the table entry and that’s it. Cost: on the order of a microsecond.
  • Hard (major) fault: the page must be read from disk, from the page file or from a mapped file such as DLL code. Cost: from tens of microseconds on an SSD to milliseconds on an HDD.
  • The address maps to nothing: the OS reports an access error, an access violation on Windows, a SIGSEGV signal on Linux.

After a soft or hard fault the instruction runs again and the program notices nothing, except the time it lost.
cards.deep: The first touch of freshly allocated memory is a page fault too: that is the moment the OS hands out a zeroed page. On Linux you can see the counts with ps -o min_flt,maj_flt -p PID or in the output of /usr/bin/time -v; on Windows, in the process performance counters. A null dereference in .NET also starts as an access error: pages near address zero are never mapped, and the runtime turns that fault into a NullReferenceException.

cards.q: Match the event with what it means
pairs: The page is already in RAM, it only needs mapping
The page has to be read from disk
A cache of finished address translations

cards.title: One address, two processes
cards.body:
Run a program twice and print the address of the same variable: the numbers may match. There’s no conflict: each process has its own page table, and the same virtual page leads to different physical pages in each.

A process can’t even name another process’s memory: every address it uses is translated through its own table. That’s what isolation means.

The reverse happens too: one physical page can be visible in several processes. That’s how the OS shares the code of system libraries and the runtime: it’s loaded into RAM once and mapped into every process that needs it.
cards.deep: ASLR, the random placement of modules, stacks and heaps at startup, makes matching addresses rarer and gets in the way of attacks, but the rule stays the same. You can read another process’s memory only through the OS (ReadProcessMemory on Windows, process_vm_readv on Linux, with the right permissions) or by agreeing on shared memory up front; in .NET that’s MemoryMappedFile. Shared library pages are marked copy-on-write: a process that tries to write gets its own copy.

cards.q: Two processes write different numbers to the same virtual address at the same time. What does each of them read back?
options: Each reads its own number
Both read the number of whoever wrote last
The second process gets an access error

wrong.1: That would happen if the address were physical. But the processes have different page tables.
wrong.2: There’s no error: in each process the address maps to that process’s own page.

cards.explain: The same virtual address in two processes goes through two different page tables and ends up in different physical pages.

cards.title: How much is 64 bits
cards.body:
A pointer in a 64-bit process takes 8 bytes, but today’s x86-64 CPUs use only 48 bits of a virtual address, which is 256 TB. Half goes to the kernel and half to the process: 128 TB of user space on both Windows and Linux.

For comparison, a 32-bit process sees only 4 GB of addresses, and on Windows it gets 2 GB of them by default.

The takeaway: a 64-bit process practically never runs out of addresses. What runs out is something else: physical memory and how much the OS is willing to promise. That’s the next lesson.
cards.deep: The top 16 bits of a 48-bit address must repeat bit 47 (a canonical address), which is why user addresses look like 0x0000_7FFx_xxxx_xxxx and kernel addresses start with 0xFFFF. Newer CPUs support five-level page tables and 57-bit addresses; Linux then hands out addresses above 128 TB only to programs that explicitly ask for them. A 32-bit process with the LargeAddressAware flag gets up to 4 GB on 64-bit Windows.

cards.q: A program reads a freshly allocated page for the first time. Put the steps in order
items: An instruction accesses a virtual address
The MMU finds no translation in the TLB and walks the page table
The entry is marked "not in memory", so the CPU raises a page fault
The OS takes a free physical page, zeroes it and fills in the entry
The instruction runs again and reads 0
cards.explain: This is a soft fault: no disk involved, the OS just finds a physical page and zeroes it. It zeroes it so the process can’t see someone else’s data.

cards.q: What is true about virtual memory? Select all that apply.
options: Every process has its own address space
The OS maps memory in whole pages
A virtual address is the same as a cell number in RAM
A hard page fault costs about as much as an L1 cache read
One physical page can be visible in several processes
cards.explain: A virtual address is translated through the page table and can lead anywhere. A hard fault is a disk read: it costs tens of thousands of times more than an L1 read, or worse.

cards.q: A RAM read takes on the order of 100 ns. How much longer does a hard page fault served from an SSD take?
options: About a thousand times longer or more
About twice as long
The same: both are memory
It’s faster: the disk caches
cards.explain: A hard fault from an SSD takes tens or hundreds of microseconds, three orders of magnitude more than a RAM access. With a spinning disk it’s milliseconds, another one or two orders worse. That’s why a program that runs short of RAM slows down so abruptly.

lessons.title: Reserve and commit
lessons.sub: Why a process has several different memory numbers

cards.title: Two steps: claim the addresses, then back them
cards.body:
Getting memory from the OS can take two steps.

Reserve: the process says "this range of addresses is mine". The OS just makes a note in the address space map. It costs neither RAM nor page file space.

Commit: the OS promises that the pages in the range will have something behind them, and counts them against a global limit made up of RAM plus the page file. But a physical page still appears only on first touch, through that same soft page fault.
cards.deep: On Windows both steps are done by VirtualAlloc: the MEM_RESERVE flag reserves, MEM_COMMIT commits. The reverse operations are VirtualFree with MEM_DECOMMIT (give back the promise, keep the addresses) and MEM_RELEASE (give back the addresses). Reservations come in multiples of 64 KB, commits in pages. Touching a page that is reserved but not committed is an access error.

cards.q: Claim 1 GB of addresses, but back only the first 64 KB with memory
cards.code:
void* p = VirtualAlloc(null, 1 << 30, ___, PAGE_NOACCESS);
VirtualAlloc(p, 64 * 1024, ___, PAGE_READWRITE);
cards.explain: First the whole range is reserved, then the first 64 KB are committed. The other addresses are taken but cost nothing until someone commits them.

cards.title: Linux: mmap and overcommit
cards.body:
On Linux the same two steps go through mmap: a range mapped with PROT_NONE is the counterpart of a reservation, and mprotect with read and write access is the counterpart of a commit.

The big difference is overcommit. By default Linux doesn’t keep strict count of its promises: it refuses only obviously impossible requests and grants the rest, betting that not all of that memory will be needed at once. Physical pages appear on first touch, just as on Windows.

If RAM and swap do run out, there’s no exception: the kernel starts the OOM killer, which kills a process with SIGKILL. The process simply vanishes, with no stack trace and no catch.
cards.deep: The mode is set in /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory: 0 is the heuristic (default), 1 allows everything, 2 is strict accounting against CommitLimit from /proc/meminfo. In a container the cgroup sets its own ceiling: go over the memory limit and the kernel kills the process inside the container, while the orchestrator sees exit code 137 (128 plus the SIGKILL number).

cards.q: Why can a program on Linux die from lack of memory not at the moment it allocates, but later?
options: Pages are handed out on first touch, there may not be enough of them then, and the OOM killer comes
mmap always reports errors with a delay
The garbage collector postpones the allocation until the next collection
cards.explain: With overcommit, an allocation is only a promise. Real memory is needed at the first write, and if there is none, the kernel picks a victim and kills it.

cards.title: How much memory does the process use? Depends what you count
cards.body:
• Virtual size (VSZ on Linux): every address in use, reserved, committed or mapped from files. For a .NET process that’s hundreds of gigabytes, and that’s fine.
  • Private bytes (commit): committed memory that belongs to this process alone, what the OS has promised it. Grows when you leak.
  • Working set (RSS on Linux): pages sitting in physical memory right now, including shared library pages.

What’s promised hasn’t been touched yet, and what’s been touched the OS can evict, so the numbers drift apart. In the Memory column, Task Manager shows the private working set by default, which is yet another number.
cards.deep: The working set can shrink without the program doing anything: under pressure the OS takes pages away and they go to standby. If the process touches them again, bringing them back is a soft fault. On Linux the most precise view is /proc/PID/smaps_rollup: it has Rss, Pss (shared pages divided between the processes) and anonymous memory. The private working set on Windows is the working set without shared pages.

cards.q: Match each number with what it counts
pairs: Every address in use, even with no memory behind it
Committed memory of this process alone
Pages that are in RAM right now

cards.title: How the CLR gets memory for the heap
cards.body:
At startup the garbage collector reserves a large contiguous range of addresses, hundreds of gigabytes in a 64-bit process. Addresses are free, and the heap knows it has room to grow.

From there the heap commits memory in chunks as it grows, and after a collection it can hand unneeded chunks back to the OS (decommit). So:

  • the virtual size is huge from the first second;
  • private bytes follow the size of the heap;
  • the working set is whatever the program has touched recently.
cards.deep: Since .NET 7 the heap is made of regions: by default 4 MB for ordinary objects and 32 MB for large ones. The initial reservation for regions is 256 GB by default, more on machines with a very large amount of RAM; the GCRegionRange setting changes it. GCHeapHardLimit caps the heap; in a container with a memory limit it defaults to 75% of that limit. From code you can see the numbers through GC.GetGCMemoryInfo(): HeapSizeBytes, TotalCommittedBytes, TotalAvailableMemoryBytes.

cards.q: A service on .NET 9 shows a virtual size of 260 GB and a working set of 300 MB. What does that mean?
options: All is well: addresses are reserved, and about 300 MB sit in RAM
A 260 GB leak
The process wrote 260 GB to the page file
cards.explain: A huge virtual size in .NET is the address reservation for the heap. It uses neither RAM nor the page file. You hunt leaks by private bytes and the size of the managed heap.

cards.q: Which line shows how much of the process’s memory is in RAM right now?
cards.explain: WorkingSet64 is the working set, the pages in physical memory. VirtualMemorySize64 is all addresses, PrivateMemorySize64 is committed private memory, and GC.GetTotalMemory is how many bytes the GC estimates managed objects take.

cards.title: OutOfMemoryException with RAM to spare
cards.body:
OutOfMemoryException doesn’t mean "RAM ran out". Typical causes:

  • The commit limit is exhausted. Windows has already promised all of RAM and the page file to processes. Actual RAM use may be low, since the promises are untouched, but the OS won’t make new ones.
  • The GC heap limit is reached. In a container or with GCHeapHardLimit, the runtime throws at its own boundary even if the machine has gigabytes free.
  • No contiguous range of addresses. A 32-bit problem: 2–4 GB of addresses get fragmented and a big array has nowhere to go.
  • The object is too big. An array longer than Array.MaxLength can’t be created no matter how much memory you have.

And on Linux without limits it may never get as far as an exception: the OOM killer kills the process.
cards.deep: Before an operation that is certain to need a lot of memory, you can ask in advance: MemoryFailPoint checks whether there’s room and throws InsufficientMemoryException before the work starts rather than halfway through. If OOM hits a 64-bit process on a big server, first check the container limits and the GC settings in runtimeconfig.json.

cards.q: What can cause an OutOfMemoryException while Task Manager shows gigabytes of free RAM? Select all that apply.
options: The commit limit is exhausted: RAM and the page file are already promised
A process in a container hit the GC heap limit
A 32-bit process couldn’t find a contiguous range of addresses
Too many threads are waiting on a lock
The garbage collector is off by default
cards.explain: Waiting on a lock costs no memory, and the garbage collector is always on. The other three are the classics: the memory is promised, you hit your own ceiling, or there were no consecutive addresses.

cards.q: A 64-bit process calls VirtualAlloc with MEM_RESERVE for 1 GB a hundred times and writes nothing. What grew?
options: Only the virtual size
The working set, by 100 GB
Private bytes, by 100 GB
Nothing: Windows refuses on the second call
cards.explain: A reservation is only addresses. 100 GB fits easily into 128 TB of user space, and no commit or RAM is used.

lessons.title: The stack and CPU caches
lessons.sub: The stack limit, cache lines and locality

cards.title: A thread’s stack is a range claimed in advance
cards.body:
Every thread has its own stack. It’s a reserved range of addresses that gets committed bit by bit as the stack grows (it grows downward, toward lower addresses). Allocating on the stack just moves the stack pointer, which makes it almost free.

The size is set up front and doesn’t change:

  • for the main thread of a Windows program it’s usually 1 MB, a value written into the exe header;
  • for the main thread on Linux it follows ulimit -s, usually 8 MB;
  • for threads created by .NET the runtime picks the default, and it depends on the OS and the version. Need a different one? Pass it to the constructor: new Thread(work, maxStackSize).
cards.deep: Check the exact defaults for new threads on your own platform: on Linux the runtime doesn’t inherit the main thread’s 8 MB but sets its own size, around one and a half megabytes. On Linux and macOS the DOTNET_DefaultStackSize environment variable changes it (a hexadecimal number of bytes). The thread pool creates its threads with the default size, so deep recursion inside a request handler runs into exactly that limit.

cards.title: What goes into a stack frame
cards.body:
Every method call adds a frame. It holds:

  • the return address and saved registers;
  • arguments that didn’t fit into registers;
  • local value types: int, double, whole structs;
  • local references, 8 bytes of address, while the object itself is on the heap;
  • stackalloc buffers.

What isn’t on the stack: class instances, variables captured by a lambda (they move into a closure object on the heap), and locals of an async method that live across an await (they become fields of the state machine).
cards.deep: This is a model, not a promise: the JIT can keep a local only in a register and never touch the stack, and it can spread the fields of a small struct across registers. The opposite happens too: in .NET 9–10 the JIT learned to place objects that never leave the method on the stack in some cases (escape analysis). "Classes live on the heap" is still the right model, but the JIT chooses the actual location.

cards.q: What ends up in the stack frame of Draw? Select all that apply.
options: The whole struct p
The reference list, 8 bytes
The List<int> object itself
The 64 bytes of buf
The list’s internal array
cards.explain: The List<int> object and its internal array are on the heap; the stack holds only the reference to the list. The struct and the stackalloc buffer sit right in the frame, unless the JIT moved something into registers.

cards.title: The guard page and StackOverflowException
cards.body:
Just below the committed part of the stack sits a guard page. Touch it and the OS commits the next page and moves the guard further down. That’s how the stack grows on demand.

When the stack reaches the end of its reservation, there’s nowhere left to grow: a stack overflow. In .NET a StackOverflowException can’t be caught: the runtime terminates the process immediately. Neither catch nor finally runs.

Typical causes: infinite recursion, recursion over deep data (a long chain, a degenerate tree), a huge stackalloc. The rule: if recursion depth depends on input, rewrite the traversal with an explicit Stack<T> or check the headroom with RuntimeHelpers.EnsureSufficientExecutionStack().
cards.deep: EnsureSufficientExecutionStack throws InsufficientExecutionStackException when little stack is left; that’s an ordinary exception you can catch. There’s also a version without an exception: TryEnsureSufficientExecutionStack. Recursive parsers and expression compilers protect themselves this way. On Linux the guard page is a protected area: touching it raises SIGSEGV, the runtime recognizes the overflow, prints a message and terminates the process.

cards.q: A chain of 10 million nodes. Which line won’t work the way the author intended?
cards.explain: Ten million nested calls won’t fit on the stack, and StackOverflowException can’t be caught: the process will terminate. Walk the chain with a loop instead.

cards.title: Caches: memory is far, the cache is near
cards.body:
The CPU works faster than RAM can answer, so caches sit between them. Orders of magnitude for latency (exact numbers depend on the CPU):

  • L1: about 1 ns, tens of KB per core;
  • L2: a few ns, from hundreds of KB to a couple of MB per core;
  • L3: on the order of 10 ns, tens of MB shared by all cores;
  • RAM: on the order of 100 ns.

Memory arrives in the cache not byte by byte but in cache lines of 64 bytes. Read one int and the 15 next to it come along. And if you read sequentially, the prefetcher spots the pattern and pulls in the next lines ahead of time.
cards.deep: In cycles at 3–4 GHz: L1 is 4–5 cycles, L2 around 12–15, L3 a few dozen, RAM hundreds. 64 bytes is the line size on x86-64 and most ARM CPUs; on Apple M-series chips it’s 128 bytes. Address translation is cached too, in the TLB, and scattered access over a large amount of memory misses both caches at once.

cards.q: Order these from fastest to slowest
items: CPU register
L1 cache
L3 cache
Main memory
Soft page fault
Hard page fault from an SSD
cards.explain: A register is a fraction of a nanosecond, L1 about 1 ns, L3 on the order of 10 ns, RAM on the order of 100 ns, a soft fault on the order of a microsecond, a hard fault from an SSD tens to hundreds of microseconds.

cards.title: An array of structs versus an array of references
cards.body:
If Point is a struct of two ints, a Point[] stores the points back to back, 8 bytes each: 8 points per cache line, and a traversal walks straight through memory.

If Point is a class, the array stores only references. Each point is a separate object: 16 bytes of overhead (the header and the type pointer) plus 8 bytes of data. To read pts[i].X you have to load the reference and follow it. Freshly created objects often sit next to each other, but after the program has run for a while and collections have happened, that’s not guaranteed.

For a million points: structs are about 8 MB read sequentially; classes are 8 MB of references plus about 24 MB of objects, and each hop can cost a cache miss.
cards.deep: The next step is a "struct of arrays": if a loop reads only X, keep X in one array and Y in another, and every cache line carries 16 useful numbers instead of 8. ECS engines and vectorization with Vector<T> are built on this. The price is less convenient code, so it’s done only in hot loops, after measuring.

cards.task: Step through both versions: where do the points lie in one block, and where do you have to follow a reference to each?

steps.note: An array of structs is one object. Room for all three points is right inside it, back to back.
The point is written straight into the slot. Neighboring slots are neighboring bytes, in the same cache line.
No new objects: a traversal reads memory strictly in sequence.
One object in total: 24 bytes of points in one block.
An array of classes stores only references, 8 bytes each. All null for now.
Each point is a separate object with its own header. The array holds just the address.
To read X, the CPU first reads the reference and then follows it: a second memory access.
Four objects in total. Where the points end up after collections is not the array’s call.

cards.q: Why is this traversal several times slower than with the loops swapped?
options: Elements adjacent in i are 16 KB apart: every read is a new cache line
A multidimensional array checks bounds twice
Adding longs is slower than adding ints
It isn’t: loop order doesn’t matter
cards.explain: In C# an int[,] is stored row by row: m[i, j] and m[i, j + 1] are neighbors. A row is 4096 × 4 bytes = 16 KB. The last index should change in the inner loop; then the traversal is sequential and one cache line serves 16 reads.

cards.title: False sharing: threads get in each other’s way without sharing data
cards.body:
Two threads each count into their own slot: the first writes to counts[0], the second to counts[1]. There’s no race and the result is correct. Yet it runs slower than a single thread.

The reason: the slots are adjacent and sit in the same cache line. To write, a core must own the line exclusively. Every write by one core takes the line away from the other, and it bounces between their caches. This is false sharing.

Remedies: accumulate in a local variable and write once at the end; keep hot fields at least 64 bytes apart; give each thread its own data.
cards.deep: Core caches coordinate through a coherence protocol (the MESI family): only one core can hold a line it writes to in modified state. Some Intel CPUs fetch lines in pairs, which is why hot fields are sometimes spaced 128 bytes apart. The .NET libraries do this themselves, for example in ConcurrentQueue: the head and tail of the queue are separated by padding.

cards.q: Each thread gets its own counter. Spread the array’s counters across different cache lines
cards.explain: With a 64-byte element, the Value fields of neighboring elements are 64 bytes apart and never land in the same cache line. Size = 8 would give you a plain long array, with eight counters per line.

lessons.title: Final: memory through the OS's eyes
lessons.sub: Pages, reserve and commit, the stack and caches

cards.task: Step through the call to Draw: what lives in the frame, what lives on the heap, and what is left after the method returns?

steps.note: The struct is 8 bytes right in Main's frame. Space for the frame was taken with a single stack pointer move on method entry; the OS is not involved.
The call pushes a new frame: return address, saved registers, locals. The parameter at is a copy of the whole struct.
The frame holds only an 8-byte reference. The List<int> itself is on the heap, in memory the GC reserved and committed from the OS in advance.
The number is in the frame too. Or only in a register: that is up to the JIT.
The frame is gone: the stack pointer moved back, and the stack pages still belong to the thread. The list is now garbage — the GC removes it, not the method return.

cards.q: Pages are 4 KB. Which two addresses are on the same page?
cards.explain: The low 12 bits are the offset; the rest is the page number. The first pair shares the page number (0x7FF6_1234_5), with offsets 0x000 and 0xFFF — the start and end of the page. 0x…5FFF and 0x…6000 are adjacent bytes, but on different pages.

cards.q: The life of a page obtained through VirtualAlloc. Put the steps in order
items: MEM_RESERVE: the address range is marked as taken
MEM_COMMIT: the OS counts the pages against the commit limit
First write: a soft page fault, and the OS hands out a zeroed physical page
The page joins the process working set
MEM_DECOMMIT: the promise is returned, the addresses are still taken
MEM_RELEASE: the addresses are free again
cards.explain: Virtual size grows at step one, private bytes at step two, the working set at steps three and four. Going back happens in reverse: first the promise is returned, then the addresses.

cards.q: A Linux process maps 1 GB read-write with mmap and writes one byte into every 4 KB page of the first 100 MB. Roughly how much did VSZ and RSS grow?
options: VSZ by 1 GB, RSS by 100 MB
VSZ and RSS by 1 GB
VSZ and RSS by 100 MB
VSZ by 1 GB, RSS barely grew
cards.explain: VSZ counts all taken addresses — the whole gigabyte right after mmap. A physical page appears on first touch, and every page of the first 100 MB was touched, so RSS gains about 100 MB.

wrong.3: One write per page is enough: the page fault brings in a whole physical page for it.

cards.q: Match the symptom to the cause
pairs: The kernel killed the process for exceeding the memory limit
The process vanished after deep recursion, finally never ran
OutOfMemoryException on Windows with free RAM
Virtual size 260 GB, working set 300 MB
Address space reserved for the GC heap
Two threads write to adjacent array cells and slow down

cards.q: n comes from a network request. Which line can terminate the process with no exception to catch?
cards.explain: A stackalloc sized by input can run past the stack reservation — that is a stack overflow, and the runtime terminates the process. A huge new int[n] throws an ordinary OutOfMemoryException that you can catch. For large, unpredictable sizes use an array or ArrayPool; stackalloc only with a size check.

cards.q: Which are true about CPU caches? Select all.
options: Reading one int brings the whole cache line into the cache — usually 64 bytes
Walking an int[,] with the outer loop over rows is faster than over columns
An array of structs is read sequentially, an array of classes by following references
False sharing corrupts data: the result becomes wrong
The more threads write to adjacent cells, the faster the work goes
cards.explain: False sharing is a speed problem, not a correctness one: the data is right, but the cache line bounces between cores. That is why adding threads that write to one line does not speed things up, and often slows them down.

cards.q: A request handler on the thread pool parses JSON recursively, and the client controls the depth. How do you protect it?
options: Check RuntimeHelpers.EnsureSufficientExecutionStack() and catch InsufficientExecutionStackException
Wrap the parsing in catch (StackOverflowException)
Increase the main thread stack in the exe header
Call GC.Collect() before parsing
cards.explain: That method throws an ordinary exception while there is still stack left — you can catch it and return an error to the client. Even more robust: cap the depth or rewrite the walk with an explicit Stack<T>.

wrong.1: StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET: the process terminates immediately.
wrong.2: A bigger stack only moves the limit: the client will send deeper nesting. Besides, pool threads do not necessarily take their stack size from the exe header.
wrong.3: The stack is not managed by the garbage collector.

cards.q: new byte[1_500_000_000] works in a 64-bit process but throws OutOfMemoryException in a 32-bit one on the same machine. Why?
options: A 32-bit process has no contiguous free address range that large
In a 32-bit process an array cannot be longer than a million elements
A 32-bit process cannot commit more than 1 GB in one call
32-bit processes have no page file
cards.explain: An array must occupy one contiguous address range. A 32-bit process has only 2–4 GB of addresses, already split among modules, stacks and the heap. A 64-bit process has 128 TB of addresses — there is always room.

lessons.sub: Task Manager, top and what the GC itself knows

cards.title: Numbers nested like dolls
cards.body:
In unit 1 you saw that a process has several numbers for "used" memory. For .NET add one more layer — what the garbage collector knows. From the inside out:

  • live objects — what the roots can reach;
  • the managed heap — live objects, plus garbage not yet collected, plus gaps between objects (fragmentation);
  • the GC commit — memory the GC has committed for the heap, with headroom for new allocations;
  • private bytes of the whole process — the heap plus everything unmanaged: thread stacks, JIT-compiled code, runtime structures, native library buffers.

The working set sits to the side: it is the part of all this that is in RAM right now.
cards.deep: Typical orders of magnitude for a service: hundreds of megabytes of live objects, a slightly larger heap, a GC commit noticeably larger than the heap (especially with Server GC, where every core has its own heap and its own budget), and tens or hundreds of megabytes of unmanaged memory between private bytes and the GC commit. If that gap grows, the leak is not in the managed heap.

cards.q: A service has 2 GB of private bytes, while the GC reports a 300 MB managed heap. Where is the rest?
options: In unmanaged memory: native libraries, stacks, runtime structures
In objects the GC has not counted yet
In the reserved address range of the heap
In the page file, so it does not matter
cards.explain: Private bytes are the commit of the whole process, and the heap is only part of it. A reservation is not counted in private bytes, and the heap already includes uncollected garbage. 1.7 GB outside the heap is a reason to look for a native leak.

wrong.2: A reservation is just addresses. It grows virtual size, not private bytes.

cards.title: What Task Manager and top show
cards.body:
Task Manager shows the private working set in its "Memory" column: the process’s pages in RAM, minus shared ones. It is neither the heap size nor the commit. On the "Details" tab you can enable a commit size column — that is closer to private bytes.

top on Linux:

  • VIRT — all of the process’s addresses; for .NET that is hundreds of gigabytes of reservation;
  • RES — resident memory (RSS), shared pages included;
  • SHR — the part of RES the process may share with others: libraries, mapped files.

None of these tools knows what a managed heap is.
cards.deep: In a container there is one more number — what the cgroup counts (memory.current in cgroup v2). It also includes the page cache of files the process has read, so it can be larger than RSS. The .NET runtime sees the cgroup limit and derives its heap limit from it. For a precise breakdown of RSS on Linux, look at /proc/PID/smaps_rollup, as in unit 1.

cards.q: Match the column with what it counts
pairs: All addresses, including the heap reservation
The process’s pages in RAM, shared ones included
Pages that can be shared with other processes

cards.title: GC.GetTotalMemory: cheap but approximate
cards.body:
GC.GetTotalMemory(false) returns the managed heap size excluding fragmentation. Dead objects that have not been collected yet are included: after a burst of temporary allocations the number grows, after a collection it drops.

GC.GetTotalMemory(true) first lets the collector collect garbage and run finalizers — it triggers full collections until the number stops changing noticeably. You get close to "live only", but at the price of a full blocking collection, which on a large heap is a long pause.

Rule: false for metrics and logs, true only in tests and experiments.
cards.deep: The documentation used to call the result "the number of bytes currently thought to be allocated". The wording is more precise now: the heap size minus fragmentation, that is, minus free objects. The gc-heap-size counter of the old EventCounters was computed exactly through GetTotalMemory(false). How much has been allocated over the life of the process is a different question, answered by GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes() (since .NET Core 3.0).

cards.q: Which line can stop all threads for a full garbage collection?
cards.explain: GetTotalMemory(true) triggers full collections itself and waits for finalizers. The other calls only read counters: GetGCMemoryInfo returns data about a past collection, GetTotalAllocatedBytes without precise does not stop threads, WorkingSet asks the OS.

cards.title: GC.GetGCMemoryInfo: a snapshot of the last collection
cards.body:
Since .NET Core 3.0 you can ask the GC for details, and since .NET 5 you can choose which collection: GCKind.Any, Ephemeral, FullBlocking, Background. All numbers are as of that collection, not now.

  • HeapSizeBytes — the heap size, fragmentation included;
  • FragmentedBytes — free gaps inside the heap;
  • TotalCommittedBytes — how much memory the GC has committed;
  • PromotedBytes — how much survived that collection;
  • GenerationInfo[i] — size and fragmentation of each generation before and after the collection;
  • PauseDurations, PauseTimePercentage — how long threads were stopped.
cards.deep: GenerationInfo is indexed like this: 0, 1, 2 are the generations, 3 is the LOH, 4 is the POH. Index is the sequence number of the collection; if it has not changed between two calls, you are looking at the same collection. There is also memory pressure data: MemoryLoadBytes, HighMemoryLoadThresholdBytes, TotalAvailableMemoryBytes — the GC uses them to decide when to compact more aggressively. In a container TotalAvailableMemoryBytes reflects the limit.

cards.q: Estimate the volume of live objects from the last full blocking collection
cards.code:
var info = GC.GetGCMemoryInfo(GCKind.___);
long live = info.___ - info.___;
cards.explain: After a full blocking collection all garbage is gone, and the heap is live objects plus free gaps. Subtract fragmentation from the heap size. TotalCommittedBytes includes headroom, and an ephemeral collection did not touch generation 2.

cards.title: A big heap is not yet a leak
cards.body:
The collector does not remove garbage immediately. It runs when a generation has used up its allocation budget. Until then the garbage stays in the heap and is counted in every number.

That is why a heap graph under load is a sawtooth: growth, a collection, a drop. The height of the teeth says little. A leak looks different: the floor of the sawtooth grows — the heap size after full collections, from one to the next, under steady load.

Also: Server GC keeps a separate heap and a separate budget per core, so gigabytes of heap on a 32-core machine can be normal.
cards.deep: Since .NET 9, DATAS is on by default for Server GC: the number of heaps and the budgets adapt to the load, and a lightly loaded service no longer inflates its heap across all cores. In .NET 8 DATAS existed but had to be enabled by a setting. The GC may not return memory to the OS right after a spike — decommit follows its own rules too.

cards.q: Which sign points most strongly to a leak in the managed heap?
options: The heap size after each full collection grows from one to the next under steady load
Under load the heap saws between 200 MB and 900 MB
The process virtual size is 260 GB
The working set grew in the first minute after startup and then stays flat
cards.explain: A sawtooth is the collector working normally, a huge virtual size is an address reservation, growth at startup is warm-up. A leak shows as a rising floor: what survives full collections gets bigger every time.

cards.title: Managed or native leak
cards.body:
Compare two graphs: the process’s private bytes and the GC heap.

  • They grow together — the leak is in the managed heap. Heap snapshots show it, and the rest is technique (lesson 3).
  • The heap is flat, private bytes grow — memory goes around the GC: Marshal.AllocHGlobal without a free, a native library, unreleased OS handles, multiplying threads. A managed heap snapshot shows almost nothing here.
  • The heap grows, but there are few live objects — fragmentation: look at FragmentedBytes and pinned objects.
cards.deep: A common hybrid: a small managed wrapper object holds a big native buffer. The heap snapshot shows thousands of 32-byte objects, and behind them gigabytes of native memory. The hint is a type with a finalizer or a SafeHandle whose count keeps growing. The native memory itself is hunted with native tools: on Linux, for example, heaptrack; on Windows, OS heap tracing via ETW.

cards.q: What increases the process’s private bytes but not the managed heap? Select all.
options: Marshal.AllocHGlobal in a loop without FreeHGlobal
A native image-decoding library does not free its buffers
A static List<byte[]> that keeps getting new arrays
Short-lived objects subscribing to an event of a long-lived one
String concatenation in a loop
cards.explain: AllocHGlobal and native buffers take memory around the GC. The static list and the event subscription are leaks, but in the managed heap. Concatenation produces garbage the GC will collect.

lessons.title: The tools
lessons.sub: Counters, heap snapshots, traces and dumps

cards.title: Five tools, five questions
cards.body:
• dotnet-counters — what is happening right now: heap size, collections, pauses, allocation rate;
  • dotnet-gcdump — which types occupy the heap and who holds them;
  • dotnet-trace — what happened over a span of time: every collection, who allocates;
  • dotnet-dump — the full memory of the process: field values, threads, everything at once;
  • PerfView — an analyzer for Windows: opens traces and snapshots, compares them.

The first four are cross-platform .NET utilities. They install as global tools: dotnet tool install --global dotnet-counters. With the .NET 10 SDK you can also run them without installing: dnx dotnet-counters.
cards.code:
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-counters
dotnet-counters ps        # which .NET processes are visible
cards.deep: All four talk to the runtime through the diagnostic port: a named pipe on Windows, a Unix socket in the temp folder on Linux and macOS. Hence the common problems: the tool must run as the same user as the process (or as root), with the same TMPDIR, and for a container you either install the tool inside or expose the socket and pass --diagnostic-port. Back in .NET Framework none of this existed: there were Windows performance counters, ETW and WinDbg with SOS.

cards.title: dotnet-counters: the heap’s pulse
cards.body:
dotnet-counters monitor attaches to a process and refreshes a table every second. collect writes the same to CSV or JSON.

Since .NET 9 the runtime publishes the System.Runtime meter with new names. For memory, watch:

  • dotnet.gc.last_collection.heap.size — the heap by generation after the last collection;
  • dotnet.gc.last_collection.heap.fragmentation.size — the gaps;
  • dotnet.gc.last_collection.memory.committed_size — the GC commit;
  • dotnet.gc.heap.total_allocated — total allocated; its growth gives the allocation rate;
  • dotnet.gc.collections and dotnet.gc.pause.time — collections and pauses;
  • dotnet.process.memory.working_set.
cards.code: dotnet-counters monitor -n Shop --counters System.Runtime[dotnet.gc.last_collection.heap.size,dotnet.gc.heap.total_allocated]
cards.deep: If the app runs on .NET 8 or older, there is no System.Runtime meter, and the tool shows the old EventCounters: gc-heap-size, gen-0-size, gen-2-size, loh-size, poh-size, alloc-rate, time-in-gc, gc-fragmentation, gc-committed (since .NET 6), working-set. Without --counters it shows all of System.Runtime by default. The same metrics can be exported to OpenTelemetry and viewed on a dashboard — counters is for a quick look without any setup.

cards.q: Match the question with the System.Runtime counter in .NET 9+
pairs: How many bytes per second the code allocates
How long threads stood still in collections
Whether the heap has many gaps
How much of the process is in RAM now

cards.q: Save the counters of process 1902 to a table so you can plot them later
cards.code: dotnet-counters ___ -p 1902 --refresh-interval 5 --format ___ -o gc.csv
cards.explain: monitor only draws a table in the terminal; collect writes to a file. The formats of collect are csv and json; nettrace and speedscope are dotnet-trace formats.

cards.title: dotnet-gcdump: the heap graph without values
cards.body:
dotnet-gcdump collect -p 1902 asks the runtime to perform a full generation 2 collection and, during it, to emit events about every object and the references between them. The tool builds a graph from them and writes a .gcdump file.

The file holds types, sizes, references and roots. No field values: no strings, no numbers. So the file is small, safe to hand over, and good for the question "what takes up memory and who holds it".

The price: a full blocking collection, a long pause on a large heap. You open a .gcdump in Visual Studio or PerfView; on Linux you can get a type table: dotnet-gcdump report file.gcdump.
cards.deep: The events go through a buffer inside the process itself, which can grow up to 256 MB — keep that in mind in a container with a tight limit. On a very large heap events can be dropped and the snapshot comes out incomplete; take a full dump then. By default collect waits 30 seconds (-t changes the timeout). Visual Studio can open two .gcdump files and compare them.

cards.q: A cache holds thousands of strings. You need to see which URLs exactly are in them. What do you capture?
options: A process dump with dotnet-dump
A heap snapshot with dotnet-gcdump
Counters with dotnet-counters
A trace with the gc-collect profile
cards.explain: Object contents exist only in a full memory dump: dumpheap finds the strings, dumpobj shows their text. A .gcdump holds only types, sizes and references, and counters and gc-collect know nothing about individual objects.

wrong.1: A heap snapshot shows how many strings there are and who holds them, but not their text: a .gcdump has no field values.

cards.title: dotnet-dump: all of memory, plus SOS
cards.body:
dotnet-dump collect -p 1902 writes a dump. --type sets the kind: Full (the default, all memory including module images), Heap (all memory except mapped images), Mini and Triage (stacks and modules, no heap). Memory analysis needs Full or Heap. The file is as big as the process’s memory and contains everything: passwords, tokens, customer data.

dotnet-dump analyze file opens a console with SOS commands:

  • dumpheap -stat — types by total size, the largest at the bottom;
  • dumpheap -mt <MT> — addresses of objects of one type;
  • dumpobj <address> — an object’s fields;
  • gcroot <address> — the path from a root to the object;
  • eeheap -gc, finalizequeue, gchandles — heap segments, the finalization queue, handles.
cards.deep: You can also get a dump at the moment of a crash, without the tool: the environment variables DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump=1 and DOTNET_DbgMiniDumpType (1 — Mini, 2 — Heap, 3 — Triage, 4 — Full). In a container collect needs the ptrace capability, and taking a full dump can temporarily raise memory use — with a hard limit the container risks being killed. Back in .NET Framework the same was done with WinDbg and the SOS extension; dotnet-dump has the same commands, without a native debugger.

cards.q: Put the steps of a dump analysis in order
items: dotnet-dump collect -p 1902 --type Full
dotnet-dump analyze core_20261012_101500
dumpheap -stat
dumpheap -mt 00007f6c20a67498
gcroot 00007f6ad09421f8
cards.explain: First take the dump and open it. Then statistics by type — find the suspicious type and its MT. By MT, list the instances and take an address from it. And for that address, the path to a root.

cards.title: dotnet-trace: who allocates
cards.body:
A heap snapshot shows what survived. If the problem is that the code allocates a lot and the GC runs nonstop, you need a trace.

dotnet-trace collect -p 1902 --profile gc-verbose records the events of every collection (reason, generation, pause) and a sample of allocations: roughly every 100 KB of allocated memory, an AllocationTick event with the object type and the call stack. Aggregating them shows which methods allocate the most. The gc-collect profile records only collections, with minimal overhead.

The result is a .nettrace file. You open it in PerfView or Visual Studio.
cards.code: dotnet-trace collect -p 1902 --profile gc-verbose --duration 00:00:00:30
cards.deep: Profiles have changed between tool versions: in recent dotnet-trace, running without --profile enables dotnet-common and dotnet-sampled-thread-time, and collect no longer has the old cpu-sampling profile. The profiles of your version: dotnet-trace list-profiles. The speedscope format is fine for CPU stacks, but GC events need nettrace. AllocationTick is a sample, not every allocation: rare small allocations may not make it in.

cards.q: Counters show 2 GB of allocations per second and 40 gen0 collections per second, but the heap does not grow. What do you capture to find the culprit?
options: A dotnet-trace trace with the gc-verbose profile
Two dotnet-gcdump snapshots, then compare them
A dotnet-dump dump of type Mini
dotnet-counters with a 1-second interval
cards.explain: The heap does not grow, so the objects die quickly and snapshots barely contain them. The answer to "who allocates" comes from allocation stacks in a trace. A Mini dump has no heap, and counters know nothing about stacks.

cards.title: PerfView
cards.body:
PerfView is Microsoft’s free analyzer for Windows. It collects traces through ETW — with kernel events and every process on the machine — and opens .nettrace and .gcdump files captured on Linux.

For memory it has three key things:

  • GCStats — a table of every collection in a trace: generation, reason, pause, heap size before and after;
  • a heap snapshot (Memory → Take Heap Snapshot) and a view of the paths to roots;
  • Diff — comparing two snapshots or two traces against a baseline.
cards.deep: On a large heap PerfView by default builds the snapshot from a sample of objects and scales the numbers, so its sizes are approximate — a full dump gives exact figures. Traces and snapshots captured on Linux are analyzed by moving the file to a Windows machine. Back in the .NET Framework era PerfView and WinDbg were the main tools; today PerfView is still the most detailed viewer of GC events.

cards.q: Match the task with the tool
pairs: A quick look at whether the heap grows
Which types hold memory, a file without data
Field values at the moment of a failure
A table of every collection with pauses on Windows

lessons.title: Hunting a leak
lessons.sub: Two snapshots, the difference and the path to a root

cards.title: The method: two snapshots and a diff
cards.body:
A leak in .NET is not "forgot to free" but "someone still holds a reference". The GC will not collect an object while there is a path to it from a root. The job is to find what grows and who holds it.

  • Make sure it is a leak: the floor of the sawtooth rises under steady load (lesson 1).
  • Warm the service up so caches and the JIT have done their work, and take snapshot A.
  • Run a known number of operations: say, 1000 requests.
  • Take snapshot B and compare it with A.
  • Pick a type whose instance count grew by about 1000 or a multiple of it, and find the path from a root to any of its instances.
cards.deep: Pick a round, noticeable number of operations so the growth is recognizable: +1000 objects for 1000 requests is clearly "one per request". A dotnet-gcdump snapshot performs a full collection itself, so garbage does not get into the diff. A full dump keeps the garbage, so in dotnet-dump count with dumpheap -stat -live — reachable objects only.

cards.q: Put the steps of a leak hunt in order
items: See in the counters that the heap after full collections keeps growing
Warm the service up and take the first snapshot
Run 1000 identical requests
Take the second snapshot and compare it with the first
For the type that grew, find the path to a root
Fix it and repeat the same snapshots
cards.explain: First you confirm the problem, then you get a diff under a known load, then you look for who holds it. The last step is the same measurement after the fix: the growth should be gone.

cards.title: How to read a diff
cards.body:
In a snapshot comparison (Visual Studio, PerfView) every type has a growth in instance count and in size.

  • Look at the count, not only the size. At the top by size there are almost always string and byte[] — they are leaves; something holds them.
  • Look for your own types: OrderSnapshot, Session, ViewModel. They are closer to the cause than the strings inside them.
  • Tell an object’s own size (exclusive) from its retained size (inclusive) — everything that would die along with it. A small dictionary can retain a gigabyte.
cards.deep: Retained size is computed from the dominator tree: object X dominates Y if every path from the roots to Y goes through X. PerfView and Visual Studio build this tree approximately — the heap graph is reduced to a spanning tree, and an object reachable by two paths has its size attributed to one of them. That is why "inclusive" can differ between tools.

cards.q: After 1000 requests the snapshot diff is: +1000 OrderSnapshot, +3000 string, +1000 byte[], and one List<OrderSnapshot> grew. Where do you start?
options: With OrderSnapshot: find the path to a root and see whose list it is
With string: there are the most of them
With byte[]: the arrays take the most space
Nowhere: 1000 objects is just warm-up
cards.explain: The strings and arrays are most likely fields of OrderSnapshot: three strings and an array per order snapshot. Your own type growing by exactly one per request plus a growing list is direct evidence. Warm-up was done before the first snapshot.

cards.title: Roots and the retention path
cards.body:
Roots (GC roots) are where the collector starts its walk:

  • static fields — alive as long as their type, usually the whole life of the process;
  • local variables and arguments on thread stacks that will still be used;
  • GC handles: strong, pinned — created by GCHandle.Alloc, the runtime and libraries;
  • the finalization queue — objects waiting for a finalizer are temporarily alive.

The retention path is the chain of references from a root to the object. gcroot in dotnet-dump and the paths view in Visual Studio and PerfView give it to you. Read top to bottom and look for a link that should not be there.
cards.deep: An event subscription is a reference from the publisher to the subscriber: the delegate stores in its _target field the object whose method will be called. So a long-lived publisher holds everyone who subscribed and never unsubscribed. System.Threading.Timer is a special case: the runtime’s timer queue holds the callback, but not the Timer object itself. If nothing references the Timer, it gets collected and stops; the leaking timer is one kept in a long-lived place and never stopped. An async method awaiting a task that never completes holds its state machine through that task’s continuation.

cards.q: The OrderWindow was closed long ago, but gcroot shows it is alive. Which link should not be there?
cards.code:
HandleTable:
    000001F2A0011388 (pinned handle)
    -> 000001F2B4C01000 System.Object[]
    -> 000001F2B4C2A3D0 MyApp.PriceFeed
    -> 000001F2B4C2A460 System.EventHandler<MyApp.PriceChangedEventArgs>
    -> 000001F2B4D88E10 MyApp.Views.OrderWindow
    -> 000001F2B4D99000 MyApp.Views.OrderViewModel
cards.explain: PriceFeed is a long-lived service; it is supposed to live. But its event holds a delegate, and the delegate holds the closed window: the window subscribed to PriceChanged and did not unsubscribe on close. The fix is to unsubscribe in Closed or Dispose.

cards.title: The usual culprits
cards.body:
• Events. A short-lived object subscribed to an event of a long-lived one and never unsubscribed.
  • Static collections and caches without eviction. A static Dictionary as a "cache" that is only ever added to. Or a MemoryCache without a SizeLimit and expirations.
  • Timers. A timer in a long-lived object that nobody stopped: it holds the callback, and the callback holds this.
  • Closures. A lambda stored for a long time holds everything it captured — sometimes the whole object via this.
  • Registrations on a long-lived token. token.Register(...) on an application-wide token without disposing the registration.
cards.deep: A closure captures variables, not values, and the compiler puts all captured variables of a method into one closure object. If two lambdas in a method captured different variables and one of them lives long, it holds both. Another old source is thread-local data ([ThreadStatic], ThreadLocal<T>) on thread-pool threads: the threads live long, and the data lives with them.

cards.q: Which of these causes a leak in a long-running service? Select all.
options: static readonly Dictionary<string, Report> Cache that is only ever added to
A request handler subscribes to an event of a singleton service and never unsubscribes
A local List<T> inside a method, filled with a million items
Every request adds a lambda that captured this to a static List<Action>
An array rented from ArrayPool and given back with Return
cards.explain: The static dictionary, the singleton’s event and the static callback list outlive the request and hold everything they reference: a lambda with this holds the whole handler. The local list dies when the method returns, and the pooled array went back to the pool — that is reuse, not a leak.

cards.title: Less obvious culprits
cards.body:
• A stuck finalizer thread. Finalizers run on a single thread. If someone’s finalizer waits on a lock or goes to the network, the queue grows, and objects with finalizers — and everything they hold — are not freed. The sign: finalizequeue shows thousands of objects ready for finalization.
  • Fragmentation. Few live objects, but a big heap: buffers pinned for a long time prevent compaction. Look at FragmentedBytes and gchandles.
  • Native memory behind small wrappers — lesson 1.
cards.deep: You can see the finalizer thread in a dump: clrthreads shows it marked Finalizer, and clrstack for it shows where it is stuck. Finalizers must not block, and resources are better released through Dispose than left to a finalizer. Long pinning is a typical trace of old code with fixed or GCHandle.Alloc(..., Pinned) held for the whole run; for long-lived buffers .NET 5+ has the POH: GC.AllocateArray<T>(n, pinned: true).

cards.q: The heap grows. In a dump, finalizequeue shows 400,000 objects ready for finalization, and the finalizer thread’s stack is sitting in Monitor.Enter. What is going on?
options: Some finalizer is waiting on a lock, and the whole finalization queue is stuck
The garbage collector is turned off
The objects have too many fields
This is expected: finalizers always run at process exit
cards.explain: There is one finalizer thread. While it waits on a lock, new objects pile up in the queue and stay alive with everything they hold. The fix is to remove the lock from the finalizer and release resources through Dispose.

cards.title: Fixed it? Prove it
cards.body:
After the fix, repeat the same measurement: warm-up, snapshot, 1000 requests, snapshot. The growth of your type should drop to zero.

To keep the leak from coming back, write a test. Create the object in a separate method, hand back a weak reference (WeakReference), run a collection and check that the object is dead.

The separate method with NoInlining matters: in a Debug build the JIT extends the lifetime of locals to the end of the method, and an object created in the test itself may survive the collection.
cards.deep: Put GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers() between two GC.Collect() calls: the first collection finds the garbage, the finalizers run, the second removes what finalizable objects were holding. Do not run such tests in parallel with others that allocate heavily — the result gets flaky. There are libraries with memory assertions too, but their mechanism is the same.

cards.q: Finish the test: a closed window must not stay in memory
cards.explain: A collection, waiting for finalizers, another collection — then check IsAlive. Target would return the object itself, while Assert.False expects a bool. KeepAlive would do the opposite and extend the object’s life.

lessons.title: Final: measuring
lessons.sub: Numbers, tools and leaks

cards.q: A week under steady load: private bytes grew from 1 to 4 GB, while dotnet.gc.last_collection.heap.size stays around 400 MB the whole time. What next?
options: Look for a leak outside the managed heap: native libraries, AllocHGlobal, handles, threads
Take two .gcdump snapshots and compare: the leak is in the managed heap
Nothing: that is Server GC keeping headroom
Call GC.Collect() once a minute
cards.explain: The heap is flat while the process commit grows — so memory is taken around the GC. Managed heap snapshots will not show it. Server GC headroom shows up in the GC commit, not in 3 GB on top of the heap.

wrong.1: The snapshots will show the same 400 MB as the counter: it is not the heap that grows.

cards.q: Match the API with what it returns
pairs: The heap minus fragmentation, uncollected garbage included
How much memory the GC has committed
How much was allocated over the life of the process

cards.q: A service on .NET 9. Watch the heap size by generation after each collection
cards.code: dotnet-counters monitor -n Shop --counters System.Runtime[___]
cards.explain: last_collection.heap.size is broken down by gen0, gen1, gen2, loh and poh. total_allocated is cumulative allocations, working_set is the process’s RAM, pause.time is pauses.

cards.q: What is true about the tools? Select all.
options: dotnet-gcdump collect triggers a full generation 2 collection
dotnet-dump collect without --type writes a Full dump
A .gcdump shows the values of string fields
A Mini dump is suitable for hunting a heap leak
dotnet-trace with the gc-verbose profile records sampled allocations with stacks
cards.explain: A heap snapshot is built during an induced full collection, dotnet-dump takes Full by default, gc-verbose gives AllocationTick with stacks. A .gcdump has no field values, and a Mini dump has no heap.

cards.q: A dotnet-dump analyze session. Which command explains why an object is still alive?
cards.code:
> dumpheap -stat -live
> dumpheap -mt 00007ffa1c2b4a10
> dumpobj 000001f2b4d88e10
> gcroot 000001f2b4d88e10
> finalizequeue
cards.explain: gcroot prints the path from a root to the object — that is the answer to "who holds it". dumpheap finds objects, dumpobj shows fields, finalizequeue shows the finalization queue.

cards.q: Put the steps of verifying a fixed leak in order
items: Warm the service up
Take a heap snapshot
Run 1000 requests
Take a second snapshot
Confirm that the growth of your type is near zero
cards.explain: The same measurement as during the hunt: warm-up, snapshot, a known load, snapshot, comparison. Using the same method guarantees the vanished growth is thanks to the fix.

cards.q: Snapshot diff after 1000 requests: +1000 RequestContext, +1000 <>c__DisplayClass5_0, +1000 Action, and the invocation list of the static event AppEvents.Reloaded keeps growing. The most likely explanation?
options: Every request subscribes a lambda that captured RequestContext to the static event and never unsubscribes
RequestContext is a struct and gets boxed
The compiler creates a DisplayClass on every call of any method
It is garbage the collector has not collected yet
cards.explain: DisplayClass is the closure object, Action is a delegate over it, and a growing invocation list means delegates pile up in it. The static event is a root: it holds the delegate, the delegate holds the closure, the closure holds RequestContext. And garbage does not get into heap snapshots: a snapshot is built during a full collection.

cards.q: Server GC, 32 cores. Under steady load the heap saws up to 6 GB, and after full collections it has stayed around 1.5 GB for a week. Is it a leak?
options: No: the floor of the sawtooth is not rising; the height comes from the collector’s budgets
Yes: 6 GB is too much for a service
Yes: the heap should return to zero after a collection
Impossible to say without a full dump
cards.explain: The sign of a leak is a growing heap size after full collections. It stays put. The tall teeth are the generation budget, which is large with Server GC. If memory matters more, look at DATAS (default for Server GC since .NET 9) or the GCConserveMemory setting.

units.title: Inside the heap
units.blurb: What an object is made of: the header, the sync block and the MethodTable, how the CLR lays out and aligns fields, how arrays and strings sit in memory. The SOH, LOH and POH, regions in .NET 7+ and the .NET 8 non-GC heap.

source.title: Microsoft Learn: The large object heap

lessons.title: Header and MethodTable
lessons.sub: What sits before the fields and how much an object weighs

cards.title: A reference does not point at the start of the object
cards.body:
In the Deeper C# course you saw two bookkeeping words in front of an object's fields. Now more precisely, for x64:

  • −8: the object header — 8 bytes, of which 4 are used and the other 4 are padding;
  • 0: the MethodTable pointer — 8 bytes. This is where the reference points;
  • +8: the instance fields.

The reference targets the type pointer because it is needed most often: a virtual call, a cast, GetType — one read at the reference address. The header is rarely needed, and it is one step back, at −8.
cards.deep:
In the runtime sources this is ObjHeader (file src/coreclr/vm/syncblk.h): on a 64-bit platform it has a padding field m_alignpad and a 32-bit m_SyncBlockValue. On x86 the header and the type pointer are 4 bytes each, and the minimum object is 12 bytes.

The header formally belongs to the object but sits "before" it. That is why the allocator zeroes memory ahead: the header of the next object is already zero when it gets allocated.

cards.q: What does the reference Order o point at in a 64-bit process?
options: The word holding the MethodTable pointer inside the object
The object header
The first field of Order
Directly at the MethodTable of Order
cards.explain: A reference is the address of the type-pointer word. The header is 8 bytes earlier, the fields 8 bytes later. The MethodTable itself is a separate structure, one per type.

wrong.1: The header sits at a negative offset: ref − 8.
wrong.3: There is one MethodTable per type, and it lives outside the object heap. The object holds only a pointer to it.

cards.title: 32 header bits: one of three things
cards.body:
The top bits of the header are flags, and the rest of the space holds one of three things:

  • a thin lock: the owning thread id (16 bits) and the recursion depth (6 bits). This is how lock works while there is no contention;
  • the default hash code — 26 bits, written by RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode (and by a non-overridden GetHashCode);
  • a sync block index — the number of an entry in the sync block table, a separate structure in native memory.

If an object needs more than fits in 32 bits — say, both a hash and a lock — the CLR gives it a sync block: it moves the hash and the monitor state there and writes the index into the header.
cards.deep:
The constants are in syncblk.h: BIT_SBLK_IS_HASH_OR_SYNCBLKINDEX says the low 26 bits hold a hash or an index, BIT_SBLK_IS_HASHCODE tells them apart. The BIT_SBLK_FINALIZER_RUN flag is set by GC.SuppressFinalize, and the collector uses BIT_SBLK_GC_RESERVE while it works, with all threads stopped.

The monitor also needs a sync block in its "heavy" state: threads waiting for the lock, a call to Monitor.Wait. The System.Threading.Lock type from .NET 9 does not touch another object's header: lock on it calls methods of the Lock object itself.

cards.q: What the header contents mean
pairs: Nobody locked the object or took its hash
Owning thread id and recursion depth
An entry number in a separate table

cards.q: After which line will the object definitely have a sync block?
cards.explain: The first lock is a thin lock in the header, released on exit. GetHashCode writes the hash into the now free header. The second lock has no room left: the CLR moves the hash into a sync block and writes the index into the header.

cards.title: MethodTable is the type's passport
cards.body:
There is one MethodTable per type: a million Order objects hold a million pointers to the same structure. It lives not in the GC heap but in loader memory (the loader heap). It contains:

  • BaseSize — the instance size in bytes, header included;
  • ComponentSize — the element size for arrays and strings;
  • flags: does it have a finalizer, does it contain references, is it an array;
  • the parent, the interface map, the virtual method slots.

The collector needs the MethodTable all the time. From it, it learns the object size to step to the next object, and where the references inside are that must be traced.
cards.deep: The description of references — the GCDesc — sits right before the MethodTable, at negative offsets: a list of "series", ranges of the object where references follow one another. Rarely needed type data (field descriptors, links to metadata) is moved out to a separate EEClass structure. You can look at all of this in a debugger with the SOS extension: !dumpobj, !dumpmt. Each closed generic has its own MethodTable: List<int> and List<string> are different types.

cards.q: The collector walks the heap object by object. How does it know where the current object ends?
options: From the MethodTable: BaseSize, plus length × ComponentSize for arrays and strings
The object size is stored in its header
The GC keeps a separate table with the sizes of all objects
Objects in the heap are separated by zero markers
cards.explain: The size is not stored in the object: it follows from the type. For a plain object it is BaseSize; for an array or a string it is BaseSize plus the length times the element size, rounded up to 8 bytes.

wrong.1: The header has only 32 bits of flags, hash and lock — no size.

cards.title: What is not in the object
cards.body:
Each instance holds only the header, the type pointer and the instance fields. Everything shared by the type is stored once:

  • static fields — in separate per-type memory, not in every object;
  • method code — machine code from the JIT, one per type;
  • the virtual method table — in the MethodTable.

So methods and statics do not make objects heavier. A million instances of a class with a hundred methods weigh the same as a million instances of a class with one method and the same fields.
cards.deep: Exactly how the runtime lays out statics has changed from version to version. One detail will be useful later: CoreCLR keeps a static struct field in a separate box — one box per field for the whole lifetime, and writes change its contents. In .NET 8 such boxes for structs without references moved to the non-GC heap — more on it in lesson 4.

cards.q: What is stored in every instance of Order? Select all.
options: The object header
The MethodTable pointer
The fields Id and Note
The field Count
The slot of the virtual method Total
cards.explain: Count is a static field, there is one per type. The Total slot is in the MethodTable, not in the object. The instance holds 8 bytes of header, 8 bytes of type pointer, an int and a reference — 32 bytes in total.

cards.title: How much an object weighs: the arithmetic
cards.body:
The formula for a plain object on x64: 16 bytes (header and type pointer) + fields with alignment, the total rounded up to 8 and no less than 24 bytes.

  • new object() — 24: no fields, but nothing goes below the minimum;
  • a class with one int — 24: 16 + 4, rounded to 24;
  • a boxed int or long — 24;
  • a class with three int fields — 32: 16 + 12 = 28, rounded to 32.

You can check it with the thread's allocation counter: it counts bytes exactly.
cards.deep:
The 24-byte minimum is defined in the runtime as MIN_OBJECT_SIZE = two pointers + the header. One reason: in place of dead objects the collector leaves a "free object" — a fake array with its own type pointer and length, and it must fit into any gap.

Do not confuse this with Unsafe.SizeOf<T>(): for a class it returns 8 — the size of a reference, not of the object. For a struct it returns the size of its fields without a header.

cards.q: How many bytes does an object of this class take on the x64 heap?
cards.explain: 16 bytes of bookkeeping plus 12 bytes of fields is 28. Objects are aligned to 8 bytes, so it is 32.

wrong.1: That is before alignment. On x64 an object size is always a multiple of 8.
wrong.2: 24 is 16 + 8. Three ints need 12 bytes.

cards.q: Measure how many bytes new Order() allocates
cards.explain: The thread counter grows by exactly the allocated size. GetTotalMemory shows an approximate heap size and depends on collections. KeepAlive stops the JIT from treating the object as unused — in .NET 9–10 it can place objects that never leave the method on the stack, and then the counter would show zero.

lessons.title: Field layout
lessons.sub: Who decides the field order and where the gaps come from

cards.title: Source order is not memory order
cards.body:
For a class the C# compiler writes auto layout into the metadata: "lay it out as you see fit". And the CLR lays it out its own way:

  • 8-byte fields first, and among them references come first;
  • then 4-byte, 2-byte and 1-byte fields;
  • nested structs at the end.

Each field sits at an offset that is a multiple of its size. Large fields in front, small ones behind — this leaves almost no gaps between them. The offsets in the example were measured on .NET 9, x64, and are counted from the first field.
cards.deep:
The logic is in MethodTableBuilder::PlaceInstanceFields (src/coreclr/vm/methodtablebuilder.cpp): fields are grouped by size, groups are placed from large to small, and references take the start of the pointer-size group. That way all references of an object form one contiguous "series", and the GCDesc describes them with a single entry — easier for the collector to walk.

The exact order is an implementation detail, not a contract. Code that relies on the field offsets of a class may break on another runtime version or another platform.

cards.q: How many bytes does an object of this class take on x64?
cards.explain: The CLR puts Time first (+0), followed by Side (+8) and Flags (+9). 10 bytes of fields round up to 16, plus 16 bytes of bookkeeping — 32.

wrong.1: That is what the source order would give: byte, a 7-byte gap, long, byte, another 7-byte gap. But a class has auto layout.
wrong.2: On x64 an object size is always a multiple of 8.

cards.title: Alignment: where the gaps come from
cards.body:
Natural alignment: a field of N bytes sits at an address that is a multiple of N. long — a multiple of 8, int — 4, short — 2. The CPU reads an aligned value in one access, and it never straddles a cache line.

There is a correctness guarantee too: reading and writing an aligned reference is atomic. Another thread never sees "half an address". Reference safety under races rests on this.

The price is padding: empty bytes between fields and at the end of the object, so that the next object also starts at an address that is a multiple of 8.
cards.deep: The CLI specification (ECMA-335, section I.12.6.6) guarantees atomic reads and writes of aligned values no larger than a pointer. That is why long is atomic in a 64-bit process but not in a 32-bit one, and decimal and large structs are not atomic anywhere.

cards.q: In what order will the CLR lay out the fields of this class? From the lowest offset to the highest.
items: object R
long L
int I
short S
byte B
cards.explain: First the 8-byte group, with the reference first in it: R (+0), L (+8). Then I (+16), S (+20), B (+22). That is exactly what .NET 9 x64 does; the order inside a group is an implementation detail.

cards.title: Inheritance: base fields first
cards.body:
Base class fields sit at the start, derived class fields after them. The CLR cannot interleave them: the base class code already accesses its fields at fixed offsets, and they must stay the same in the derived class.

If the base fields end off an 8-byte boundary, the CLR tucks small derived fields into the tail — a byte, for example. References do not move like that: they stay in their group, and a gap may remain.
cards.deep: A deep hierarchy with one bool per level loses bytes to padding: each level starts its group of large fields at an alignment boundary. That is one reason to keep "hot" types with millions of instances flat.

cards.q: What is true about class layout in CoreCLR? Select all.
options: Base class fields come before derived class fields
The CLR puts references at the start of the 8-byte field group
The field order in the class source defines the order in memory
An object size on x64 is a multiple of 8
A bool field takes 1 bit
cards.explain: Classes have auto layout, the source order does not matter. A bool field takes a whole byte: the CPU cannot address a single bit.

cards.title: Structs: Sequential until there is a reference
cards.body:
For a struct the C# compiler writes sequential layout: fields in memory in declaration order, with gaps for alignment. The order matters for native interop and for MemoryMarshal.

But if the struct contains a reference, the CLR silently switches to auto layout: references cannot be passed to native code as is anyway, and the collector prefers them grouped together.
cards.code:
struct Seq    { byte A; long L; byte C; }     // 24 bytes: A, 7-byte gap, L, C, 7-byte gap
struct Sorted { long L; byte A; byte C; }     // 16 bytes
struct WithRef { byte A; object O; byte C; }  // 16 bytes: O, A, C — reordered
cards.deep: methodtablebuilder.cpp says exactly that: if the parent is not Object/ValueType/Sequential, or the type has reference fields, Sequential is replaced by Auto. The marshalling layout is a separate story: Marshal.SizeOf computes the native struct by the marshaller's rules. The reverse also exists: [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Auto)] on a struct lets the CLR reorder fields, but such a struct cannot be passed to native code.

cards.q: What does Unsafe.SizeOf<S>() return?
cards.explain: A struct without references is sequential: A (+0), a 7-byte gap, B (+8), C (+16), another 7 bytes up to a multiple of 8. Put B first and it becomes 16.

wrong.1: 16 is what a class with these fields would get, or a struct with reordered fields. But a struct without references keeps the source order.
wrong.2: 10 is the sum of the field sizes. Without Pack = 1 alignment does not go away.

cards.q: A network packet header must take exactly 10 bytes, in the field order of the protocol
cards.explain: Sequential keeps the field order, Pack = 1 removes the gaps: 1 + 8 + 1 = 10 bytes. Auto would reorder the fields, and Explicit requires a FieldOffset on every field. An unaligned long is slower to read, so Pack = 1 is for data formats only.

cards.title: Explicit and "version 2"
cards.body:
LayoutKind.Explicit with [FieldOffset] sets offsets by hand — this is how unions are made. One restriction: a reference cannot overlap a non-reference and cannot be misaligned. Otherwise the collector would take a number for an address. Such a type will not load: TypeLoadException.

Version 2. Reordering the fields of a class in a new library version is safe: IL accesses a field by a metadata token, and the CLR computes the offset when it loads the type. But for a struct that is written to a file or a socket as bytes, the field order is part of the format: old files will be read wrong.
cards.deep: The exception message names the cause directly: "contains an object field at offset 0 that is incorrectly aligned or overlapped by a non-object field". Two references at the same offset are allowed. The compiler does not catch it: the type loader checks it on first use of the type, that is, when the JIT compiles a method that uses it.

cards.q: Library v2 reordered the private fields of the public class Order. The app was built against v1 and not rebuilt. What happens?
options: Everything works: the CLR computes field offsets at load time
MissingFieldException on field access
v1 methods read the wrong fields
TypeLoadException when Order is loaded
cards.explain: IL has no offsets — only field tokens. The CLR builds the layout when it loads the type, and all code, library and app alike, uses the same one. Concrete offsets appear only in machine code, and the JIT produces it after the type is loaded.

cards.q: A struct holds a binary file record and is written with MemoryMarshal.AsBytes. In v2 two int fields were swapped. What happens to old files?
