options: The values of the two fields are read swapped
Nothing: the CLR fixes the order itself
An exception on read
Nothing: structs have auto layout
cards.explain: A struct without references has sequential layout, and the bytes in the file follow the field order. Change the order and you change the format. Such structs are versioned explicitly: a version number in the file header, new fields only at the end.

lessons.title: Arrays and strings
lessons.sub: The length inside the object, the terminator and the cost of small strings

cards.title: An array: the length before the elements
cards.body:
An array is a variable-size object. After the type pointer comes the length: a 4-byte int and, on x64, 4 more bytes of padding. Right after them come the elements, back to back, with no gaps.

  • new byte[0] — 24 bytes: header, type, length;
  • new byte[10] — 24 + 10 = 34 → 40;
  • new int[4] — 24 + 16 = 40;
  • new object[3] — 24 + 3 × 8 = 48: the slots hold references, the objects themselves live elsewhere.

The element type is not stored in the object: int[] and string[] have their own MethodTables, and the element size (ComponentSize) is recorded there too.
cards.deep: In the runtime this is ArrayBase from object.h: the m_NumComponents field and, on a 64-bit platform, pad. The length is 32-bit, so there are at most Array.MaxLength elements (2,147,483,591, .NET 6+). The array can still exceed 2 GB in bytes: modern .NET allows large objects on 64-bit by default, while .NET Framework needed gcAllowVeryLargeObjects.

cards.q: How many bytes does new long[3] take on x64?
cards.explain: 24 bytes of bookkeeping (header, type, length with padding) plus 3 × 8 bytes of elements — 48.

wrong.1: That is 16 + 24: you forgot the 8 bytes for the length.
wrong.2: The elements live inside the array object, not separately.

cards.title: Multidimensional and jagged
cards.body:
int[2, 3] is one object. After the total length (6) it stores the length of each dimension and the lower bounds, and then all 6 elements back to back, row by row. In total 16 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 24 = 64 bytes.

int[2][] with two rows of 3 is three objects: an outer array of references (40 bytes) and two 40-byte arrays somewhere in the heap. 120 bytes in total, plus an extra hop through a reference on every access.
cards.code:
var grid = new int[2, 3];   // 1 object, 64 bytes

var rows = new int[2][];    // 40 bytes: two references
rows[0] = new int[3];       // + 40 bytes
rows[1] = new int[3];       // + 40 bytes
cards.deep: A one-dimensional array with a zero lower bound (an SZ array in CLR terms) has its own IL instructions ldelem/stelem, and in simple loops the JIT often removes the bounds check. Access to a multidimensional array goes through the array type's Get/Set/Address methods; since .NET 7 the JIT expands them into direct code, but every index is still checked against its lower bound.

cards.q: Match the expression to the object size on x64

cards.title: A string: length, characters and a zero at the end
cards.body:
A string also keeps its length inside: after the type pointer there is an int with the character count, followed by the UTF-16 characters, 2 bytes each. And after the last character the CLR puts one more: the null terminator '\0'. It is not counted in Length.

The base size of a string is 8 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 22 bytes (header, type, length, terminator). Then 2 bytes per character and rounding to 8:

  • "a" — 22 + 2 = 24;
  • "abc" — 22 + 6 = 28 → 32;
  • "hello" — 22 + 10 = 32.
cards.deep: In the runtime this is StringObject: the fields m_StringLength and m_FirstChar. Strings and arrays are the only variable-size objects: their MethodTable has a non-zero ComponentSize. A string in memory is always UTF-16. A UTF-8 literal "..."u8 from C# 11 is not a string but a ReadOnlySpan<byte> over data in the assembly itself; it creates no heap object.

cards.q: How many heap bytes does new string('x', 0) allocate?
options: 0 — it returns string.Empty
cards.explain: For a zero length the constructor returns the ready-made empty string and allocates nothing. Likewise Substring(0) and ToString() on a string return the string itself.

wrong.2: That is what an empty string would weigh if one were actually created. But there is only one empty string in the process.

cards.title: The cost of small strings
cards.body:
Let us count a million distinct strings of 10 Latin characters — keys from a file, say.

  • each string: 22 + 20 = 42 → 48 bytes;
  • a million strings — 48 MB;
  • a string[] holding them — another 8 MB of references.

The useful text is 10 MB in ASCII. The rest is UTF-16 (twice the bytes for Latin text), the bookkeeping of every object and alignment. With millions of strings this is where most of the memory goes. Remedies: do not keep several copies of equal strings, store data as UTF-8 in a byte[], parse input through Span<char> without creating substrings.
cards.deep: For deduplication, use your own pool on a HashSet<string> or a Dictionary with lookup by ReadOnlySpan<char> via GetAlternateLookup (.NET 9): a string is created only if there is no such one yet. string.Intern is worse for this: interned strings live until the process ends.

cards.q: Roughly how much memory does a string[] with a million distinct 10-character strings take?
options: About 56 MB
About 20 MB
About 10 MB
About 28 MB
cards.explain: Each string is 48 bytes (22 + 20, rounded to 8), a million strings is 48 MB, plus 8 MB of references in the array.

wrong.1: That is just the characters in UTF-16. You forgot the bookkeeping of every string and the array of references.
wrong.2: That is what the text would weigh in a single-byte encoding without a single object.

cards.title: Why the terminator
cards.body:
Native APIs (Win32, libc) expect a string with a zero at the end. Thanks to the terminator .NET can hand them a string without copying: fixed pins the string and gives a pointer to the first character, and a zero already sits after the last one.

The marshaller does the same for LPWStr parameters: it passes a pointer straight into the string if the string does not need to change. The trap: a .NET string may contain '\0' inside — for C# it is an ordinary character, but native code sees the end of the string there.
cards.deep: Never write into a string through such a pointer: strings are immutable, and literals are also shared by the whole process (interned). For a buffer that native code will fill, use a char[], a Span<char> from stackalloc, or string.Create.

cards.q: Which line allocates a new heap object every time it runs?
cards.explain: A literal is created once per process. The empty string is the ready-made string.Empty. Substring(0) and ToString() return the same string. But Substring(1) copies "bc" into a new 32-byte object.

cards.q: What is true about arrays and strings in CoreCLR? Select all.
options: The length is stored inside the object, before the elements
A '\0' sits after the last character of a string, and Length does not count it
int[2, 3] stores the dimension lengths and lower bounds in the object itself
An int[][] with two rows is a single heap object
A string stores its text in UTF-8
cards.explain: A jagged array is an outer array of references plus one object per row. The text of a string in memory is always UTF-16.

cards.q: Complete the string size formula for x64
cards.code:
static long StringSize(int length) =>
    (___ + 2L * length + 7) & ~7L;  // round up to 8
cards.explain: 22 = 8 bytes of header + 8 of type pointer + 4 of length + 2 of terminator. For "abc": 22 + 6 = 28 → 32.

lessons.title: SOH, LOH, POH and regions
lessons.sub: Where an object lands and how the heap is built physically

cards.title: The managed heap is several heaps
cards.body:
You saw generations 0, 1 and 2 in the .NET under the hood course. Physically, different heaps with different rules stand behind them:

  • SOH (small object heap) — ordinary objects, generations 0–2. The collector compacts it, sliding live objects together;
  • LOH (large object heap) — objects of 85,000 bytes and more. Collected only together with generation 2, not compacted by default;
  • POH (pinned object heap, .NET 5) — objects that never move;
  • the non-GC heap (.NET 8) — objects the collector never collects at all.

Your code allocates in generation 0, in the LOH or in the POH. Objects get into generations 1 and 2 only by surviving a collection.
cards.deep: In the GC sources the LOH and POH together are called the UOH (user old heap): objects there are "old" from birth and are collected together with generation 2. That is why GC.GetGeneration returns 2 for them right away. In the internal numbering the LOH is generation 3 and the POH is 4.

cards.title: The threshold is the object size, not the length
cards.body:
An object goes to the LOH when its full size — header, type pointer and length included — is at least 85,000 bytes. For a byte[] the bookkeeping is 24 bytes, so the boundary is a length of 84,976:

  • new byte[84_976] — exactly 85,000 bytes → LOH;
  • new byte[84_975] — 84,999 → SOH;
  • new string('x', 50_000) — 22 + 100,000 → LOH.

With collections it is often not the object itself that is large but its internal array: a List<int> is small, but its int[] of 30,000 elements is already in the LOH.
cards.code:
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(new byte[84_975])); // 0: SOH
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(new byte[84_976])); // 2: straight to the LOH
cards.deep: The threshold is configurable: System.GC.LOHThreshold in runtimeconfig.json (.NET Core 3.0+), and only upwards from the default. The effective value is visible in GC.GetConfigurationVariables() under the name LOHThreshold. The number 85,000 came from performance tuning, it is not a power of two.

cards.q: What goes straight to the LOH? Select all.
options: new byte[84_990]
new int[20_000]
new string('x', 45_000)
new long[10_000]
The internal array of new List<int>(30_000)
cards.explain: byte[84_990] is 85,014 bytes. A 45,000-character string is 90,022. The list's array is an int[30,000], 120,024 bytes. But int[20,000] and long[10,000] are 80,024 bytes each — that is the SOH.

cards.title: The LOH is not compacted — by default
cards.body:
Moving objects of a hundred kilobytes and more is expensive, so in the LOH the collector does a sweep: dead objects become free blocks, and a free list is built from them. A new large object looks for a fitting gap there. If the gaps are smaller than needed, memory grows even though there is plenty of free space in total. That is fragmentation.

You can compact the LOH on demand: GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode = CompactOnce. The next blocking generation 2 collection compacts the LOH, and the mode switches back to Default by itself.
cards.deep: The mode appeared in .NET Framework 4.5.1. The runtime may also compact the LOH on its own: for example, when System.GC.ConserveMemory is set (.NET 6+, values 1–9) and fragmentation is too high. But the best remedy is not to create large temporary arrays: rent them from ArrayPool<T>. More on that in the "Allocation" unit.

cards.q: Ask for the LOH to be compacted at the next full collection, and run it
cards.explain: The enum has only two values: Default and CompactOnce. There is no "always compact" — the mode is one-shot and resets after the collection.

cards.title: POH: a heap for pinned objects
cards.body:
Native code and devices need a buffer address that will not move. You can pin an object in the SOH — fixed or GCHandle.Alloc(..., Pinned) — but it becomes a rock in the middle of generation 0: the collector cannot move it or compact the memory around it.

The POH (.NET 5) solves this: objects there never move, so there is no need to pin them. To allocate an array in the POH — GC.AllocateArray<T>(length, pinned: true), or GC.AllocateUninitializedArray<T>(length, pinned: true) without zeroing.

The POH is collected together with generation 2 and is not compacted. It suits long-lived I/O buffers, not short-lived temporary ones.
cards.deep: In .NET 5–7, with pinned: true the type T could not be a reference type or contain references; since .NET 8 the restriction is gone. The API offers arrays only — you cannot allocate an ordinary object in the POH. A separate POH limit under a hard heap limit is set with System.GC.HeapHardLimitPOH.

cards.q: A 4 KB buffer lives for the whole lifetime of a service, and its address is constantly passed to native I/O. How should you allocate it?
options: GC.AllocateArray<byte>(4096, pinned: true)
new byte[4096] and GCHandle.Alloc(buf, GCHandleType.Pinned) forever
new byte[100_000] so it lands in the LOH — nothing moves there
stackalloc byte[4096] in Main
cards.explain: The POH was made exactly for this: the object never moves and does not get in the way of compacting generation 0.

wrong.1: It works, but a pinned object in the SOH gets in the way of compaction and fragments the young generations until it is promoted to generation 2.
wrong.2: The LOH is not compacted only by default: CompactOnce or ConserveMemory can move it. Only pinning or the POH guarantee an object stays put.
wrong.3: The stack does not outlive the method, and you cannot hand it to asynchronous I/O.

cards.title: Segments and regions
cards.body:
Before .NET 7 the heap was made of segments — large chunks of address space. Generations 0 and 1 lived together in one "ephemeral" segment, generation 2 and the LOH in their own. Free space inside a segment could not be given to another generation. A segment went back to the OS only when it became completely empty; otherwise only the tail after the last live object was released.

Since .NET 7, on 64-bit Windows and Linux the heap is made of regions: small blocks, by default 4 MB for the SOH and 32 MB for the LOH and POH. Each region belongs to one generation. Regions that survived a collection can be "promoted" to an older generation as a whole, and empty ones go back to a shared list to be given to any generation or to the OS.

As in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit: at startup the GC reserves a large address range for regions — 256 GB by default — but commits memory only as needed.
cards.deep: The range is visible in GC.GetConfigurationVariables() as GCRegionRange; with a hard heap limit it is smaller — five times the limit. The region size is changed with DOTNET_GCRegionSize (.NET 7+) or System.GC.RegionSize in runtimeconfig.json (.NET 10). An object larger than a region gets a region of its own size. In .NET 7 the old segments implementation shipped as a separate clrgc library that could be plugged in with DOTNET_GCName in case of regressions.

cards.q: A .NET 8 service on Linux without memory limits. top shows a VIRT of over 256 GB for the process, while RES is 300 MB. What is it?
options: The GC reserved an address range for regions — this is not used memory
A leak in the LOH
The service allocated 256 GB in the POH
The process's swap file
cards.explain: A reservation of addresses costs nothing physically, as we covered in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit. Used memory is RES and committed pages, not VIRT.

wrong.1: A leak would grow RES and the heap size, not just the virtual address space.

cards.title: The non-GC heap: frozen segments in .NET 8
cards.body:
Some objects live until the process ends and hold no references the GC needs to know about. In .NET 8 the runtime puts them on the non-GC heap (also called frozen): the collector neither collects nor moves it. It holds:

  • string literals;
  • the Type objects returned by typeof(T);
  • empty arrays from Array.Empty<T>();
  • the boxes of static struct fields without references.

The win is in machine code: the address of such an object never changes, and the JIT bakes it right into the instruction, without a read through an intermediate cell.
cards.code:
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration("hello"));        // 2147483647
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(typeof(string))); // 2147483647
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(new object()));   // 0
cards.deep: This is a documented .NET 8 change: GC.GetGeneration may return int.MaxValue for objects on the non-GC heap — do not use the result as an array index. What exactly goes there is an implementation detail: for example, typeof for a type from a collectible context does not, otherwise the type could never be unloaded. The idea grew out of Native AOT's frozen segments, where such objects are prepared at build time.

cards.q: Where does the object land in .NET 8+?
Which line prints 2147483647 on .NET 8+?
cards.explain: a is 0, b (LOH) and c (POH) are 2: these heaps are collected together with generation 2. The literal lives on the non-GC heap, and GetGeneration returns int.MaxValue for it.

lessons.title: Final: inside the heap
lessons.sub: Header, layout, arrays and heaps

cards.q: An object was used as a Dictionary key (its hash taken via the non-overridden GetHashCode), and then it is locked on. What happens to the header?
options: The hash already occupies the header, so the CLR creates a sync block and writes its index into the header
The thin lock overwrites the hash, and the key gets lost
lock throws SynchronizationLockException
The hash is recomputed after leaving the lock
cards.explain: The 32 header bits hold only one thing: a thin lock, a hash or a sync block index. When both are needed, the hash and the monitor state move into a sync block, and the hash does not change.

cards.q: How many bytes does an object of this class take on x64?
cards.explain: Auto layout: Next (+0), Value (+8), Kind (+12). 13 bytes of fields → 16, plus 16 of bookkeeping — 32.

wrong.1: That is what the source order would give: byte, a 7-byte gap, a reference, an int, a 4-byte gap. But the CLR reorders class fields.

cards.q: Put the parts of new int[4] in order from the lowest address to the highest (x64)
items: Object header
MethodTable pointer
Array length (4 bytes)
Padding (4 bytes)
Elements [0]…[3]
cards.explain: The header is at ref − 8, the type pointer at the reference address, then the length padded to 8 bytes and the elements back to back. 24 + 16 = 40 bytes in total.

cards.q: What goes straight to the LOH? Select all.
options: new double[11_000]
new char[40_000]
new string('x', 45_000)
new object[12_000]
new Guid[5_000]
cards.explain: double[11,000] is 88,024 bytes, a 45,000-character string is 90,022, object[12,000] is 96,024. char[40,000] and Guid[5,000] are 80,024 bytes each, below the 85,000 threshold.

cards.q: What does Unsafe.SizeOf<S>() return?
cards.explain: A reference inside a struct switches it to auto layout: B (+0), A (+8), C (+9), rounded to 16. Sequential with gaps would give 24.

wrong.1: That is what sequential layout would give. But with a reference inside, the CLR lays the struct out like a class.

cards.q: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: An entry in a separate table for the hash and the monitor
Where the references sit inside an object
The size of an array element or a string character
A heap block that belongs to one generation
Literals and typeof results that are never collected

cards.q: Allocate a long-lived buffer for native I/O that will never move
cards.code: byte[] buf = GC.___<byte>(64 * 1024, ___: true);
cards.explain: pinned: true puts the array in the POH — objects there do not move, need no pinning and do not get in the way of SOH compaction.

cards.q: What changed in the heap with the move to regions in .NET 7?
options: The heap is split into small regions that can pass between generations and go back to the OS one by one
The LOH threshold grew to 4 MB
The collector stopped dividing objects into generations
Objects in the SOH no longer move
cards.explain: Generations, the LOH threshold and compaction stayed. The physical structure changed: instead of large segments, regions of 4 MB (32 MB for the LOH and POH) that move flexibly between generations.

cards.q: Library v2 reordered the fields of a public struct without references. The app writes it to a file as bytes via MemoryMarshal. What breaks?
options: Reading files written by v1: the byte order is part of the format
Nothing: the CLR computes offsets at load time
Type loading: TypeLoadException
Nothing: structs have auto layout
cards.explain: For access from IL the reordering is safe — offsets are computed at load time. But a struct without references has sequential layout, and its bytes in the file follow the field order.

units.title: Allocation
units.blurb: Why new in .NET is nearly free — a pointer bump in the thread's allocation context — and when it takes the slow path or goes to the LOH. Hidden allocations in closures, boxing, iterators, params, strings and async; ArrayPool, stackalloc, string.Create and measuring bytes per call.

lessons.title: The fast path: bumping a pointer
lessons.sub: Allocation context, 8 KB chunks and zeroing in advance

cards.title: What new actually does
cards.body:
In C#, new Order() is one line. The compiler turns it into the IL instruction newobj, and the JIT turns that into a call to a runtime allocation helper followed by the constructor.

The helper does three things:

  • finds room of the right size;
  • makes sure that room is zeroed;
  • writes the type pointer (MethodTable) at the start of the object.

Only then does the constructor run. This whole lesson is about why the first two steps cost almost nothing in .NET.

cards.title: The thread's allocation context
cards.body:
Every thread has an allocation context — two pointers into the generation 0 heap: alloc_ptr is where free space begins, alloc_limit is where it ends. Between them lies a chunk of memory the collector handed to this thread in advance, usually about 8 KB.

Allocating an object means moving alloc_ptr forward by its size. If the move did not cross alloc_limit, the job is done. This is called bump pointer allocation.
cards.deep: In the dotnet/runtime sources this is the gc_alloc_context struct (gcinterface.h). Besides the two pointers it holds the counters alloc_bytes and alloc_bytes_uoh — how many bytes the thread allocated on the SOH and on the large heaps. The chunk size comes from the CLR_SIZE constant in gc.cpp — 8 KB plus a small margin. If an object is bigger than a chunk but below the LOH threshold, the collector hands out a chunk sized for it.

cards.q: Why does every thread get its own allocation context instead of one shared pointer for the whole heap?
options: Bumping your own pointer needs neither a lock nor an atomic operation
So that objects from different threads cannot reference each other
So that the collector can collect each thread's heap separately
The memory model requires it: a write to a shared pointer is invisible to other cores
cards.explain: A shared pointer would have to be bumped with Interlocked or under a lock, and every thread would fight over one cache line. A thread-local pointer is touched only by its own thread: plain reads and writes. Synchronization is needed only when the chunk runs out and the thread goes to the collector for a new one.

wrong.1: Objects from different chunks reference each other freely: there is one heap, chunks are just a way to hand it out.
wrong.2: Collection works by generations and regions, not by threads. Chunks of different threads live in the same generation 0.

cards.title: Zeros in advance, in bulk
cards.body:
The spec promises that the fields of a new object are default. If the runtime zeroed each object separately, every new would pay for an extra loop.

Instead the collector zeroes the whole chunk at once when it hands it to a thread. After that the fast path cleans nothing: the memory under the pointer is already zero. All that is left is writing the type pointer — and the object is ready, even if the constructor is empty.

That is why new int[1000] does not walk 1000 elements: the zeros were laid down earlier, with one memset per chunk.
cards.deep: Zeroing cannot be skipped for objects with references: the collector must see either null or a real address in those fields. Arrays of primitives have a loophole — GC.AllocateUninitializedArray<T> (.NET 5+): memory is not zeroed if the type contains no references. The gain shows only on large arrays: for an array under 2 KB the method simply calls new T[]. This is, for example, how ArrayPool allocates new buffers of primitive types.

cards.q: Put the fast-path steps for new Order() in order
items: Read alloc_ptr from the thread's context
Add the object size
Compare the result with alloc_limit
Store the new alloc_ptr
Write the type pointer
Call the constructor
cards.explain: First check that the object fits, then bump the pointer, then write the MethodTable into already zeroed memory. The constructor is called by JIT-generated code after the helper returns.

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body:
The fast path is on the order of ten machine instructions: a load, an add, a compare, two stores. No free-block search like a classic malloc, no locks.

So new in .NET is cheap at the moment of the call. You pay later:

  • every few megabytes of allocations a generation 0 collection runs;
  • the collector copies survivors into an older generation.

Hence the rule: short-lived garbage is nearly free; what costs is lots of allocations in a hot loop (frequent collections) and objects that live "a bit longer than needed" (copying).
cards.deep: Then and now: bump pointer allocation has been in the CLR since version one, .NET Framework allocated the same way. The surroundings changed: in .NET 7 the heap moved to regions, and chunks are carved from generation 0 regions rather than an ephemeral segment. In .NET 9–10 the JIT sometimes skips the allocator altogether: an object that never leaves the method can be placed on the stack (escape analysis). Do not rely on it in code — it is an optimization, not a guarantee.

cards.q: A thread creates three small objects in a row. Where do they most likely live?
options: Right next to each other in this thread's chunk
In random spots of the heap wherever a free hole was found
In three different regions, one per object
On the thread's stack until a field references them
cards.explain: Each new bumps the same alloc_ptr, so the objects land back to back. That is free locality: objects created together are usually read together, and neighbors share cache lines (see the cache lesson in the unit "Memory through the OS’s eyes"). A compacting collection preserves their order.

cards.title: When the chunk runs out
cards.body:
If an object does not fit in what is left of the chunk, the fast path reports failure and the thread takes the slow path — to the collector for a new chunk.

The tail of the old chunk where the object did not fit is not silently lost: the collector marks it as a free object — a dummy object that fills the hole so the heap can be walked object by object.

With an 8 KB chunk and objects of 30–100 bytes, the slow path fires roughly once per hundred allocations. The rest of the time it is a pointer bump.
cards.deep: The heap must be "walkable": the collector and the debugger step through it, reading each object's type pointer and computing its size. So every unused hole is dressed up as an object of the special Free type with a length. In a dump (for example, !dumpheap -stat in SOS) they show up as the Free row — that is heap fragmentation.

cards.q: Complete the fast-path model
cards.explain: Check that the new end did not cross the chunk boundary; the object starts at the old Ptr; the new Ptr is its end. No zeroing needed: the chunk is already zero.

cards.q: What is true about the allocation context? Select all.
options: Each thread has its own
Its memory is zeroed in advance, when the chunk is handed out
Every new takes a global heap lock
An object that does not fit in the rest of the chunk takes the slow path
The chunk covers the whole of generation 0 at once
cards.explain: Only the slow path takes a lock, and not for every object. A chunk is about 8 KB: if a thread got all of generation 0, other threads would have nowhere to allocate and the collector could not track its budget precisely.

cards.q: Match the term and its meaning
pairs: Where the next object will start
A piece of generation 0 given to a thread
A placeholder for the unused tail
IL instruction that allocates and calls the constructor

lessons.title: The slow path and the LOH
lessons.sub: When a pointer bump is not enough and who starts a collection

cards.title: When the fast path will not do
cards.body:
Pointer bumping works for most objects. But in some cases the JIT or the fast path itself sends the allocation to the collector — down the slow path:

  • the chunk ran out — the object did not fit in what was left;
  • the object is large — 85,000 bytes or more, it belongs in the LOH, not generation 0;
  • the type has a finalizer — the object must also be registered in the finalization queue.

The first case is decided at allocation time. A finalizer and the size of an ordinary object are visible to the JIT in advance: for such types it calls the slow helper right away. The size of an array is known only at run time, so a large array is sent down the slow path by the helper itself.
cards.deep: You can see this in CEEInfo::getNewHelperStatic (jitinterface.cpp): the slow helper CORINFO_HELP_NEWFAST is the default, and the fast CORINFO_HELP_NEWSFAST is chosen only if the type has no finalizer, is not a COM object and is smaller than LARGE_OBJECT_SIZE. For arrays the size is known only at run time, so the helper itself checks the threshold.

cards.q: Which allocations always take the slow path? Select all.
options: new Plain()
new WithFinalizer()
new Person("Ann")
new double[20_000]
new string('x', 10)
cards.explain: A finalizer is a reason for the slow path, and a double[20,000] weighs over 160,000 bytes and goes to the LOH. A record is an ordinary class without a finalizer. A 10-character string is a small object, fast path.

cards.title: What the slow path does
cards.body:
The slow path is a collector function whose job is to give the thread a new chunk. Roughly in this order it:

  • takes the heap lock — chunks are handed out to all threads from a shared place;
  • checks the generation 0 budget: how much more can be allocated before the next collection;
  • looks for room: a free block left over from the last collection (the free list), or an untouched part of a generation 0 region, and if there is none — takes a new region;
  • zeroes the chunk, turns the tail of the old chunk into a free object and updates the thread's alloc_ptr/alloc_limit.

That is hundreds or thousands of instructions, but it happens once per many allocations.
cards.deep: In Server GC each core has its own heap, and the slow path can move a thread to another, less loaded heap (balancing). Small and large objects use different locks: more_space_lock_soh and more_space_lock_uoh in gc.cpp. So a thread allocating large arrays does not get in the way of threads with small objects — but threads with large arrays do get in each other's way.

cards.q: Put the slow-path steps in order
items: The object did not fit in the rest of the chunk
Take the heap lock
Check the generation 0 budget
Find a free piece and zero it
Give the thread a new alloc_ptr and alloc_limit
Retry the fast path
cards.explain: The slow path starts with a fast-path miss and ends with the thread getting a fresh chunk, where the object is allocated with an ordinary bump. If the budget is exhausted, a collection happens between the third and fourth steps.

cards.title: The budget: new starts the collection
cards.body:
The collector does not watch the clock. Generation 0 has an allocation budget — how many bytes may be allocated before the next collection. Every chunk handed out is charged against it.

When the budget is exhausted, the slow path starts a collection right on this thread, and a new that normally costs nanoseconds waits for the collection to finish. All other managed threads are stopped meanwhile.

The key consequence: collection frequency is proportional to the allocation rate. Half the garbage per second means half as many generation 0 collections.
cards.deep: The budget is not fixed: the collector recomputes it after every collection — based on how many objects survived — within a lower and an upper bound. The initial size of generation 0 depends on the CPU cache size (L3), and is larger for Server GC. Besides allocation, collections are triggered by an explicit GC.Collect, a low-memory signal from the OS and some internal events — more on triggers in the unit "How a collection works".

cards.q: A service allocates 2 GB of short-lived objects per second, and almost all die in generation 0. What will you see in the counters?
options: Many generation 0 collections per second with a small heap
A heap growing by 2 GB per second until OutOfMemoryException
Rare but long full collections
Nothing: the collector does not account for short-lived objects
cards.explain: Every few megabytes of budget there is a generation 0 collection. Dead objects cost nothing to mark, so collections are short and the heap does not grow. The price is frequent thread suspensions: cut them down and the gain shows immediately.

wrong.1: Garbage does not pile up: each generation 0 collection reclaims its memory.
wrong.2: Full collections are triggered by older generations and the LOH filling up, and almost nothing reaches them here.

cards.title: The LOH: large objects apart
cards.body:
An object of 85,000 bytes or more — the whole object counts, header included — is allocated not in generation 0 but in the LOH (large object heap). In practice it is almost always an array, or a long string: a string of 50,000 characters weighs over 100,000 bytes.

How such an allocation works:

  • always the slow path, through its own lock;
  • room is found among the LOH free blocks, and the whole object is zeroed — for a megabyte array that is noticeable work;
  • the LOH has its own budget. Once it is exhausted, a generation 2 collection runs — that is, a full one.

The structure of the LOH itself is covered in the unit "Inside the heap".
cards.deep: The threshold can be changed with the System.GC.LOHThreshold setting in runtimeconfig.json (since .NET Core 3.0) — only upward from 85,000. By default the LOH is not compacted; free blocks are reused via a list, so alternating arrays of different sizes cause fragmentation; a one-off compaction is enabled with GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode. Then and now: in 32-bit .NET Framework, double arrays of 1000 elements or more went to the LOH below the threshold — for 8-byte alignment.

cards.q: Which of these objects lands in the LOH (64-bit process)?
options: new string('a', 50_000)
new int[20_000]
new object[10_000]
new List<long>(5_000)
cards.explain: A char takes 2 bytes, so a 50,000-character string is over 100,000 bytes. int[20,000] is about 80,000 bytes, object[10,000] is 10,000 references of 8 bytes, also about 80,000. List<long>(5,000) is a small object plus an internal array of 40,000 bytes. All three are below the threshold.

wrong.2: A reference in a 64-bit process is 8 bytes: 80,000 bytes plus the header, the 85,000 threshold is not reached.
wrong.3: The List itself is a small object, and its long[5,000] array is about 40,000 bytes.

cards.title: A temporary large buffer is an expensive habit
cards.body:
A common sight in services: every request allocates a one-megabyte buffer, which is garbage a millisecond later. From the code's point of view, no big deal. From the collector's point of view:

  • every buffer is a slow path plus zeroing a megabyte;
  • the buffers quickly eat the LOH budget;
  • each time it runs out — a full collection that walks the whole heap, not just young objects.

In the counters this shows up as frequent generation 2 collections while hardly any old objects are added. The cure is reusing the buffer — a pool (lesson 4).

cards.q: A service runs several full collections per second. Which line is the prime suspect?
cards.explain: A megabyte per request is the LOH: slow path, zeroing and fast exhaustion of the LOH budget, after which a generation 2 collection runs. The dictionary and the string are small short-lived objects that die in generation 0.

cards.q: Match the event and its consequence
pairs: The slow path hands out a new one
A generation 0 collection right inside new
Registered in the finalization queue on creation
Straight to the LOH, bypassing generation 0

lessons.title: Hidden allocations
lessons.sub: Where no new is written, yet an object appears

cards.title: The new you cannot see
cards.body:
The most expensive allocations in hot code are not the ones written out. The C# compiler and the libraries create objects for you: for a lambda, for a boxed number, for an iterator, for an argument array.

How to find them:

  • look at what the compiler turned the code into — a decompiler to IL or to "lowered" C#;
  • measure bytes per call — that is lesson 4;
  • in an allocation profiler, look at which types get created: <>c__DisplayClass, Box, <Where>d__ — the names of compiler-generated classes give the culprit away.
cards.deep: The compiler picks names with angle brackets so that they cannot be written in C#: <>c__DisplayClass0_0 is a closure, <>c is the singleton for non-capturing lambdas, <Read>d__3 is the state machine of an iterator or async method named Read. These are Roslyn implementation details and may change, but they have stayed this way for years.

cards.title: Closures and delegates
cards.body:
How a lambda captures variables is covered in the unit "Delegates, events and closures" of the "Deeper C#" course. Here — only the cost:

  • no capture — the delegate is created once and cached in a static field, free after that;
  • capturing this — a new delegate every time the lambda expression is evaluated;
  • capturing a local or a parameter — a closure object (display class) plus a delegate.

The trap: the closure is created on entry to the scope of the captured variable, not where the lambda is written. If a parameter is captured — on entry to the method, even if the branch with the lambda never runs.
cards.code:
items.Where(x => x > 0);       // cached delegate
items.Where(x => x > _min);    // a delegate per call
items.Where(x => x > limit);   // closure + delegate
cards.deep: Method groups: items.Select(Parse) with a static Parse created a new delegate on every call before C# 11; starting with C# 11 the compiler caches it like a non-capturing lambda. An instance method group (items.Select(this.Parse)) always produces a new delegate: it is bound to a specific object.

cards.q: How many heap objects does the call Find(list, 10, fast: true) create?
options: One — the closure
Zero — the lambda was never reached
Two — the closure and the delegate
One — the delegate
cards.explain: limit is a parameter, so its storage moves into the closure object, which is created on entry to the method: from then on the parameter lives only there. The delegate is created when the lambda expression is evaluated, and the fast branch never gets there. The fix is to move the branch with the lambda into a separate method.

cards.title: Boxing
cards.body:
A value type that ends up where an object or an interface is expected gets boxed: a heap object with a header, a type pointer and a copy of the value. For an int that is 24 bytes for the sake of 4.

Where it hides:

  • old APIs taking object: string.Format("{0}", n), ArrayList, Hashtable;
  • a struct passed as an interface: IComparable c = point;
  • calling non-overridden ToString, Equals, GetHashCode on a struct — they are declared in ValueType.

Generics (List<int>, IEquatable<T>) work without boxing: the JIT generates separate code for each value type.
cards.deep: Enum.HasFlag used to box its argument; since .NET Core 2.1 the JIT expands it into a bit test. Interpolation $"{n}" with C# 10 on .NET 6+ goes through DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler with the generic AppendFormatted<T> — no boxing. But string.Format with numeric arguments still boxes today.

cards.q: n is an int, list is a List<int>. Where does boxing happen (C# 12, .NET 8)? Select all.
options: object o = n;
IComparable c = n;
list.Add(n);
string.Format("{0}", n);
var s = $"{n}";
cards.explain: object and an interface are explicit boxing. string.Format takes object — boxing too. List<int> stores an int as is. Interpolation since C# 10 calls the generic AppendFormatted<int> and writes the number straight into a buffer; the only allocation is the final string.

cards.title: Iterators, LINQ and foreach over an interface
cards.body:
The compiler turns a method with yield return into an iterator class, and every call of the method is a new object. Every LINQ operator is such an object plus a delegate; details are in the unit "LINQ and its cost" of the "Deeper C#" course.

Less visible is foreach. On List<T>, GetEnumerator() returns a struct List<T>.Enumerator: iteration without a single allocation. But if the list is passed as IEnumerable<T>, the interface method is called, it returns IEnumerator<T> — and the struct gets boxed.
cards.deep: An iterator saves one object: it implements both IEnumerable and IEnumerator, and the first GetEnumerator on the same thread returns this. A second enumeration of the same sequence creates a copy. In .NET 10 the JIT learned, in some cases (primarily arrays behind IEnumerable<T>), to devirtualize the enumeration and avoid the heap enumerator — but it is an optimization you cannot rely on in an API.

cards.q: All three methods are called with a List<int>. Which one creates a heap object on every call?
options: Sum2
Sum1
Sum3
All three
cards.explain: Sum2 enumerates through IEnumerable<int>.GetEnumerator(), and the struct enumerator gets boxed. Sum1 sees the concrete List<int> and takes the struct. Sum3 calls Count and the indexer through the interface — interface calls, but not allocations.

wrong.2: An interface call costs an indirect jump but creates no object: Count and the indexer return int.

cards.title: params and strings
cards.body:
params object[] means a new array on every call (an empty one is the shared Array.Empty), and value-type arguments get boxed on top. Since C# 13 there is params ReadOnlySpan<T>: the compiler puts the arguments in a stack buffer, no heap needed. In .NET 9 such overloads were added to, for example, string.Join, string.Concat, Path.Combine — recompiling is enough.

Strings are immutable, every change is a new string:

  • a + b + c — one call to string.Concat, one string;
  • s += x in a loop — a new string on every iteration, each copying everything accumulated so far;
  • interpolation $"..." (C# 10+) builds the text in a rented buffer and creates one final string.
cards.deep: For params ReadOnlySpan<T> the compiler generates a struct with the [InlineArray] attribute in the stack frame; if all the arguments are primitive constants, the data comes straight from the metadata section. The span overload wins overload resolution over the array one, so an old call string.Join(",", a, b, c) quietly stops creating an array after moving to .NET 9.

cards.q: A report of 10,000 lines takes minutes to build. Which line is to blame?
cards.explain: result += creates a new string and copies the whole report so far into it. For n lines that is n copies of growing length, O(n²) bytes; the long intermediate strings also end up in the LOH. The interpolation in the var line = … line is one short string per order. The cure is a StringBuilder or writing to a stream.

cards.title: async: the state machine moves to the heap
cards.body:
The compiler turns an async method into a struct — a state machine (in a Release build; in Debug it is a class and is always allocated on the heap). While the method runs synchronously, it lives on the stack. The cost depends on how the method finishes:

  • finished without waiting — the machine stayed on the stack. A non-generic Task comes ready-made from a cache; a Task<T> is created anew (except for cached bool, small int and null); a ValueTask<T> carries the result inside — zero allocations;
  • the first real await of an incomplete operation — the state machine is copied to the heap.

The mechanics are covered in detail in the course "Async/await in depth".
cards.deep: Since .NET Core 2.1 the state machine is copied into an AsyncStateMachineBox<TStateMachine> object, which itself derives from Task<TResult>: one allocation instead of several in .NET Framework (the task, the boxed machine, the continuation delegate). The Task<int> cache covers values from -1 to 8 — an implementation detail, not a contract.

cards.q: The value is in the cache and the method returns it without awaiting. How many heap objects does the call create?
options: Zero
One — a Task<Item>
One — the state machine
Two — the state machine and a task
cards.explain: The method never reached await, so the state machine stayed a struct on the stack, and the ValueTask<Item> holds the result right inside. With Task<Item> there would be one new task object on every cache hit.

cards.q: Match the construct and what it creates on the heap
pairs: x => x > limit (limit is a local)
Calling a method with yield return
foreach over a List<T> as IEnumerable<T>
The state machine on the heap

lessons.title: Measure, then stop allocating
lessons.sub: Bytes per call, MemoryDiagnoser, ArrayPool, stackalloc and string.Create

cards.title: Measure first
cards.body:
Before removing allocations, find out how many there are. The most precise counter at hand is GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread(): how many bytes the current thread has allocated over its lifetime. The runtime keeps it in the same allocation context, so the call is cheap and the "after minus before" difference is exact to the object.

Two rules:

  • warm the code up with one call first: the first call pulls in the JIT, static constructors, lazy caches;
  • the counter is per thread: if the work moves to another thread (Task.Run, the thread pool), it will not see it.
cards.deep: The counter is the allocation context's alloc_bytes plus alloc_bytes_uoh minus the unused remainder of the current chunk — which is why it is exact even though chunks are handed out 8 KB at a time. .NET Framework got this method only in version 4.8; before that you had to look at AppDomain.MonitoringTotalAllocatedMemorySize or at performance counters.

cards.q: The measurement shows 0 bytes, although the profiler sees thousands of objects per call. Why?
options: The work ran on a pool thread, and the counter only counts the current thread
The counter ignores objects the GC has already collected
Without a warm-up the counter always returns 0
GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread counts only the LOH
cards.explain: ProcessBatch ran on another thread, so its bytes went into that thread's context. This kind of measurement needs GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes — the sum over all threads. The counter is monotonic: collections never decrease it.

wrong.1: The counter counts what was allocated, not what is alive: collected objects are not subtracted from it.

cards.title: All threads and BenchmarkDotNet
cards.body:
GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise) (.NET Core 3.0+) is how much the whole process has allocated. With precise: false the result may miss the remainders of the threads' current chunks; true is more exact but noticeably more expensive.

To compare code variants, use BenchmarkDotNet with the [MemoryDiagnoser] attribute. The table gains columns:

  • Allocated — bytes per operation;
  • Gen0, Gen1, Gen2 — how many collections of each generation happened per 1000 operations.

In a running service, watch the allocation rate: the allocation rate counter in dotnet-counters (covered in the unit "How to measure").

cards.q: MemoryDiagnoser reports for a method: Allocated = 160 B, Gen0 = 0.0153. What does it mean?
options: Each call allocates 160 bytes; there are about 0.015 generation 0 collections per 1000 calls
Each call allocates 160 bytes and triggers 0.0153 collections
The method keeps 160 bytes alive, 1.5% of which survive generation 0
The whole run allocated 160 bytes, with almost no collections
cards.explain: Allocated is bytes per operation, the GenN columns are collections per 1000 operations. That is one generation 0 collection per roughly 65,000 calls: 160 bytes × 65,000 ≈ 10 MB — the order of a generation 0 budget.

wrong.1: The number in the Gen0 column is per 1000 operations, not per one.

cards.title: ArrayPool<T>: rent and return
cards.body:
A temporary buffer does not have to be allocated anew. ArrayPool<T>.Shared is a shared pool of arrays:

  • Rent(n) hands out an array of length at least n — usually the next power of two, so always remember your own length;
  • Return(array) gives it back; by default the contents are not cleared, for secrets there is clearArray: true;
  • after Return the array is no longer yours.

Inside, the pool has a per-thread cache and sets of arrays per core, so Rent and Return almost always avoid locks. For the buffers from the LOH lesson this is the cure: a megabyte is allocated once and lives in generation 2 instead of being created for every request.
cards.deep: The shared pool keeps arrays from 16 to 2³⁰ elements long, one bucket per power of two; for a bigger request it allocates a plain array and drops it on return. Under memory pressure the pool trims unused arrays by itself. Failing to return an array is not a leak — the GC collects it, the pool just does not help. A custom pool with other limits is ArrayPool<T>.Create(maxArrayLength, maxArraysPerBucket).

cards.q: The checksum sometimes does not match. Which line is wrong?
cards.explain: Rent(count) returned an array of at least count elements, usually more. Checksum(buf) also covers the tail, which holds the previous renter's data. It should be Checksum(buf.AsSpan(0, count)).

cards.title: stackalloc + Span: small things go on the stack
cards.body:
Span<T> and stackalloc themselves are covered in the unit "Performance" of the "Deeper C#" course. Here is a working pattern for memory: a small buffer comes from the stack, a large one from the pool.

Keep the threshold small — usually hundreds of bytes, up to a couple of kilobytes: the thread stack is limited (the stack lesson in the unit "Memory through the OS’s eyes"), and an overflow cannot be caught. Never pass a size taken from input to stackalloc without a check.
cards.deep: stackalloc zeroes the buffer: locals in .NET are zero-initialized (the localsinit flag in IL). The [SkipLocalsInit] attribute (C# 9, requires AllowUnsafeBlocks) turns it off for a method or a type — then the buffer holds garbage and must not be read before it is written. The gain shows on buffers of hundreds of bytes in hot methods.

cards.q: Complete the "small on the stack, large from the pool" pattern
cards.explain: The stackalloc branch does not touch the heap; the pool branch rents an array and must return it. new byte[512] would work, but it would allocate a heap object on every call.

cards.title: string.Create: a string without an intermediate buffer
cards.body:
If the length of the final string is known up front, you can fill it in place. string.Create(length, state, action) allocates a string of the needed length and hands you its characters as a Span<char>. One allocation — the string itself, no StringBuilder and no temporary char[].

The state is passed as an argument and the lambda is marked static: that way it captures nothing and the compiler caches the delegate.
cards.deep: Strings are immutable for everyone who can see them — but inside string.Create nobody has seen the string yet, so writing to it is safe. Do not keep the span beyond the lambda: after it returns, the string becomes an ordinary immutable one. Interpolation $"..." since C# 10 often gives a comparable result with no manual work; string.Create is for when the format is unusual or you need the exact length.

cards.title: Delegates: cache and static
cards.body:
The compiler caches a non-capturing lambda by itself. So the task is to get rid of the capture. Good APIs take the state as a separate argument for this: ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd, string.Create, ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem, CancellationToken.Register.

The static keyword before a lambda (C# 9) turns "I hope there is no capture here" into a compiler check. If the delegate does carry state but is always the same, create it once and keep it in a field.

cards.q: The code returned an array to the pool and kept reading from it. What happens?
options: Usually it works, but sometimes it sends someone else's data: the array may already belong to another renter
An ObjectDisposedException when the array is accessed
Nothing bad: Return only marks the array while references to it exist
The GC collects the array and Send reads freed memory
cards.explain: The pool does not know you still hold a reference and checks nothing. The next Rent on this or another thread may get the same array and write to it while your Send runs. The bug does not crash, it silently corrupts data — which is why Return goes in finally, after the last use.

wrong.3: The array is an ordinary managed object: while a reference to it exists, the GC leaves it alone. The problem is different — shared ownership.

cards.q: Match the task and the tool
pairs: A temporary buffer of hundreds of KB
A 128-byte buffer in a hot method
A string of known length built from parts
A GetOrAdd factory in hot code
A static lambda with state as an argument

lessons.title: Final: allocation
lessons.sub: Fast and slow paths, hidden objects, pools and measurements

cards.q: The profiler says each new takes nanoseconds, yet the process spends 30% of its time in GC. What do you cut first?
options: The volume of allocations in hot code
The number of threads, so there are fewer allocation contexts
The size of the allocation context chunk
Nothing — call GC.Collect() at the start of every request
cards.explain: new itself is cheap, but every few megabytes exhaust the generation 0 budget and start a collection. Fewer bytes per second means fewer collections. A manual GC.Collect only adds collections.

cards.q: When does new take the slow path? Select all.
options: The thread's chunk has no room left for the object
The object weighs 85,000 bytes or more
The type has a finalizer
The class is sealed
The object is created inside a loop
cards.explain: A new chunk, the LOH and registration in the finalization queue all need the collector. sealed and loops do not affect the allocation path.

cards.q: Which array ends up in the LOH (64-bit process)?
options: new long[11_000]
new long[10_000]
new byte[80_000]
new string('x', 40_000)
cards.explain: long[11,000] is 88,000 bytes of data plus a header, above the 85,000 threshold. long[10,000] and byte[80,000] are about 80,000 bytes. A string of 40,000 two-byte characters is also about 80,000.

cards.q: Logging is almost always off, yet every call creates a closure object. How do you get rid of it?
options: Move the branch with the lambda into a separate method that takes r as a parameter
Mark the lambda static
Move the IsEnabled check inside the lambda
Replace the lambda with a local function that captures r
cards.explain: The parameter r is captured, so the closure is created on entry to Handle, before the check. In a separate method the closure is created only when that method is called. static will not compile — the lambda captures r. A local function converted to a delegate also needs a heap closure.

wrong.1: static forbids capture, and there is a capture here — a compile error.
wrong.3: While a local function is called directly, its state can live in a struct on the stack. But here it is converted to a delegate for Log, and the state needs the heap.

cards.q: The loop runs a million times. On which line is a heap object created on every iteration?
cards.explain: foreach over IEnumerable<Order> calls the interface GetEnumerator, and the List<Order>.Enumerator struct gets boxed. A parameter of type List<Order>, or IReadOnlyList<Order> with a for loop, would remove the allocation.

cards.q: Measure how many bytes one call to Parse allocates on this thread
cards.explain: The thread counter is monotonic and exact to the object, and the "after minus before" difference is the bytes of one call. GetTotalMemory shows the live heap, not what was allocated, and changes with collections.

cards.q: A method almost always completes synchronously and returns a number from a cache, usually in the hundreds. What does switching Task<int> to ValueTask<int> give you?
options: It removes the task allocation on the synchronous path
It removes the state machine from the stack
Nothing: Task<int> is cached for any value
It speeds up awaiting incomplete operations
cards.explain: Without an await the state machine lives on the stack anyway, but a Task<int> for a value like 300 is created anew — the cache covers only a few small numbers. ValueTask<int> carries the result inside. On the asynchronous path there is almost no difference.

cards.q: ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1000) — what array length will you most likely get?
cards.explain: The shared pool sorts arrays into power-of-two buckets and hands out the smallest that fits — 1024. That is why you then work with buf.AsSpan(0, 1000), not the whole array.

cards.q: Match the tool and what it shows
pairs: Bytes allocated by the current thread
Bytes allocated by the whole process
Allocation speed in a running service

units.title: How a collection works
units.blurb: What triggers a collection and how the generation is chosen, how threads are stopped at safepoints, marking from roots through GC info and the card table, the plan that picks sweep or compact, moving objects and updating references.

source.title: Book of the Runtime: Garbage collection design

lessons.title: When a collection starts
lessons.sub: Generation budgets, GC.Collect and low-memory signals

cards.title: Allocations trigger collections
cards.body:
The garbage collector does not run on a timer, and it does not watch for objects becoming garbage. Most of the time a collection is triggered by an allocation.

Every generation has an allocation budget: how many bytes may be allocated in it before the next collection. Every new spends the Gen 0 budget. Once the budget is gone, the next allocation triggers a collection.

The check is not in every new. A thread allocates by bumping a pointer inside its own allocation context, and it looks at the budget only on the slow path, when the context is used up and it needs a new chunk. The unit "Allocation" covers this in detail.
cards.deep:
The runtime derives the starting Gen 0 budget from the CPU cache size: the Workstation GC sources take 4/5 of the largest cache per logical processor (no less than 256 KB) and then multiply the result by 5/8, so the minimum budget ends up at about half of that cache. After that the budget is tuned after every collection. You can set it by hand with the GCgen0size setting, and DATAS mode (unit "GC modes") deliberately keeps Gen 0 small.

Why the cache: if Gen 0 fits in the cache, freshly allocated objects are still hot when the collector walks them.

cards.q: At what moment does a thread check whether it is time to start a collection?
options: When its allocation context runs out and it goes to get a new chunk of memory
On every new, before bumping the pointer
On a runtime timer, roughly every 100 ms
When the last reference to an object is set to null
cards.explain: The fast path of new is a pointer bump with no checks. The budget is checked on the slow path, when the thread asks the heap for a new chunk for its allocation context.

wrong.3: The GC does not count references and does not know when an object became garbage. That only comes out during marking.

cards.title: The budget is alive: it is recomputed after every collection
cards.body:
A budget is not a constant. After a collection the GC looks at the generation's survival rate: what share of objects survived.

  • Few survived: the collection was productive, the budget can stay small.
  • Many survived: the collection freed almost nothing. The budget grows: collecting often is pointless, let more garbage pile up.

A key detail: the budgets of older generations are spent not by new but by promotion. Survivors of a Gen 0 collection move to Gen 1 and spend its budget. Survivors of a Gen 1 collection spend the Gen 2 budget. Large objects spend the LOH budget directly.
cards.deep: In the GC sources this is the generation's "dynamic data": dd_new_allocation goes down on allocation or promotion, and when it reaches zero or below, the budget counts as exhausted. The new budget is computed from survival and clamped between the generation's minimum and maximum. The limits depend on the mode (Workstation or Server), the version and settings, so do not trust specific numbers from articles without measuring.

cards.q: Whose budget does this event spend?
pairs: An object survived a Gen 0 collection
An object survived a Gen 1 collection

cards.title: A collection is triggered: which generation to collect?
cards.body:
The trigger is almost always "the Gen 0 budget ran out". But the collector may go deeper. First it decides which generation to condemn:

  • it checks the budgets of older generations: Gen 1 budget exhausted, it collects 0 and 1; Gen 2 budget exhausted, a full collection;
  • LOH budget exhausted: also a full collection, because LOH is only collected together with Gen 2;
  • it adds heuristics: low memory, heavy fragmentation, expensive cross-generation references.

So a thread that allocated a small object may end up starting a full collection: Gen 0 was the last straw, but everything gets collected.
cards.deep: In gc.cpp this is the function generation_to_condemn. With background GC enabled, a full collection usually becomes a background one: Gen 2 is marked while the program keeps running. The unit "GC modes" covers this.

cards.q: A loop allocates byte[200_000] arrays, and each becomes garbage right away. Which collections will happen?
options: Full collections: an exhausted LOH budget leads to a Gen 2 collection
Only Gen 0 collections: the array became garbage immediately
None: LOH is never collected
Gen 1 collections: large objects start in Gen 1
cards.explain: 200,000 bytes is above the LOH threshold. Such arrays spend the LOH budget, and only a Gen 2 collection can free LOH. Temporary large arrays are a classic source of frequent full collections; the fix is a pool (ArrayPool).

wrong.1: A Gen 0 collection does not touch LOH: it only looks at the youngest generation.

cards.title: GC.Collect: a collection on demand
cards.body:
GC.Collect() is an induced collection. Without arguments it is a full blocking collection. The overloads let you choose:

  • generation: collect generations 0 up to the given one;
  • mode: Forced (same as Default) collects now; Optimized lets the GC decline if the collection would be unproductive; Aggressive (.NET 7+) compacts everything and returns as much memory to the OS as possible;
  • blocking: false allows a background collection;
  • compacting: true demands compaction. Without it the GC decides between sweep and compact itself.

Legitimate reasons: tests and measurements, the end of a one-off heavy phase (data loaded, moving on to work), before the app goes idle. Otherwise the collector knows better when to collect.
cards.deep:
Aggressive is strict about arguments: only for the oldest generation, only with blocking: true and compacting: true, otherwise ArgumentException. The overload without compacting fills it in for you.

GCCollectionMode.Default currently equals Forced. An induced collection is counted in GC.CollectionCount like any other, and in a trace it has its own reason, Induced, so stray GC.Collect calls in someone else's library are easy to find.

cards.q: The app has finished loading and wants to return as much memory as possible to the OS. Fill in the call
cards.code: GC.Collect(2, GCCollectionMode.___, blocking: true, compacting: ___);
cards.explain: Aggressive (.NET 7+) does a full blocking compacting collection and gives the freed memory back to the OS. With compacting: false this mode throws ArgumentException.

cards.title: Low memory: three signals
cards.body:
Besides budgets, the state of the machine also pushes collections.

  • OS notification. On Windows the runtime subscribes to the "memory is low" signal (memory resource notification). The finalizer thread waits for it and, once it arrives, starts a collection with reason LowMemory right away. Linux has no such notification.
  • Memory load. At the start of every collection the GC checks what share of physical memory is in use, taking a container limit into account. Above a threshold (90% by default) it does full compacting collections more often.
  • Heap hard limit. In a container with a memory limit, the heap is limited to 75% of that limit by default (but no less than 20 MB). Near the limit the GC collects more aggressively.

And the last line of defense: if memory cannot be allocated, the GC runs a full compacting collection and only after that throws OutOfMemoryException.
cards.deep: The load threshold is changed by GCHighMemPercent, the heap limit by GCHeapHardLimit or GCHeapHardLimitPercent in runtimeconfig.json or DOTNET_ variables. The "out of space" reasons appear in a trace as OutOfSpaceSOH and OutOfSpaceLOH. A collection on the OS notification is requested as a Gen 0 collection with a "low memory" flag, and the GC picks the depth itself based on memory load.

cards.q: An app with no GC settings runs in a container with a 1 GB memory limit. What limit will the managed heap have?
options: About 750 MB: 75% of the container limit
Exactly 1 GB: the whole container limit
All of the host RAM: the GC knows nothing about containers
None: the heap grows until the kernel kills the process
cards.explain: In a container with a memory limit the runtime sets a heap hard limit itself, 75% of the limit, to leave room for native memory, stacks and code. You can change it with GCHeapHardLimit or GCHeapHardLimitPercent.

cards.title: How to find out why a collection happened
cards.body:
Every collection begins with a GCStart event, and it has a Reason field. The main values: AllocSmall (SOH budget), AllocLarge (LOH budget), Induced (GC.Collect), LowMemory, OutOfSpaceSOH/OutOfSpaceLOH. dotnet-trace collects it, and PerfView shows it in its table of collections.

Without tracing, a lot is visible from code: GC.CollectionCount(n) is how many collections of a generation happened, GC.GetGCMemoryInfo() gives data about the last collection.
cards.code:
var info = GC.GetGCMemoryInfo();
Console.WriteLine(info.Index);              // collection number
Console.WriteLine(info.Generation);         // which generation was collected
Console.WriteLine(info.Compacted);          // whether it compacted
Console.WriteLine(info.PauseDurations[0]);  // the pause

cards.q: Put in order: from new to work resuming
items: new does not fit in the allocation context
Slow path: the Gen 0 budget is exhausted
The GC picks a generation by the older budgets
Collection: survivors are promoted and spend older budgets
New budgets from survival rates
The allocation proceeds
cards.explain: The trigger is the Gen 0 budget; the depth is chosen from the budgets of older generations. After the collection the budgets are recomputed, and the thread gets its memory.

lessons.title: Suspending threads
lessons.sub: Cooperative and preemptive mode, safepoints and hijacking

cards.title: Why the program has to stop
cards.body:
The collector reads references and moves objects. If a managed thread runs at the same time, it may write a reference into an object that was already scanned, or hold in a register an address the GC is about to change. The result is a lost live object or a pointer into nowhere.

So before a blocking collection the runtime suspends the execution engine (Suspend EE): all managed threads freeze, the collection runs, then the threads are released (Restart EE). Even a background collection needs short pauses at its start and end.

cards.title: Two thread modes
cards.body:
Every thread that has ever entered managed code has a mode flag.

  • Cooperative: the thread runs managed code and may touch the heap. A collection cannot start while it is in this mode: it has to be brought to a stop.
  • Preemptive: the thread is in native code, waiting in the kernel, or sleeping. It has promised not to touch the managed heap, and the GC does not wait for it.

It works like a lock on the heap: cooperative mode holds it, preemptive mode has released it. Entering cooperative mode again checks whether a collection is in progress, and if so, the thread waits for it to end.
cards.deep: In CoreCLR the mode is kept in the thread field m_fPreemptiveGCDisabled, and the "suspension in progress" flag in the global g_TrapReturningThreads. Every switch to cooperative mode checks it: returning from P/Invoke, entering from native code through a callback, leaving a wait. See the "Threading" document of the Book of the Runtime in the dotnet/runtime repository.

cards.q: Which threads does the collector not need to wait for? Select all.
options: A thread in Thread.Sleep(5000)
A thread waiting in Monitor.Wait
A thread inside a P/Invoke call to ReadFile
A thread spinning a managed addition loop
A thread currently executing new List<int>()
cards.explain: Sleeping, waiting and native calls happen in preemptive mode: such threads do not touch the heap. A thread in managed code is in cooperative mode: it has to be brought to a safepoint.

cards.title: Safepoint: where a thread can be stopped
cards.body:
Stopping a thread at an arbitrary instruction is not enough: the GC must know exactly which registers and stack slots hold references at that moment. In the middle of a computation a reference may sit in a register nothing is recorded about.

Places where this information exists are safepoints. The JIT defines them when it writes the GC info for a method:

  • partially interruptible code: only call sites to other methods and GC poll checks are safe;
  • fully interruptible code: almost every instruction is safe, except the prolog and epilog.

Full interruptibility costs space: the GC info gets bigger. The JIT picks the mode with heuristics: for example, it usually makes a method with a call-free loop fully interruptible, otherwise a thread in such a loop could not be stopped.

cards.q: Why not just freeze a thread through the OS and start collecting right away?
options: At an arbitrary point the GC does not know which registers and stack slots hold references
The OS cannot suspend threads
A frozen thread holds the heap lock forever
Suspending through the OS takes seconds
cards.explain: The OS can stop a thread, and the runtime uses that. But then it needs an exact map of references for the current instruction, and that exists only at safepoints.

cards.title: How a thread is brought to a safepoint
cards.body:
The thread that started the collection sets a global "suspension in progress" flag and goes through all threads in cooperative mode:

  • Interruption. The thread is paused with OS facilities and inspected. If it is in fully interruptible code, it is redirected to a stub that switches it to preemptive mode and waits for the collection to end.
  • Return address hijacking. If the code is partially interruptible, the runtime replaces the return address of the top frame. The method finishes, "returns" into the stub and stops there.
  • GC poll. In partially interruptible code the JIT may insert a check of the flag. When it sees the flag, the thread enters the runtime by itself and stops.

The runtime repeats the pass until nobody is left in cooperative mode.
cards.deep: On Windows the thread is paused with SuspendThread, and on newer Windows versions the runtime can step in through a special user-mode APC. Linux and macOS have no SuspendThread: the thread is interrupted with a signal, and the signal handler does the same check.

cards.q: Put the suspension steps in order
items: The initiating thread sets the "suspension in progress" flag
It finds threads in cooperative mode
It interrupts them or replaces their return address
Each reaches a safepoint and waits in preemptive mode
The collection runs
Restart EE: the flag is cleared, threads are released
cards.explain: While even one thread is in cooperative mode, the collection does not start. Threads in native code will see the flag only when they try to return to managed code.

cards.title: Why native code does not get in the way
cards.body:
Before a P/Invoke call the stub records a transition frame, marking where the managed part of the stack ends, and switches the thread to preemptive mode. While the native function runs, the managed frames below it are frozen: the GC walks them calmly and updates references in them.

Native code must not hold "raw" addresses of movable objects. That is why the marshaller pins arrays and strings for the duration of the call.

On the way back the stub switches the thread to cooperative mode and checks the flag. If a collection is running, the thread waits. Native code that calls a managed method through a callback waits the same way.

cards.q: A thread sleeps in usleep(5_000_000) through P/Invoke. Another thread starts a collection. What happens?
options: The collection runs at once; if usleep returns during it, the thread waits for it to end
The collection waits 5 seconds until usleep returns
The runtime interrupts usleep to collect garbage
The collection scans only the stacks of the other threads
cards.explain: A thread in P/Invoke is in preemptive mode, the GC does not wait for it. Its managed frames are frozen and get walked as usual. The thread can get back into managed code only after Restart EE.

wrong.3: The managed frames below the native call hold roots too. The GC walks them, starting from the transition frame.

cards.title: SuppressGCTransition: the flip side
cards.body:
Switching to preemptive mode and back costs little, but for a tiny native function called millions of times it is a noticeable share. For such cases there is the [SuppressGCTransition] attribute: a call without the transition.

The price: the thread stays in cooperative mode while the native function runs. If the function is long, collections in the whole process wait for it to finish. If it blocks or calls managed code, you can get a hang or corrupted state.

The rule from the documentation: only for very short functions that do not block, do not throw and do not call into the runtime.
cards.code:
[LibraryImport("native")]
[SuppressGCTransition]
internal static partial long ReadCounter();  // a few instructions

cards.q: Which call can hold up collections in the whole process for a full second?
cards.explain: With SuppressGCTransition the thread stays cooperative for the whole second of sleep, and any collection in the process waits for it. usleep and Thread.Sleep go into preemptive mode and do not get in the way.

cards.title: The cost of suspension
cards.body:
A GC pause is suspending threads, the GC work and restarting threads. Usually suspension is a small share of the pause, but there are exceptions:

  • many threads in cooperative mode: each has to be brought to a safepoint;
  • a thread in a long call with SuppressGCTransition;
  • a thread without a CPU: an overloaded machine or CPU throttling in a container. Until the thread gets CPU time, it will not reach the stub.

In a trace this shows up as the GCSuspendEEBegin/GCSuspendEEEnd events; PerfView shows suspension time as a separate column in its table of collections. If the pause is long but the collection itself is short, look for the problem in suspension.

cards.q: Match the term and its meaning
pairs: A thread in managed code, the GC waits for it
A thread in native code or a wait, the GC does not wait for it
A point where it is known where references are
Replacing the return address of the top frame
A flag check inserted into code by the JIT

lessons.title: Marking
lessons.sub: Roots, precise collection, the card table and the write barrier

cards.title: The mark phase: find everything alive
cards.body:
Threads are stopped, and marking begins. The collector takes each root and follows references, marking every object it reaches. You saw how reachability works in ".NET inside out"; here is how it is built internally.

  • Where the mark lives. Not in a separate table but in the object itself: the GC sets the lowest bit of the type pointer (MethodTable). Pointers are aligned, that bit is always zero, so it is free.
  • How the walk goes. Not by recursion but with its own mark stack: take an object, mark it, push its unmarked neighbors.
  • Where the walk stops. Only condemned generations are marked. In a Gen 0 collection, Gen 2 objects are neither walked nor marked.
cards.deep: In gc.cpp the mark is set by set_marked: MethodTable | 1, and the bit is cleared after the collection. The pinned flag is kept elsewhere, in a bit of the object header. If the mark stack overflows, the GC remembers an "overflow" address range and rescans it later, so even a very deep chain does not crash the collector.

cards.title: Roots: the full list
cards.body:
Where the walk starts:

  • Thread stacks: the stack slots and registers of every managed frame that currently hold live references.
  • Static fields: the CLR keeps them in its own structures and reports them to the collector as roots.
  • GC handles: strong and pinned ones (GCHandle.Alloc, Normal and Pinned). Weak handles are not roots: they are cleared if the object is not marked.
  • The finalization queue: objects ready for their finalizer are kept alive until it has run.
  • Older generations: when collecting younger ones, references from Gen 2 into Gen 0 also act as roots. More on that below.
cards.deep: A trace shows this breakdown literally: the GCMarkWithType event reports how many bytes were marked from each root type: Stack, Finalizer, Handle, Older (references from older generations) and others. It shows what keeps survivors alive: for example, a huge Older next to a small Stack means Gen 0 is being held by references from Gen 2.

cards.q: What keeps an object alive during a collection? Select all.
options: A local variable that will still be read later in the method
A static field
GCHandle.Alloc(obj, GCHandleType.Weak)
The finalization queue: the finalizer has not run yet
A WeakReference<T> to the object
cards.explain: A live local, a static and the finalization queue are roots. Weak handles and WeakReference built on them do not hold the object: after marking they are cleared if it is not marked.

cards.title: GC info: precise collection
cards.body:
How does the GC know a stack slot holds a reference and not the number 140 billion? The JIT tells it.

  • For every method the JIT writes GC info: which registers and frame slots hold live references at each safepoint. Interior pointers (ref, Span), which point into the middle of an object, are flagged separately.
  • The runtime unwinds the stack frame by frame and, for each frame, asks the GC info about the current instruction address.
  • For heap objects the type knows the same: the MethodTable holds a GCDesc, the offsets of reference fields.

This is a precise collector. It never mistakes a number for a reference, so it can move objects and rewrite references. A conservative collector treats anything that looks like an address as a reference and cannot move such objects: it might have been a number.
cards.deep: GC info explains what you saw in ".NET inside out": in optimized code a variable lives only until its last use, and an object may become garbage before the method ends.
