In Debug the JIT extends lifetimes to the end of the method. Slots whose address is taken and leaks out are marked "untracked" by the JIT: they count as live for the whole method. The CoreCLR sources also have an undocumented conservative stack scanning mode (gcConservative), but by default collection is precise.

cards.q: Why can a precise collector move an object referenced from the stack, while a conservative one cannot?
options: The precise one knows the slot is a reference and can rewrite it; the conservative one does not, it might be a number
A conservative collector cannot copy memory
A precise collector does not look at the stack at all
A conservative collector works only with LOH
cards.explain: To move an object, every reference to it must be rewritten. You cannot rewrite a "maybe reference": if it was a number, the program breaks. So conservative collectors pin everything the stack "seems" to point at.

cards.title: The problem: references from old to young
cards.body:
A Gen 0 collection is cheap because it does not walk Gen 2. But a Gen 2 object may reference a new object:

cache.Add(key, new Entry()): the cache has long been in Gen 2, the Entry was just created. No root points at Entry directly. Without looking into Gen 2, Entry would be counted as garbage.

Walking all of Gen 2 would throw away the whole point of generations. The solution is the card table: the heap is split into small areas, "cards", and each has a bit meaning "there is a reference into a younger generation here". A Gen 0 collection looks only at objects in marked cards and treats the references found there as roots.
cards.deep: On a 64-bit platform a card covers 256 bytes of heap, and card bits are packed into 32-bit words. Above the cards there is one more level, card bundles: a bit per group of words, so a collection can quickly skip large clean areas.

cards.task: Cache has long been in Gen 2 and holds a new Entry. Make Temp get removed while Entry survives a Gen 0 collection and moves to Gen 1.

cards.title: The write barrier: who marks the cards
cards.body:
The program's own code marks the cards. Every store of a reference into the heap, into an object field or an array element, is turned by the JIT into a call to the write barrier helper. It stores the reference, checks whether it points into the younger generations, and if so marks the card that contains the field's address.

  • A store into a local variable needs no barrier: the stack is scanned in full anyway.
  • Neither does storing null or a number: the JIT inserts no barrier.
  • A struct with references copied into an object field also goes through the barrier, once for each reference field.

The price is a few instructions and a conditional branch on every reference store. That is why writing a reference field is slightly more expensive than writing an int.
cards.code:
class Node { public Node? Next; public int Value; }

n.Value = 5;      // a plain store
n.Next = other;   // store + write barrier
n.Next = null;    // null: no barrier needed
cards.deep: The classic x64 barrier only checks that the new value falls into the younger generations' range, and marks a whole byte of the table: eight cards, 2 KB of heap. With regions (.NET 7+) there are barrier variants that compare the generations of the source and destination regions and can set a single bit. The runtime patches the barrier code on the fly: the younger generation bounds and the table address are baked into the instructions. If the JIT is not sure the store goes into the heap (for example, through a ref), it calls a "checked" barrier that first looks whether it is the heap.

cards.q: On which line will the JIT insert a write barrier call?
cards.explain: Only head.Next = new Node() writes a reference into a field of a heap object. var head = new Node() and the last line write a reference into a local variable; the rest write numbers.

cards.title: The cost of cards and a side effect
cards.body:
When collecting younger generations, the GC goes through the marked cards: for each object in such a card it looks at its references, and everything that points into the condemned generations is marked live. If a card has no young references left, its mark is cleared.

Two consequences:

  • A dead old object keeps young ones alive. A Gen 2 object may have become garbage long ago, but a Gen 0 collection does not check that: Gen 2 is not marked. Its references, through the cards, hold the young objects until the next full collection.
  • Many cards make Gen 0 collections expensive. A large Gen 2 array that keeps receiving fresh objects marks cards along its whole length. Gen 0 collections start spending time scanning them.
cards.deep: The GC tracks how productive the card scan was and takes it into account when deciding whether to collect Gen 1 right away: then fewer references end up "older" than the young objects. The usual fix is in the data: do not keep a long-lived collection that young objects keep pouring into, or store value types in it instead of references.

cards.q: Object Old in Gen 2 is already unreachable but references Young in Gen 0. A Gen 0 collection runs. What happens to Young?
options: It survives and moves to Gen 1: a reference from a marked card counts as a root
It is removed: Young cannot be reached from the roots
It is removed together with Old
The Gen 0 collection first checks whether Old is alive
cards.explain: A Gen 0 collection does not mark Gen 2 and does not know Old is dead. Old's card is marked, and the reference to Young from it acts as a root. Only a full collection frees both.

wrong.3: To check that, it would have to mark Gen 2, exactly what a Gen 0 collection avoids.

cards.q: Where does the GC learn where references are?
pairs: GC info written by the JIT

lessons.title: Planning
lessons.sub: Plugs, the brick table and the choice: sweep or compact

cards.title: After marking comes a decision
cards.body:
The marks are set: the living are separated from the dead. Space can be freed in two ways:

  • Sweep: live objects stay where they are, and the holes between them become free chunks.
  • Compact: live objects slide together, and the free space gathers into one chunk at the end.

Which is better is not known in advance. So between marking and cleanup comes the plan phase: the GC simulates compaction, computing where each live object would move and how much space that would free, and only then decides.

cards.title: Plugs and gaps
cards.body:
The plan walks the condemned generation in order, from lower addresses to higher ones. It can step from object to object because each object's size is known from its MethodTable.

  • Consecutive live objects merge into a plug, which is moved as one piece.
  • Dead objects between plugs form a gap.

For every plug the GC computes a new address: plugs "slide" toward the start, keeping their order. The difference between the old and new address is the relocation distance. It is written right into the gap before the plug: that memory is dead, nobody minds, and no extra memory is needed during the collection.
cards.deep: To quickly find the plug for any address later, there is the brick table: the heap is split into "bricks" (4 KB on a 64-bit platform, 2 KB on 32-bit), and for each brick it stores the offset of the root of that brick's plug tree. Plugs within a brick are linked into a binary tree by address. So answering "where did address X move" means: find the brick, walk down the tree, add the relocation distance.

cards.q: Why does the GC write plug information into the gap before it rather than into a separate table?
options: The gap is dead memory that can be overwritten, and nothing new has to be allocated during the collection
It makes the write barrier faster
The GC is not allowed to keep separate tables in the heap
So that an object in the plug knows its new address after the collection
cards.explain: A collection often happens exactly when memory is short. Keeping the plan in space that is being freed anyway avoids asking the OS for memory in the middle of a collection.

cards.q: Put the phases of a blocking compacting collection in order
items: Suspend threads
Choose the generation
Mark: tag the living
Plan: new addresses and the decision
Relocate: rewrite references
Compact: copy the plugs
Resume threads
cards.explain: First references are rewritten to the new addresses, and only then are objects physically copied. If the plan decides to sweep, sweep runs instead of relocate and compact.

cards.title: How the choice is made: sweep or compact
cards.body:
Compaction is expensive: copy every survivor and rewrite every reference to it. It pays off only when it frees a lot. The logic is visible in the GC sources: compaction is chosen if:

  • it was demanded: GC.Collect(..., compacting: true), Aggressive mode, a forced-compaction setting;
  • this is the last collection before OutOfMemoryException;
  • fragmentation is high by two measures at once: in bytes and as a share of the generation size;
  • memory load is high, and compacting a full collection would return a noticeable amount;
  • otherwise there would not be enough space for the generations or new allocations.

If none of the conditions holds, it sweeps.
cards.deep: This is the decide_on_compacting function in gc.cpp. The fragmentation thresholds live in the generation's dynamic data and depend on the generation and the mode. The GC records the reason in the GCPerHeapHistory trace event (the compaction mechanisms field), and you can inspect it in PerfView.

cards.q: When will the plan definitely choose compaction? Select all.
options: GC.Collect(2, GCCollectionMode.Forced, blocking: true, compacting: true)
GC.Collect(2, GCCollectionMode.Aggressive, blocking: true, compacting: true)
A full collection right before throwing OutOfMemoryException
A plain GC.Collect() with no arguments
Any Gen 0 collection
cards.explain: compacting: true, Aggressive and the collection before OOM turn compaction on explicitly. GC.Collect() with no arguments is a full blocking collection, but the plan itself decides between sweep and compact. For Gen 0 compaction is common but not mandatory.

cards.title: Generations in the plan
cards.body:
The plan also decides which generation survivors end up in: Gen 0 survivors become Gen 1, Gen 1 survivors become Gen 2.

Then. Before .NET 7 the young generations lived in one contiguous ephemeral segment, and a generation boundary was just an address. Compaction moved objects and boundaries, and that is how survivors "moved" into the older generation.

Now. Since .NET 7 the heap consists of regions, and each region has its own generation. Survivors can be compacted into Gen 1 regions. And if almost everything in a region survived, copying makes no sense: the plan simply moves the whole region to the older generation, sweeping the gaps in place.
cards.deep: In the .NET 8 sources such regions are called "swept in plan" (SIP), and the threshold is 90% survival relative to the region size. If almost everything that survived in a region is held by references from Gen 2 (through cards), the region may be moved straight to Gen 2. The threshold is an implementation detail and may change.

cards.q: .NET 8. In a Gen 0 region, 95% of objects survived the collection. What will the plan most likely do?
options: Move the whole region to Gen 1 without copying objects
Copy all the objects into Gen 1 regions
Leave the region in Gen 0 until the next collection
Move the survivors to LOH
cards.explain: Copying 95% of a region to gain 5% of space is a bad deal. The plan labels the region with the new generation and sweeps the holes. Objects do not move, and references to them need no rewriting.

cards.title: Pinned objects in the plan
cards.body:
A pinned object (fixed, GCHandle with Pinned, the marshaller in P/Invoke) cannot move: native code is looking at its address. The GC records the pinned flag during marking.

The plan is built around such objects: their plug stays in place, and neighboring plugs slide only up to it. The gap before a pinned object does not disappear: it becomes a free chunk, that is, fragmentation.

One short pin costs almost nothing. The trouble is many pinned objects in the young generation: they chop it into pieces. For long pins there is a separate heap since .NET 5, the POH (unit "Advanced").
cards.deep: To avoid fragmenting the older generation, the GC may leave a pinned object and its neighbors in the younger generation instead of promoting them; this is called demotion. fixed is cheaper than GCHandle: the JIT just marks the stack slot as pinning in the GC info, and the pin exists only for collections that happen inside the block.

cards.q: From which line on can the GC no longer move buf (until Free is called)?
cards.explain: The Pinned handle does the pinning. A Span does not pin: it is an interior pointer, and the GC simply rewrites it during compaction. AddrOfPinnedObject only reads the address of an already pinned object.

cards.title: LOH and POH: a plan without moving
cards.body:
For LOH compaction is not planned by default: copying megabyte-sized arrays is expensive. LOH is swept, and the holes go to the free list.

Exceptions:

  • ask for it once: GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode = GCLargeObjectHeapCompactionMode.CompactOnce; the next blocking full collection compacts LOH, and the mode resets;
  • with a heap hard limit (for example, in a container) and with the GCConserveMemory setting, the GC decides by itself when to compact LOH.

POH is never compacted, and that is its whole point: it holds objects that must not move.

cards.q: Compact LOH once, at the next full collection
cards.explain: CompactOnce applies to one blocking full collection, after which the mode goes back to Default. GC.Collect() is such a collection right now; without it, compaction happens at the next blocking full one.

lessons.title: Sweep and compact
lessons.sub: The free list, moving objects and updating references

cards.title: Sweep: holes go to the free list
cards.body:
If the plan decided to sweep, live objects stay where they are. The GC walks the gaps between plugs:

  • neighboring dead objects merge into one chunk;
  • the chunk is formatted as a free object: a fake object with a special "Free" type and a length;
  • large enough chunks go onto the generation's free list, sorted by size.

Space is later taken from that list: when promoting survivors in the next collection, when allocating in LOH.

The cost of sweep is walking the generation. No copying, no rewriting references. The price of being cheap is fragmentation.
cards.deep: Free objects are visible in a dump: !dumpheap -stat in SOS shows a Free row with the count and total size of the chunks. In the .NET 8 sources a chunk smaller than two minimum object sizes (48 bytes on a 64-bit platform) does not go onto the list: it stays a "Free" object, but cannot be used until the next compaction.

cards.q: Why format a free chunk as a fake "Free" object instead of leaving the dead objects there?
options: The heap is walked in order, stepping by object size: the chunk must look like an object with a length, and neighboring dead ones must merge into one
This is how the GC zeroes memory for security
Otherwise the finalizers of dead objects would run again
The free object keeps references to its neighbors for the card table
cards.explain: The plan, sweep, the debugger and dumps walk the heap object by object. A free object with type Free and a length keeps the heap walkable, and merging gives one big chunk instead of a scatter of small ones.

cards.title: Fragmentation
cards.body:
After a sweep, free memory is scattered in chunks between live objects. An object bigger than the largest chunk will not fit, even if there is plenty free in total. Then the heap needs new memory, and the process grows while the heap is "empty".

This hits LOH especially: by default it is only swept, and the objects there are large.

How much memory sits in chunks is visible from code:

cards.q: LOH has 50 free chunks of 1 MB each. The program allocates a 3 MB array. What happens?
options: No chunk fits: LOH takes new memory even though 50 MB is free
The GC glues three neighboring chunks together and puts the array there
The array is cut into three 1 MB parts
OutOfMemoryException is thrown
cards.explain: An array must be one contiguous piece. The chunks are separated by live objects, and only compaction can join them. Without it LOH grows, and the 50 MB of holes stay holes.

wrong.1: If the chunks are separated by live objects, they cannot be joined without moving those objects.

cards.title: Compact: references first, then objects
cards.body:
If the plan chose compaction, two phases follow.

Relocate: rewrite references. The GC again goes through every place that may hold references into the condemned generations: roots on stacks (using the same GC info), handles, marked cards of older generations, fields of the survivors themselves. For each reference the new address is found through the brick table: find the plug, add its relocation distance.

Compact: copy the plugs to their new places, in address order. Plugs slide toward the start, so copying works like memmove and does not overwrite anything not yet copied.

After that the allocation pointer sits right after the last survivor, and everything beyond it is one solid free area.

cards.q: Put the steps of a compacting Gen 0 collection in order
items: Mark the living from roots and cards
Split into plugs and compute new addresses
Rewrite references to the new addresses
Copy the plugs
Put the allocation pointer after the last survivor
Release the threads
cards.explain: References are rewritten before copying: while objects are still in their old places, the plan in the gaps and the brick table are intact and tell the new addresses.

cards.title: Interior pointers
cards.body:
A ref variable, a Span<T>, a reference to an array element point not at the start of an object but into its middle. These are interior pointers.

GC info flags them specially. When it finds one, the GC uses the brick table to find the start of the object it points into, marks that object, and during compaction shifts the pointer by the same distance as the object. That is why a Span over an array needs no pinning.

Finding an object's start from an arbitrary address is not cheap. That is one of the reasons interior pointers live only on the stack: ref fields exist only in a ref struct, and a Span cannot be stored in a class field.

cards.q: What will the GC rewrite in the relocate phase if array arr moved? Select all.
options: The local variable int[] a = arr on the stack
A reference field to arr in a surviving object
ref int r = ref arr[5]
The value of arr.GetHashCode() saved in a variable
A long addr into which the address of arr was written earlier via unsafe
cards.explain: The GC rewrites what it knows to be references: stack slots from GC info, fields by GCDesc, interior pointers. The hash code does not depend on the address, and a long is just a number to the GC.

cards.title: Why moving does not break the hash code
cards.body:
If objects move, an address is no good either for a hash or for identity. So the default hash code (RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode) is not an address: on the first call the runtime generates a pseudo-random number and stores it in the object header or in the sync block. The object moves, and the hash moves with it.

But anything you derived from an address yourself lies after compaction. An address from Unsafe.AsPointer without pinning may, one collection later, point at someone else's object or at a free chunk.
cards.deep: This ties to the lesson on System.Object in "Deeper C#": the object header is shared by the hash code, the lock bits and the sync block index. If an object needs both a hash and a "fat" lock, the data moves to a sync block, and the header keeps only its index.

cards.q: What can happen with this code?
options: The write may corrupt another object or free memory: arr may have moved
The GC will update p, just as it updates a ref
An AccessViolationException is guaranteed
It will not compile: AsPointer is forbidden for arrays
cards.explain: To the GC, a void* is not a reference, and it is not in the GC info. If the collection compacted the generation, p points at the old place of arr, which now holds another object or a free chunk. The bug is silent: memory gets corrupted without an exception.

wrong.1: Only places the JIT flagged as references or interior pointers are updated. A void* is not one of them.

cards.title: Which is cheaper
cards.body:
• Sweep: the cost is proportional to the size of the generation: walk it. Objects do not move, references are not touched. Holes remain.
  • Compact: the cost is proportional to the survivors: copy their bytes and rewrite references to them. No holes, allocation is a pointer bump again, objects keep their relative order and sit tightly (good for the cache).

So for Gen 0, where few survive, compaction is cheap and frequent. Compacting a large Gen 2 is expensive, so it is swept more often (and a background collection only ever sweeps, see "GC modes").

After compaction, emptied regions return to the common pool, and over time the GC gives surplus memory back to the OS (decommit): the very difference between reserve and commit from the first unit.
cards.deep: If you care more about memory than CPU, there is the GCConserveMemory setting (values 0 to 9, .NET 6+): the higher the number, the more willingly the GC compacts Gen 2 and LOH to reduce fragmentation. With regions (.NET 7+) survivors can be compacted into other regions too, not only toward the start of the same one, and empty regions go back to the free pool whole.

cards.q: Match the phase and its job
pairs: Computes new addresses and picks the cleanup method
Rewrites references to the new addresses
Copies plugs to their new places
Turns holes into the free list

lessons.title: Final: a collection from the inside
lessons.sub: Budgets, suspension, marking, the plan and cleanup

cards.q: A service allocates almost no large objects, yet the trace shows many full collections with reason AllocSmall. How is that possible?
options: The trigger is the Gen 0 budget, but the GC went deeper: the Gen 2 budget, spent by promoted survivors, was exhausted
AllocSmall means a call to GC.Collect()
Full collections are always labeled AllocSmall
This is how low memory shows up on Linux
cards.explain: The reason answers "what triggered it", while the depth is chosen by the budgets of older generations. Many survivors, many promotions, the Gen 2 budget runs out, a full collection, even though the trigger was a small allocation.

wrong.1: GC.Collect() gives the reason Induced.

cards.task: Cache in Gen 2 holds Entry. Make a Gen 0 collection remove Entry while Cache stays alive.

cards.q: What is true about suspending threads? Select all.
options: A thread in a P/Invoke call is in preemptive mode and does not delay the collection
A native call with [SuppressGCTransition] keeps the thread cooperative
A thread in a call-free managed loop is stopped by interruption: such a method is usually fully interruptible
A thread returning from native code during a collection keeps running alongside it
A safepoint is any instruction at which the OS managed to pause the thread
cards.explain: Returning from native code checks the flag and waits for the collection to end. A safepoint is only a place where the GC info describes references exactly; the OS can pause a thread anywhere, but that is not yet a safepoint.

cards.q: Assemble a whole blocking compacting Gen 0 collection
items: The Gen 0 budget runs out on the allocation slow path
Threads are brought to safepoints
Mark from roots and marked cards
Plan: plugs, new addresses, the decision to compact
Relocate: references rewritten
Compact: plugs copied
Restart EE
cards.explain: Trigger, suspension, marking, plan, rewrite references, copy, release threads. Had the plan decided to sweep, a single sweep would replace the two phases before Restart EE.

cards.q: Which line marks a card in the card table, if items has long been in Gen 2?
cards.explain: items[3] = fresh writes a reference to a young object into an element of a Gen 2 array: the write barrier marks the card. Writing a number or null needs no barrier, and assignments to local variables do not write into the heap.

cards.q: Why does a Gen 0 collection not check whether the Gen 2 object whose card holds the reference is alive?
options: That would require marking Gen 2, exactly what generations are meant to avoid
Gen 2 objects are always alive
The card table also stores whether the object is alive
The write barrier does that check at store time
cards.explain: Cards are a conservative approximation: "there may be a reference into a young generation here". The price is that dead Gen 2 objects hold young ones until a full collection.

cards.q: Match the situation and what the plan will choose
pairs: The whole region is promoted, no copying
LOH with no settings and no heap limit
Sweep: large objects are not moved

cards.q: A Span<int> points into the middle of an array. A collection compacted the generation and moved the array. What about the Span?
options: It is valid: the GC info flags the interior pointer, and the GC shifted it along with the array
The Span now points at the old place; fixed is needed
The array could not move: the Span pins it
The Span became empty
cards.explain: The GC knows interior pointers on the stack and rewrites them during relocate. Pinning is needed only when the address goes somewhere the GC cannot see it: into native code or a void*.

wrong.2: A Span does not pin. The array under it moves freely, and the Span itself is updated.

units.title: GC modes
units.blurb: Workstation and Server, background GC and the foreground collections that run during it, GCSettings.LatencyMode latency modes, DATAS in .NET 8–9, settings in runtimeconfig.json and environment variables, container limits.

source.title: Microsoft Learn: Garbage collector config settings

lessons.title: Workstation and Server
lessons.sub: One heap or a heap per core, whose thread collects and what it costs

cards.title: One collector, two modes
cards.body:
.NET has one garbage collector, but it comes in two main flavors: Workstation and Server. The algorithm is shared — generations, marking, compaction. What differs is how many heaps there are, which threads collect, and how freely the collector spends memory to gain speed.

The flavor is picked once, at process startup, and never changes afterwards. You can see which one you got from code:
cards.code:
using System.Runtime;

Console.WriteLine(GCSettings.IsServerGC);      // True or False
Console.WriteLine(GCSettings.LatencyMode);     // Interactive — see lesson 2
Console.WriteLine(Environment.ProcessorCount); // how many cores the process sees
cards.deep:
Each flavor also comes as background (the default) or non-concurrent — a second, independent switch covered in the next lesson. That makes four combinations.

Inside the runtime these are literally two builds of the same gc.cpp code: with the MULTIPLE_HEAPS macro (Server) and without it (Workstation). At startup the runtime picks the matching implementation of the IGCHeap interface.

cards.title: Workstation: whoever allocated, collects
cards.body:
In Workstation mode the process has a single managed heap. A collection runs right on the thread whose allocation triggered it: the thread asked for room for an object, the gen0 budget ran out — and that same thread suspends the others and collects.

It keeps its normal priority, like the other user threads, so the collection competes with them for CPU. In exchange there are no extra threads and no extra heaps — the memory footprint is minimal.

This is the default for an ordinary console or desktop app.
cards.deep:
"Suspends the others" means stopping managed threads at safepoints, covered in the unit "How a collection works". Threads running native code at that moment (P/Invoke) are not suspended in either mode: they are simply not allowed back into managed code until the collection ends.

With background GC on, Workstation gets one more dedicated thread — for background gen2 collections. If it has nothing to do for a while, that thread exits and is created again for the next background collection.

cards.q: A console app runs Workstation GC (non-concurrent). Thread A allocated an object and the gen0 budget is exhausted. Which thread performs the collection?
options: Thread A
A dedicated high-priority GC thread
A thread pool thread
The finalizer thread
cards.explain: In Workstation GC the collection runs on the thread that triggered it, at that thread's normal priority. Dedicated GC threads are a Server GC feature.

wrong.1: That is how Server GC works: each heap has its own GC thread.
wrong.3: The finalizer thread only runs finalizers after a collection; it does not collect garbage itself.

cards.title: Server: a heap and a thread per core
cards.body:
In Server mode the collector creates one heap per logical processor and, for each heap, a dedicated GC thread. On 16 cores that is 16 heaps and 16 GC threads. On Windows these threads run at THREAD_PRIORITY_HIGHEST.

An application thread allocates in "its own" heap — usually the one tied to its core. So 16 threads can allocate in parallel without crowding around one pointer. References across heaps are allowed: an object in heap 3 can point to an object in heap 7.

When a collection is needed, all GC threads wake up and collect all heaps at once, each its own.
cards.deep:
Each heap has its own generations, its own SOH and LOH (and POH). The collector balances allocations: if one heap is overloaded, a thread may start allocating in a neighbor. By default GC threads are pinned to cores (affinitized); System.GC.NoAffinitize turns that off and System.GC.HeapAffinitizeMask limits the set of cores.

Note that GC threads do not "live" in the background collecting all the time. A collection still stops the application — the pause is just shorter because N threads share the work.

cards.q: What is true about Server GC? Select all.
options: Every logical processor gets its own heap and its own GC thread
An object in one heap can reference an object in another
A collection does not suspend application threads
During a collection the heaps are collected in parallel
The number of heaps can be changed from code at run time
cards.explain: Application threads are still suspended for a blocking collection — Server GC shortens the pause, it does not remove it. The heap count is set at startup (only the collector itself changes it at run time, in DATAS mode — lesson 3).

cards.title: The price of Server GC: memory and CPU
cards.body:
Server GC assumes the process is the main one on the machine. It allows more allocation before the next collection: the gen0 budget is per heap, and there are many heaps. Fewer collections and higher throughput — but a noticeably bigger heap. The same service on 4 cores and on 64 cores can take very different amounts of memory.

The second bill is CPU. Twelve Server GC processes on a four-core machine: if they collect at the same time, each core gets twelve high-priority GC threads. They get in each other's way and everyone else's.

That is why, for many small processes on one machine, the documentation recommends Workstation, sometimes with background GC turned off — fewer threads and context switches.
cards.deep:
A middle ground is Server GC with a capped heap count: System.GC.HeapCount. For example, 4 heaps on a 32-core machine that runs several services. Since .NET 9, DATAS largely solves this — the collector picks the heap count itself (lesson 3).

Then and now: in .NET Framework 4.0 and earlier, Server GC was non-concurrent only; background GC for Server arrived in 4.5. In .NET (Core), Server GC is background by default.

cards.q: One 8-core VM runs 30 small background services on .NET 8, each holding tens of megabytes. Which GC mode makes the most sense?
options: Workstation — each process has one heap and no eight GC threads
Server — more GC threads, so everyone gets shorter pauses
Server with LowLatency — fewer pauses
It does not matter: the mode affects only speed, not memory
cards.explain: Thirty Server GC processes means 240 high-priority GC threads and 240 heaps with their own budgets. For small services that is wasted memory and CPU contention. Workstation is the natural choice here.

wrong.1: If the services collect at the same time, their GC threads will preempt each other on the same eight cores.
wrong.2: LowLatency does not apply to Server GC at all — it is a Workstation-only mode (lesson 2).
wrong.3: The mode strongly affects memory: Server GC has more heaps and bigger budgets.

cards.title: Who picks the default
cards.body:
The runtime itself defaults to Workstation. Server is turned on by whoever builds the app:

  • ASP.NET Core — a project on Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web: that SDK sets the ServerGarbageCollection property to true unless you set it yourself. That is why web apps run on Server GC out of the box.
  • Console, WPF, WinForms, MAUI, plain Microsoft.NET.Sdk — Workstation.

The MSBuild property only writes "System.GC.Server": true into the app.runtimeconfig.json file next to the assembly — that is what the runtime reads.

One exception to every rule: if the process has a single logical processor available, Server GC does not turn on — Workstation runs instead.
cards.code:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <!-- The Web SDK already sets true; false brings back Workstation -->
    <ServerGarbageCollection>false</ServerGarbageCollection>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
cards.deep:
There are two ways to check what actually made it into the build: open bin/.../app.runtimeconfig.json and look at configProperties, or call GC.GetConfigurationVariables() (.NET 7+) inside the process — a dictionary of the collector's effective settings, including ServerGC.

In .NET Framework the choice lived in app.config (<gcServer enabled="true"/>), and for ASP.NET under IIS the host decided. In modern ASP.NET Core in-process under IIS, the app's runtimeconfig.json still decides.

cards.q: Which line does not compile?
cards.explain: IsServerGC is read-only: the mode is chosen at process startup and cannot be changed in-process. Error CS0200. You can switch modes only in configuration, followed by a restart.

cards.title: Why Server is faster on the same heap
cards.body:
Take a 4 GB heap. In Workstation one thread marks and compacts it. In Server on 16 cores, 16 threads share the same work: each walks its own heap, and cross-heap references are handled during marking. The pause of a full blocking collection gets several times shorter.

The second reason is allocation. With Workstation all threads live in one heap, and when their allocation contexts need a new chunk they take turns getting it. With Server the heaps are separate, so the line is shorter.

Bottom line: Server GC is about throughput and short pauses on big heaps; Workstation is about saving memory and CPU.
cards.deep: Parallelism is not free: GC threads synchronize at phase boundaries (mark → plan → relocate), and the slowest one holds up everybody. If live data is spread unevenly, some threads sit idle. The collector can steal marking work from neighbors (mark stealing) to smooth out the imbalance.

cards.q: Match the trait with the mode
pairs: Collects on the thread that allocated
GC thread at the highest priority on Windows
The only mode on a single core
Workstation, even if Server was requested
Find out the mode from code

cards.q: A service moved from a 4-core machine to a 64-core one, same load, .NET 8, Server GC. The managed heap grew several times over. What happened?
options: There are now 64 heaps, each with its own gen0 budget — the collector allows more allocation before a GC
A memory leak: objects live longer on a big machine
On 64 cores Server GC turns off compaction
The heap did not grow, it is a counter bug
cards.explain: Server GC sizes its budget for throughput and heap count, not for the amount of live data. More cores means more heaps and more memory. This is exactly the problem DATAS solves — opt-in in .NET 8, on by default in .NET 9 (lesson 3). Without DATAS, System.GC.HeapCount or Workstation helps.

lessons.title: Background GC and latency
lessons.sub: Background GC, foreground collections and GCSettings.LatencyMode

cards.title: The trouble with a full GC: the pause grows with the heap
cards.body:
Collecting generations 0 and 1 is fast: there are few young live objects, and the pause is usually a fraction of a millisecond to a few milliseconds. A gen2 collection, though, walks the entire heap. With several gigabytes of live data, a blocking full collection stops the app for a long time — a stutter in a UI, a latency spike in a service.

The fix is background GC (BGC). It applies to gen2 only: the longest work — marking and sweeping — is done by a dedicated GC thread at the same time as the app keeps running.

Background GC is on by default in both modes, Workstation and Server.
cards.deep:
The switch is System.GC.Concurrent (ConcurrentGarbageCollection in a csproj). The name is left over from the old "concurrent" GC, but in modern .NET true means background GC.

Generations 0 and 1 are never collected in the background: they are fast already, and synchronizing with a running app would cost more than the collection itself.

cards.title: How background GC splits the work
cards.body:
It cannot avoid stopping the app entirely, but the stops are short:

  • a short pause at the start — the collector fixes the starting points for marking;
  • marking gen2 — on the background thread, while the app runs and changes references;
  • a short pause — to recheck what the app changed during marking;
  • sweeping — parallel again: dead objects become free space.

How does the collector know what the app changed? Through write watch: marks on the heap pages that were written to. In the second pause it rechecks only those pages, not the whole heap.

The price: background GC does not compact. If gen2 gets badly fragmented, sooner or later the collector runs an ordinary blocking compacting collection.
cards.deep:
The real sequence of phases in the runtime is more involved: an ephemeral collection usually runs right before a BGC starts, the recheck of modified pages is done several times concurrently so that the final pause is shorter, and the details change from version to version. The "pause — mark — pause — sweep" model is right in essence.

When memory runs low (physical memory load above the System.GC.HighMemoryPercent threshold, 90% by default), the collector prefers full blocking compacting collections over background ones — those actually shrink the heap.

cards.q: Put the stages of a background gen2 collection in order
items: Short thread suspension: starting points for marking
Marking gen2 in parallel with the app
Short suspension: recheck the pages modified during marking
Sweeping dead objects in parallel with the app
cards.explain: The long stages — marking and sweeping — run on the background thread, and there are two suspensions, both short. There is no compaction in this sequence: background GC only sweeps.

cards.title: Foreground collections during a background one
cards.body:
A background gen2 collection takes a long time — seconds on a big heap. Meanwhile the app keeps allocating, and the gen0 budget runs out.

So during a background collection, ordinary gen0 and gen1 collections are allowed. They are called foreground GCs. A foreground collection suspends all managed threads, including the background GC thread: it checks regularly whether it is being asked to yield and pauses its work. After the foreground collection, the background one continues from where it stopped.

The result for the app: short ephemeral pauses are always there, but the long pause of a full collection is gone.
cards.deep:
Then and now: before background GC there was concurrent GC (.NET Framework 3.5 and earlier for Workstation, 4.0 and earlier for Server). It also marked gen2 in parallel, but ephemeral collections were impossible while it ran. As soon as there was no more room for young objects, allocating threads waited for the full collection to end. Background GC arrived in .NET Framework 4 (for Workstation) and 4.5 (for Server) and lifted that restriction.

Workstation has one background thread, Server usually one per heap. Server GC background threads do not exit when idle; the Workstation one does.

cards.q: What is true about background GC? Select all.
options: It collects only generation 2
Gen0 and gen1 collections can happen during it
It compacts the heap, just more slowly than usual
A foreground collection suspends all managed threads
It removes pauses from the app entirely
cards.explain: Background GC only sweeps, without compacting — blocking collections compact. And pauses remain: two short ones in the BGC itself and the pauses of foreground gen0 and gen1 collections.

cards.title: When background GC is turned off
cards.body:
Background GC is not free: a dedicated thread (threads, for Server), extra work tracking changes, and a bit more memory — the heap grows while gen2 is being collected.

Turning it off (System.GC.Concurrent = false) makes sense when nobody sees the pauses and resources matter:

  • batch processing, where total speed matters, not the latency of a single operation;
  • hundreds of app instances on one machine — fewer threads and context switches.

For a UI and for a web service with latency requirements, background GC stays on.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <!-- batch processing: pauses do not matter, resources do -->
  <ConcurrentGarbageCollection>false</ConcurrentGarbageCollection>
</PropertyGroup>

cards.title: GCSettings.LatencyMode: the latency mode
cards.body:
The second lever can be pulled right from code at run time — the latency mode. It is the GCSettings.LatencyMode property of type GCLatencyMode, and it applies to the whole process:

  • Batch — no background collections, maximum throughput. The default when background GC is off.
  • Interactive — with background collections. The default when background GC is on, which is almost always.
  • LowLatency — gen2 is not collected at all. Workstation only, short periods only.
  • SustainedLowLatency — no blocking full collections, background ones are allowed. Workstation and Server, but only with background GC on.
cards.deep:
There is a fifth value — NoGCRegion. You cannot assign it: the setter throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. You enter that mode through GC.TryStartNoGCRegion, and the property only shows that it is active; details are in the unit "Advanced".

Numeric values of the enum: Batch = 0, Interactive = 1, LowLatency = 2, SustainedLowLatency = 3, NoGCRegion = 4.

cards.q: Match the latency mode with what it does
pairs: The usual mode with background collections
Gen2 is not collected, Workstation only
No blocking full collections, background ones allowed

cards.title: Low latency is a debt
cards.body:
Low-latency modes do not make collection cheaper — they postpone it. Garbage piles up in gen2 and the heap grows. With SustainedLowLatency the collector also does not compact gen2, so fragmentation grows.

A gen2 collection still happens if:

  • the OS signals low memory;
  • code calls GC.Collect(2).

So the mode is switched on for a specific stretch — a trading session, frame capture, an animation — and the previous one is always restored in finally. The mode is process-wide: if other threads allocate a lot meanwhile, an OutOfMemoryException can hit any of them.
cards.deep: The catch is that an unsuitable mode is silently not applied. In the collector source (GCHeap::SetGcLatencyMode), LowLatency is applied only in the build without multiple heaps, that is, Workstation, and SustainedLowLatency only if background GC is allowed. Otherwise the assignment does nothing, there is no exception, and LatencyMode returns the previous value. Check what you read back after writing.

cards.q: A Server GC service turns off blocking full collections for an hour-long trading session. Fill in the blanks
cards.explain: For Server GC and a long stretch, only SustainedLowLatency fits: LowLatency does not apply to Server, and NoGCRegion cannot be assigned. In finally the mode is restored through the same LatencyMode property — IsServerGC is read-only.

cards.q: The app is built with ConcurrentGarbageCollection = false. What does the code print?
cards.code:
GCSettings.LatencyMode = GCLatencyMode.SustainedLowLatency;
Console.WriteLine(GCSettings.LatencyMode);
options: Batch
SustainedLowLatency
Interactive
Throws InvalidOperationException
cards.explain: Without background GC the default mode is Batch. SustainedLowLatency requires background GC, so the collector silently keeps the previous mode: no exception, and the property still reads Batch.

wrong.1: SustainedLowLatency relies on background gen2 collections, and those are off. The collector simply does not apply the mode.
wrong.2: Interactive is the default when background GC is on. Here it is off.

cards.q: Which line throws an exception at run time?
cards.explain: NoGCRegion cannot be assigned: the setter throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. You enter that mode only through GC.TryStartNoGCRegion. LowLatency will not apply on Server GC, but it does not throw either.

lessons.title: DATAS, settings and containers
lessons.sub: A heap sized to the app, runtimeconfig.json and memory limits

cards.title: DATAS: a heap sized to the data, not the machine
cards.body:
Classic Server GC sizes its budget for throughput: the more cores, the more heaps and the more memory it allows itself. The same service takes very different amounts of memory on different machines, and when load drops, the heap is in no hurry to shrink.

DATAS (Dynamic Adaptation To Application Sizes) changes the goal: the heap size should be roughly proportional to the amount of long-lived data. Same work on different machines — similar heap size. Load goes up or down — the heap follows.

Versions: in .NET 8 DATAS is opt-in, from .NET 9 it is on by default. It is part of Server GC: an app on Workstation is not affected.

cards.title: What DATAS does inside
cards.body:
• Changes the heap count on the fly. It starts with one heap, like Workstation, and adds heaps when threads have to wait for memory. The ceiling is the core count, as with ordinary Server GC. When load drops, heaps are removed.
  • Caps the gen0 budget based on the amount of long-lived data: a small app gets a small budget, even on a big machine.
  • Does full compacting collections when needed to keep fragmentation from growing — that also keeps the heap compact.

The result is a hybrid: from one heap, like Workstation, to a heap per core, like Server.
cards.deep:
DATAS targets TCP (Throughput Cost Percentage): the share of time the app loses to GC pauses and allocation waits. The default target is 2%, set with System.GC.DTargetTCP (.NET 9). If the cost is above target, DATAS adds heaps.

The gen0 budget ceiling comes from a formula whose multiplier falls as 1/√(app size in MB), clamped between a minimum and a maximum. .NET 10 added System.GC.DGen0GrowthPercent, DGen0GrowthMaxFactor and DGen0GrowthMinFactor to tune it.

cards.q: An ASP.NET Core service was upgraded from .NET 8 to .NET 9 with no GC settings touched. The working set dropped several times over, and gen0 collections became noticeably more frequent. Why?
options: .NET 9 turns DATAS on by default for Server GC: fewer heaps and a smaller gen0 budget
In .NET 9 ASP.NET Core switched to Workstation GC
.NET 9 turned off background GC by default
In .NET 9 the collector stopped compacting the heap
cards.explain: The Web SDK still turns on Server GC, and since .NET 9 DATAS comes with it by default. The gen0 budget is now tied to the amount of live data, so there are more collections and less memory.

wrong.1: Web projects still use Server GC — its behavior is what changed.
wrong.2: Background GC is still on by default.

cards.title: What DATAS costs and how to turn it off
cards.body:
The memory savings are not free. In Microsoft's TechEmpower measurements on a 48-core machine, the working set dropped by over 80% while peak throughput dropped by 2–3%. Gen0 and gen1 collections become noticeably more frequent.

The second cost is startup. DATAS begins with one heap, and until it adds more, many allocating threads wait. The same happens on a sudden jump from quiet to peak.

If throughput matters more than memory, turn DATAS off:

  • System.GC.DynamicAdaptationMode = 0 (GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode in a csproj, DOTNET_GCDynamicAdaptationMode in the environment);
  • or set System.GC.HeapCount — a fixed heap count means "do not change the heap count", and DATAS turns off.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <!-- .NET 9+: back to classic Server GC -->
  <GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode>0</GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode>
</PropertyGroup>
cards.deep:
In .NET 8 the same property set to 1 turns DATAS on manually — together with ServerGarbageCollection. Without Server GC it has no effect.

Advice from the GC team: .NET 9 is not LTS, so many people will meet DATAS for the first time when moving from .NET 8 to .NET 10. Before such an upgrade, look at the counters: heap size, collection counts, percent of time in GC.

cards.q: ASP.NET Core on .NET 9, Server GC, DATAS by default. Which settings turn DATAS off? Select all.
options: System.GC.DynamicAdaptationMode = 0
System.GC.HeapCount = 8
ServerGarbageCollection = false
System.GC.ConserveMemory = 5
System.GC.RetainVM = true
cards.explain: DynamicAdaptationMode = 0 turns it off directly. HeapCount fixes the heap count, so DATAS is disabled. Workstation does not use DATAS at all. ConserveMemory and RetainVM are different knobs and work alongside it.

cards.title: Three places for settings
cards.body:
GC settings are read once, at startup. Changing a variable in a running process does nothing. There are three ways to set them:

  • csproj — some have MSBuild properties (ServerGarbageCollection, ConcurrentGarbageCollection, RetainVMGarbageCollection, GarbageCollectionAdaptationMode), the rest go through a RuntimeHostConfigurationOption item. All of it ends up in runtimeconfig.json.
  • runtimeconfig.json — the configProperties section, names like System.GC.Server, numbers in decimal.
  • Environment variables — DOTNET_gcServer, DOTNET_GCHeapCount and so on, numbers in hexadecimal.

An environment variable beats the file: the runtime checks it first. Handy for changing the mode in a container without rebuilding.
cards.code:
<PropertyGroup>
  <ServerGarbageCollection>true</ServerGarbageCollection>
</PropertyGroup>
<ItemGroup>
  <!-- HeapCount has no MSBuild property of its own -->
  <RuntimeHostConfigurationOption Include="System.GC.HeapCount" Value="4" />
</ItemGroup>
cards.deep:
The DOTNET_ prefix works since .NET 6; the old COMPlus_ is still understood. Watch the casing of names: DOTNET_gcServer and DOTNET_gcConcurrent start lowercase, the rest are DOTNET_GCHeapCount, DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit. Write the names exactly as the documentation does.

There is also runtimeconfig.template.json in the project folder: the SDK merges its configProperties into the final file at build time. You can check the result in-process with GC.GetConfigurationVariables().

cards.q: The Dockerfile says ENV DOTNET_GCHeapCount=16, Server GC is on, DATAS untouched. How many heaps will the collector get on a 32-core machine?
options: The heap count will vary: DATAS
cards.explain: Numbers in environment variables are hexadecimal: 0x16 = 22. To get 16 heaps, write DOTNET_GCHeapCount=10 or 0x10. And since the heap count is set explicitly, DATAS is off.

wrong.1: 16 would be right in runtimeconfig.json, where numbers are decimal. In the environment the same value is read as hex.
wrong.3: An explicit HeapCount turns DATAS off: the heap count is fixed.

cards.title: Knobs that hold memory in check
cards.body:
• System.GC.HeapHardLimit — a ceiling in bytes for the heap and the GC's own bookkeeping. On reaching it, the collector tries to free space, and if it cannot — OutOfMemoryException. The percentage-of-memory variant is HeapHardLimitPercent. 64-bit processes only.
  • System.GC.HeapCount — how many heaps Server GC uses. No effect on Workstation.
  • System.GC.ConserveMemory — 0 to 9 (.NET 6+): the higher it is, the more often the collector compacts the heap to save memory, including the LOH. The price is more collections and pauses.
  • System.GC.RetainVM — do not give freed memory back to the OS right away, keep it in reserve. Helps when the heap keeps growing and shrinking: fewer calls to the OS. The price is that the process looks "fat" for longer.
cards.deep:
There are per-heap limits too: HeapHardLimitSOH, HeapHardLimitLOH, HeapHardLimitPOH (.NET 5+). If any of them is set, the overall HeapHardLimit is ignored.

Another useful knob is System.GC.HighMemoryPercent: at what physical memory load the collector switches to aggressive compacting collections (90% by default). A small process on a big machine raises it; a large one, on the contrary, is made to react sooner.

cards.q: Match the setting with what it does
pairs: How many heaps Server GC uses
Save memory at the cost of frequent compaction, 0–9
Do not return freed memory to the OS right away

cards.q: runtimeconfig.template.json: Server GC with four heaps. Fill in the names
cards.explain: In runtimeconfig the names are System.GC.Server and System.GC.HeapCount. gcServer and GCHeapCount are the tails of environment variables (DOTNET_gcServer), and ServerGarbageCollection is the MSBuild property.

cards.title: Containers: the GC sees the limits
cards.body:
In a container the machine is "big", but the process got a slice of it. The runtime reads the cgroup limits (v1 and v2) and treats them as its machine:

  • Memory limit. If it is set and HeapHardLimit is not, the heap ceiling is set automatically: 75% of the limit, but no less than 20 MB. The remaining quarter is for native memory, thread stacks, JIT code.
  • CPU limit. Environment.ProcessorCount accounts for the CPU quota, and Server GC creates as many heaps as there are allowed cores. With a one-core limit, Server GC does not turn on at all.

You can check what the collector sees from code:
cards.deep:
Then and now: before .NET Core 3.0, Server GC in a container with a small memory limit often went past it — heap sizes and budgets were computed for the whole machine, and the OOM killer took the container down. Since .NET Core 3.0 the collector understands the limits, and HeapHardLimit with its 75% default arrived. cgroup v2 support came in .NET 5.

The heap ceiling does not fully protect against the OOM killer: native allocations, stacks and buffers outside the heap are not counted. If there are many of them, lower the percentage with HeapHardLimitPercent.

cards.q: A container with a 512 MB memory limit, .NET 8, no GC settings. The app keeps accumulating live objects nonstop. What happens?
options: At about 384 MB of heap the collector hits the ceiling and throws OutOfMemoryException
The heap grows to 512 MB, then the OOM killer kills the process without an exception
The collector does not know the limit and grows up to the memory of the whole node
At about 256 MB: the default ceiling is half the limit
cards.explain: With a container limit set, the default heap ceiling is 75% of it: 384 MB out of 512. On reaching it and failing to free space with a collection, the runtime throws a managed OutOfMemoryException — visible in the logs, unlike a silent kill by the OOM killer.

wrong.1: The OOM killer is possible if a lot of memory goes outside the heap, but the collector itself stops the managed heap at 75% of the limit.
wrong.2: That used to happen before .NET Core 3.0. A modern runtime reads the cgroup limits.

cards.q: A Kubernetes pod: CPU limit 2, a 16-core node, .NET 8, Server GC, DATAS not enabled. How many heaps will the collector create?
cards.explain: The runtime accounts for the container's CPU quota: Environment.ProcessorCount returns 2, and Server GC creates two heaps. With a limit of 1, Workstation would run. On .NET 9 with DATAS, the collector would start with one heap and add more, up to two.

wrong.1: That would be the case without a limit: a heap per node core. The runtime does account for the CPU quota.
wrong.2: DATAS starts with one heap, and in .NET 8 it is off by default.

lessons.title: Final: GC modes
lessons.sub: Server and Workstation, background GC, latency, DATAS and settings

cards.q: A web API on Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web, .NET 9, GC settings untouched. The container runs with a CPU limit of one core. Which collector actually runs?
options: Workstation: with a single available core, Server GC does not turn on
Server with DATAS: that is what the Web SDK sets in .NET 9
Server with one heap and one GC thread
Server without DATAS: DATAS turns off on a single core
cards.explain: The Web SDK asks for Server GC, but the runtime turns it on only if the process has more than one logical processor available — counting the container's CPU quota. With one core, Workstation runs and GCSettings.IsServerGC returns False.

wrong.2: It looks similar in structure, but it is not Server: with one core the runtime picks the Workstation implementation right away.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: Foreground gen0 and gen1 collections can run during a background gen2 collection
LowLatency is silently not applied on Server GC
DOTNET_GCHeapCount=20 gives 20 heaps
Background GC does not compact gen2
GCSettings.IsServerGC can be switched before the first collection
cards.explain: Numbers in environment variables are hexadecimal: 0x20 = 32 heaps. IsServerGC is read-only — the mode is chosen at startup. The rest is true: foreground collections run during a BGC, LowLatency is ignored on Server without an exception, and a BGC only sweeps.

cards.q: Put the milestones in time order, earliest first
items: Concurrent GC: no ephemeral collections while it runs
Background GC for Workstation (.NET Framework 4)
Background GC for Server (.NET Framework 4.5)
HeapHardLimit and the 75% container ceiling (.NET Core 3.0)
DATAS opt-in (.NET 8)
DATAS on by default for Server GC (.NET 9)
cards.explain: First concurrent GC, then background GC — for Workstation first, then for Server. .NET Core 3.0 taught the collector about container limits, and DATAS arrived in .NET 8 and became the default in .NET 9.

cards.q: This is code from a Server GC service. Which line silently fails to do what the author intended?
cards.explain: LowLatency applies only to Workstation GC. On Server the assignment changes nothing and throws no exception. Server needs SustainedLowLatency — with background GC on.

cards.q: Match the situation with the right knob
pairs: Forty small services on one machine
Batch processing, nobody cares about pauses
An hour of trading with no blocking full collections
The heap keeps growing and shrinking, many calls to the OS

cards.q: Dockerfile: Server GC and a 200 MiB heap ceiling (209715200 bytes). Fill in the values
cards.code:
ENV DOTNET_gcServer=___
ENV DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit=___
cards.explain: Boolean environment variables take 0 or 1, and numbers are read as hexadecimal: 209715200 = 0xC800000. The decimal 209715200 belongs only in runtimeconfig.json.

cards.q: A background gen2 collection is in progress, and the gen0 budget runs out. What happens?
options: A foreground gen0 collection runs: all managed threads, including the background GC thread, briefly stop
Allocating threads wait for the background collection to finish
The background collection is aborted and restarts as a blocking one
New objects go straight into gen2
cards.explain: That is the whole point of background GC: ephemeral collections can run while it is going. The background thread yields, the foreground collection runs, then the background one continues from where it left off.

wrong.1: That is how the old concurrent GC worked in .NET Framework 3.5 and earlier. Background GC lifted that restriction.

cards.q: Which of these can be changed while the process runs, without a restart?
options: GCSettings.LatencyMode
System.GC.Server
System.GC.Concurrent
DOTNET_GCHeapCount
cards.explain: The runtime reads runtimeconfig.json settings and environment variables once, when the collector initializes. The latency mode is the only one here that changes from code on the fly.

wrong.3: You can change the variable, but the process already read it at startup — it will not see the change.

units.title: Object lifetime
units.blurb: Finalization inside out: two queues, the finalizer thread, resurrection and SuppressFinalize. SafeHandle and critical finalizers, weak references and GCHandle, ConditionalWeakTable and leaks through closures, statics and timers.

lessons.title: Finalization inside out
lessons.sub: Two queues, the finalizer thread and the extra collection

cards.title: The bookkeeping starts at new
cards.body:
You already know from ".NET inside out" that a finalizer is a fallback and costs an extra collection. Now let us see how it works.

A type with a finalizer is a type that overrides Object.Finalize (in C#, the ~Name() syntax). Object.Finalize itself is empty, and the runtime ignores it.

When an object of such a type is created, the runtime immediately records a reference to it in the finalization queue. This is not a queue of dead objects: it holds every live object whose finalizer will have to run some day. The record is made on every new, even if the object is later released properly through Dispose.
cards.deep:
Because of the registration, allocating such an object does not take the fastest path: for types with a finalizer the JIT usually picks the general allocation helper instead of the inline pointer bump.

In CoreCLR both queues are a single array inside the collector (the CFinalize class in gc.cpp), split into segments: per generation for registered objects, plus separate segments for those already ready for finalization. In a dump the SOS command !finalizequeue shows them: how many objects are registered in each generation and how many are "Ready for finalization".

cards.q: Which of these objects get a finalization queue entry when created? Select all.
options: new A()
new B()
new C()
new string('x', 3)
cards.explain: B inherits the finalizer from A: what matters to the runtime is that Finalize is overridden somewhere in the chain. IDisposable has nothing to do with finalization: it is just an interface with a method. string has no finalizer.

cards.title: What a collection does: the second queue
cards.body:
A garbage collection goes like this:

  • the GC marks everything it reaches from the roots;
  • then it scans the finalization queue. Entries for unmarked objects move to another queue, the f-reachable queue (ready for finalization);
  • this second queue is a root. The GC marks again: the objects themselves and everything they reference;
  • whatever is marked survives and is promoted to the next generation, like any live object;
  • the GC wakes the finalizer thread.

The result: an object that is already dead to your program is "alive" again for this collection, along with its whole graph.
cards.deep:
The f in the name stands for finalization: the object is reachable only through this queue. While it sits there, it is a root for everything it references.

Without a dump you can check GC.GetGCMemoryInfo().FinalizationPendingCount: how many objects the last collection sent to finalization.

cards.task: F has a finalizer and holds Child, which has none. Null out f and get both removed. Watch which generation Child ends up in.

cards.q: Put the life of a finalizable object in order
items: new: an entry in the finalization queue
The last reference from the program goes away
A collection moves the entry to the f-reachable queue and marks the object graph
The finalizer thread calls Finalize
The next collection of its generation frees the memory
cards.explain: Between "became garbage" and "memory is free" there are at least two collections and a call on a separate thread. And after the first collection the object is already in an older generation, so the second one has to collect that generation.

cards.title: The cost: the whole graph gets promoted
cards.body:
The expensive part is not calling the finalizer but promotion. An object in Gen 0 moves to Gen 1 after the first collection, and a Gen 0 collection can no longer free it. If it does not make it to a Gen 1 collection, it moves to Gen 2 and waits for a full one.

Everything it references goes along: buffers, lists, strings. Hence the rule: a finalizable object should be small and a leaf. Keep only the handle in it, and big data in a class without a finalizer. That is exactly how SafeHandle is built: it holds just the handle number and a counter.

cards.q: A Bitmap class holds a 64 KB byte[] in a field and has its own finalizer that frees a native texture. What happens when a forgotten Bitmap becomes garbage?
options: The array survives at least one more collection and most likely moves to an older generation along with Bitmap
The array is freed right away: it has no finalizer of its own
The array is freed, and Bitmap stays until its finalizer runs
The GC removes the array before the finalizer runs to save memory
cards.explain: Bitmap in the f-reachable queue is a root, and the array is reachable through it, so it survives and gets promoted. Had the array been over 85,000 bytes, it would be in the LOH and wait for a full collection anyway. Better to move the texture into a small SafeHandle and drop the finalizer from Bitmap.

wrong.1: It does not need a finalizer to survive: it is referenced by an object that is currently a root.
wrong.3: The collector does not break references: a finalizer is allowed to read its own object's fields.

cards.title: One finalizer thread per process
cards.body:
All finalizers are called by one dedicated thread with raised priority. It takes entries from the f-reachable queue one at a time and calls Finalize. Three consequences:

  • a finalizer runs not on the thread that created the object: no SynchronizationContext, no UI;
  • if a finalizer hangs (waiting for a lock, a task's .Result, the network), the whole queue stops. Objects pile up in it, and memory grows for no visible reason;
  • an unhandled exception in a finalizer crashes the process, like on any other thread.

GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers() blocks the calling thread until the queue is empty. Useful in tests and measurements, almost never in production code.
cards.deep:
A growing queue shows up in FinalizationPendingCount and in a dump: lots of "Ready for finalization" while the finalizer thread's stack sits in a wait. The .NET Framework classic is a COM wrapper finalizer that needs an STA thread busy with something else.

The rule for a finalizer: nothing longer than a couple of system calls, no locks, no waits, no touching other managed objects.

cards.q: A service slowly grows in memory. The dump shows thousands of objects "Ready for finalization", and the finalizer thread is stuck in Monitor.Enter. What is going on?
options: One finalizer is waiting for a lock, and the whole finalization queue is stalled
The GC cannot keep up, Server GC is needed
Finalizers run in parallel and get in each other's way
The objects were resurrected and are never freed again
cards.explain: There is only one finalizer thread. While it waits in Monitor.Enter, nobody calls the other finalizers, so the objects and their graphs just hang in memory. The fix is in the finalizer: no locks and no waits inside.

cards.title: Order is not guaranteed
cards.body:
Say A references B, both have finalizers, and both became garbage in the same collection. Both go to the f-reachable queue, and the finalizer thread calls them in any order. The reference graph does not set the order.

So inside ~A the object B is still in memory (A holds it), but its finalizer may have already run: the file is closed, the buffer flushed, the native memory freed. Touching it means an ObjectDisposedException or, worse, working with a released resource.

The rule from ".NET inside out" follows from this: in a finalizer, touch only your own unmanaged resource.

cards.q: In the example above A and B became garbage at the same time. What is guaranteed while ~A runs?
options: The _b object is still in memory, but its finalizer may have already run
_b is null: the collector clears references to dead objects
~B runs strictly after ~A, since A references B
The _b object is already freed, touching it is an AccessViolation
cards.explain: While A is in the f-reachable queue, it is a root for B, so B's memory is intact. But the finalizer queue keeps no order. Only CriticalFinalizerObject has a weak ordering guarantee; more on it in the next lesson.

cards.title: Process exit: then and now
cards.body:
.NET Framework, on a normal process shutdown, ran the finalizers of the remaining objects (with a time limit).

.NET Core and .NET 5+ do not: finalizers are not called on exit. An object that flushed its buffer to a file only in the finalizer simply loses the data on exit.

What to do: release explicitly (using, Dispose), and for "at the very end" logic subscribe to AppDomain.CurrentDomain.ProcessExit or, in a hosted app, to IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping. The OS closes the process handles itself, but it will not flush your buffers for you.

cards.q: What is true about finalizers in .NET 8? Select all.
options: A finalizer runs on a different thread than the one that created the object
An unhandled exception in a finalizer terminates the process
On a normal process exit, the finalizers of the remaining objects are called
If A references B, the finalizer of A runs before the finalizer of B
cards.explain: Finalizers are called by a dedicated thread, and an exception on it crashes the process. On process exit .NET Core and later do not run finalizers; only .NET Framework did. Order between objects is not guaranteed.

lessons.title: Resurrection and SafeHandle
lessons.sub: ReRegisterForFinalize, SuppressFinalize, critical finalizers

cards.title: Resurrection
cards.body:
A finalizer is an ordinary method, and this inside it is an ordinary reference. Store it in a static field, and the object is reachable from a root again. This is resurrection.

What happens then:

  • the memory is not freed: the object lives on, now in an older generation;
  • its entry has left the queues, so the finalizer will not be called a second time;
  • the objects it references may already be finalized (order is not guaranteed), so a resurrected object can be half torn down.

cards.q: A Zombie object was resurrected through Last. Later Zombie.Last = null ran. What happens at the next collection of its generation?
options: The memory is freed, the finalizer is not called
The finalizer is called again, and the object is resurrected again
The object stays in memory forever: the GC leaves resurrected objects alone
The process crashes: access to a finalized object
cards.explain: The finalizer has already run, and there is no entry in the finalization queue anymore. To the collector it is an ordinary object without a finalizer: unreachable means freed.

wrong.1: For a second call the object has to be registered again through GC.ReRegisterForFinalize, and Zombie does not do that.

cards.title: GC.ReRegisterForFinalize
cards.body:
GC.ReRegisterForFinalize(obj) turns finalization back on: when the object becomes garbage again, the finalizer is called once more.

Together with resurrection this gives a "finalizer-based pool": in the finalizer the object returns itself to the pool and re-registers. Sounds thrifty, but in practice it is the worst kind of pool:

  • the object comes back only after a collection and a call on another thread, at an unknown moment;
  • every round promotes it and everything it references;
  • its fields may point at objects that are already finalized.

Pools are built explicitly: ArrayPool<T>, ObjectPool<T> and returning in Dispose.
cards.deep: In CoreCLR GC.SuppressFinalize sets a bit in the object header, and ReRegisterForFinalize clears it; if the queue entry is already gone (the finalizer has run), the runtime registers the object again. Hence a subtlety: re-registering "just in case" on a live object that still has its entry can produce a second entry and a double finalizer call. Call it only together with resurrection or after SuppressFinalize.

cards.q: Which line resurrects the object?
cards.explain: Pool.Add(this) puts the reference into a static collection, so the object is reachable from a root again. The next line resurrects nothing: it just turns the finalizer back on so the object returns to the pool next time too.

cards.title: SuppressFinalize: what it saves
cards.body:
The Dispose pattern ends with a call to GC.SuppressFinalize(this). The resource is already released, the finalizer is not needed.

The finalization queue entry stays: the registration at new is already paid for. But the object is flagged, and when a collection finds it dead, it does not move it to the f-reachable queue but frees it right away. The savings: no call on the finalizer thread, no extra collection, no promoted graph.

Conclusion: a finalizer plus Dispose with SuppressFinalize is still more expensive than no finalizer at all. That is why a class holding a SafeHandle does not need a finalizer of its own.

cards.q: In a class with a finalizer, Dispose releases the resource, but GC.SuppressFinalize was forgotten. The user dutifully calls Dispose. What do we lose?
options: Every object still goes through the f-reachable queue: an extra collection, promotion and a finalizer call
Nothing: the GC can see Dispose was already called
The resource is released twice and the process crashes
The object is never freed
cards.explain: The collector knows nothing about IDisposable. Without SuppressFinalize the object is an ordinary finalizable one to it. If Dispose(false) is idempotent, there is no harm beyond the cost, but the cost is everything from the previous lesson.

wrong.2: If the finalizer checks an "already released" flag, there is no second release. The loss is in performance.

cards.title: Why a bare IntPtr is not enough
cards.body:
A class keeps a handle in an IntPtr field and closes it in the finalizer. The Read method reads _h and passes the number to a native call. After the field is read, this is no longer used, and the JIT considers it dead.

If there are no other references, a collection can happen in the middle of the native call: the object is unreachable, the finalizer closes the handle, and Read is still using it. The old cure is GC.KeepAlive(this) after the call.

SafeHandle handles this itself: the wrapper object itself is passed to the call, the marshaller keeps it alive, increments its reference count before the call (DangerousAddRef) and decrements it after. Dispose in the middle of a call only marks the handle as closed, and ReleaseHandle runs on the last Release, exactly once.
cards.deep:
Another hole SafeHandle plugs: P/Invoke returned a handle, but it was not wrapped in time, because an exception happened between the return and creating the wrapper. For a returned SafeHandle the marshaller creates the wrapper object before the call, and after the call it only stores the number into it. That is why a derived class needs a parameterless constructor.

The counter and the "closed" and "disposed" flags live in one integer field, _state, and change through Interlocked. DangerousAddRef and DangerousGetHandle are available to you too, for when you need to pass the number to code the marshaller cannot see. Then DangerousRelease in a finally is mandatory.

cards.q: Once in a while Read returns an "invalid handle" error. Why?
options: After _h is read nobody needs the Device object: a collection during Native.Read runs the finalizer, which closes the handle
The finalizer is called before the constructor
IntPtr gets boxed, and Read receives a copy
Native.Open is called on the finalizer thread
cards.explain: The JIT tracks reference lifetimes up to their last use. this is used only to read the field; after that the object can become garbage even while its method is on the stack. The cure is SafeHandle instead of IntPtr, or GC.KeepAlive(this) after the native call.

cards.title: CriticalFinalizerObject: then and now
cards.body:
SafeHandle derives from CriticalFinalizerObject. What this gives you now: if ordinary and critical objects became garbage in the same collection, the runtime first calls all the ordinary finalizers, then the critical ones. So a wrapper class finalizer can still flush its buffer through its SafeHandle: the handle itself is closed later.

Back then, in .NET Framework, "critical" meant more. The finalizer code was compiled ahead of time (CER, constrained execution regions) so it could not fail for lack of memory for the JIT, and it ran even on a rude AppDomain unload and thread abort. .NET Core has neither Thread.Abort nor AppDomain unloading, and CERs are not supported. What remains is the ordering guarantee and SafeHandle itself.
cards.deep: In the CoreCLR collector, critical finalizers sit in the queue as a separate segment, which is where the order comes from. The guarantee is weak: it covers only objects that died in the same collection. If the wrapper survived a collection while the SafeHandle died earlier (nobody else referenced it), the order is different.

cards.q: Match the method to what it does
pairs: A collection frees the object without calling the finalizer
The finalizer is called again when the object becomes garbage
The object is reachable at least up to this line
Wait until the finalizer thread drains the queue
The handle is not closed until the matching Release

cards.title: Your own SafeHandle
cards.body:
For a native resource without a ready-made wrapper, write your own SafeHandle. Most often you derive from SafeHandleZeroOrMinusOneIsInvalid: it already has IsInvalid for the values 0 and -1.

One thing is left: ReleaseHandle. The runtime calls it exactly once, from Dispose or from the critical finalizer. Inside: only closing the handle, no exceptions, locks or touching other objects. Return true if the release succeeded.

cards.q: Complete the wrapper for a native handle
cards.explain: The base class provides IsInvalid, the reference count and the critical finalizer, and the constructor with ownsHandle comes from it. Only ReleaseHandle is overridden: Dispose and the finalizer are already written in SafeHandle and will call it once.

lessons.title: Weak references and leaks
lessons.sub: WeakReference, GCHandle, ConditionalWeakTable and who holds an object

cards.title: WeakReference<T>: a reference that does not hold
cards.body:
An ordinary reference from a live object makes its target reachable. A weak reference lets you get to the object but does not help it live: if there are no other paths from the roots, a collection frees it, and the weak reference goes empty.

You use it in two steps: TryGetTarget hands out an ordinary reference, and while you hold it in a variable, the object is alive.

Under the hood WeakReference<T> is a heap object plus an entry in the collector's handle table. The GC checks every such entry on every collection, so a million weak references cost both memory and pause time.

cards.q: What is wrong with this code on the non-generic WeakReference?
