options: A collection can happen between IsAlive and Target: Target returns null, and Print crashes
IsAlive itself extends the object's life, so it is never collected
Target throws an exception if the object was already collected
Nothing: after the IsAlive check the object is guaranteed to be alive
cards.explain: A collection can happen on any thread between two lines. Get a strong reference first, then check it. It is no accident that WeakReference<T> has only TryGetTarget and no IsAlive or Target.

wrong.2: Target does not throw: it returns null. It is the next line that crashes.

cards.title: Short and long
cards.body:
The constructor takes trackResurrection. Recall the collection order from the first lesson; weak references fit into it:

  • a short one (the default) is cleared as soon as the object is unreachable, before it moves to the f-reachable queue;
  • a long one (trackResurrection: true) is cleared only when the object is really freed, after finalization, if it was not resurrected.

For an object without a finalizer there is no difference. With a finalizer, a long reference can return an object whose finalizer has already run, and you get it in an unpredictable state. You rarely need one.
cards.code:
var shortRef = new WeakReference<Conn>(c);
var longRef  = new WeakReference<Conn>(c, trackResurrection: true);

cards.q: Conn has a finalizer. A collection ran, the finalizer has not been called yet. What do the references return?
options: shortRef is empty, longRef still returns the object
Both are empty
Both still return the object
shortRef returns the object, longRef is empty
cards.explain: The collector clears short weak references before it rescues finalizable objects, and long ones after. The object in the f-reachable queue is marked live, so the long reference still sees it. And by taking it through TryGetTarget you effectively resurrect it.

cards.title: GCHandle: four kinds
cards.body:
A weak reference is a special case of a GC handle. You can create them directly with GCHandle.Alloc:

  • Weak and WeakTrackResurrection: short and long weak;
  • Normal: strong, keeps the object alive even with no ordinary reference to it. This is how a managed object is passed to native code as a "context" through GCHandle.ToIntPtr;
  • Pinned: strong and also forbids moving the object during compaction. Only for objects with no managed references inside.

A handle is an unmanaged resource. Forget Free and the object lives forever, and a pinned one also punches a hole in the heap.
cards.deep:
For short pinning during a call, fixed is cheaper: it creates no handle, it just marks a local variable for the GC. Long-lived pinned buffers are better allocated straight in the POH since .NET 5 (GC.AllocateArray<T>(n, pinned: true)). More in the "Advanced" unit.

.NET 10 added typed wrappers GCHandle<T>, PinnedGCHandle<T> and WeakGCHandle<T>: they implement IDisposable and keep you from mixing up handle kinds.

cards.q: Match the handle kind to its behavior
pairs: Keeps the object alive, but the GC may move it
Keeps it alive and forbids moving
Goes empty as soon as the object is unreachable
Goes empty when the object is freed after finalization
Holds the value while the key is alive

cards.title: ConditionalWeakTable: an ephemeron
cards.body:
You need to attach data to someone else's objects, say metadata to widgets created by code you do not own. An ordinary dictionary keeps the keys forever. A dictionary with weak keys does not help either: if the value references the key, the dictionary holds the value, and the value holds the key.

ConditionalWeakTable<TKey, TValue> works differently: the key is weak, and the value lives exactly as long as the key, and references from the value to the key do not keep it alive. Such a pair is called an ephemeron. Keys are compared by reference, Equals is not called. The table is thread-safe.
cards.deep:
Each entry is a dependent handle: the primary object is weak, the secondary is reachable only if the primary is. Since .NET 6 it is available directly as DependentHandle. The cost: during marking the collector walks dependent handles repeatedly while new live objects keep turning up, so thousands of entries noticeably lengthen a collection.

This is not a cache: a value is not evicted under memory pressure, it lives as long as its key. For a cache use MemoryCache with a size limit.

cards.q: Metadata is stored in a Dictionary<WeakReference<Widget>, Meta>, and Meta holds a reference to its Widget. What is wrong with that?
options: The dictionary holds Meta, Meta holds Widget: the weak key solves nothing, the widgets are never freed
WeakReference cannot be a dictionary key: it does not compile
Weak keys are cleared at the next Gen 0 collection even if the widget is alive
Nothing, this is exactly how ConditionalWeakTable works
cards.explain: The path from the root: static dictionary → Meta → Widget. While a strong path exists, the weak reference does not go empty. ConditionalWeakTable solves this with a dependent handle: Meta is reachable only through a live Widget.

wrong.2: A weak reference goes empty only when the object is unreachable. It will not let go of a live widget.

cards.title: Leaks: events and closures
cards.body:
A leak in .NET is always a path from a root to an object nobody needs. The usual suspects were listed in the "How to measure" unit; here is the mechanism of the two least obvious ones. The first is closures.

All lambdas of one method that capture variables of the same scope share one closure object (a display class): the compiler puts all captured variables into it as fields. A lambda that needs only id also holds a megabyte-sized big if a neighboring lambda captured it.

One more thing: a subscription with a lambda e += () => ... cannot be undone unless the delegate is saved in a variable: a new lambda gives a different delegate, and -= finds nothing.
cards.deep:
For events of long-lived publishers there are "weak events": the subscription holds the subscriber through a weak reference (WeakEventManager in WPF, WeakReferenceMessenger in CommunityToolkit.Mvvm). The cost is extra handles and the fact that unsubscribing happens only after a collection.

A dump helps find the path that holds an object, as in the "How to measure" unit: the chain from a root to the object is the answer.

cards.q: The handler in the static Bus uses only id. What does it keep in memory?
options: A closure object with fields id and big: the array lives as long as the subscription
Just a copy of id: each lambda captures its own variables
Nothing: the lambda does not use this, so it is static
The object Start was running on
cards.explain: big and id are parameters of the same scope, the compiler puts them into one display class, and both lambdas are its methods. The delegate in Bus references that whole object. The fix is splitting into separate methods or copying what you need into a separate local in a nested scope.

wrong.3: Start is static: it has no this, so only big and id get into the closure.

cards.title: Statics, caches and timers
cards.body:
The second non-obvious one is the timer, but first the obvious. A static collection is a root. Whatever you put in and never remove lives until the process ends. Especially sneaky are "caches" on a static Dictionary without eviction: memory grows with every new key. If you need a cache, take MemoryCache with entry expiration and a SizeLimit.

A timer has a catch both ways. System.Threading.Timer registers in a static timer queue, and the queue holds the callback, and through it the object whose method it calls. If that object keeps the timer in its own field, it will not die until Dispose is called.

The flip side: the queue does not reference the Timer object itself. If you did not store it anywhere, it can be collected and stop firing.

cards.q: Which of these keep an object alive indefinitely? Select all.
options: Its method is subscribed to a static event, never unsubscribed
It is a value in a static Dictionary nobody removes anything from
A System.Threading.Timer in its field calls its method, Dispose is never called
It is a value in a ConditionalWeakTable whose key is already unreachable
A WeakReference<T> in a static list points to it
cards.explain: The first three are strong paths from a root: a static event, a static collection, the timer queue through the callback. A value in a ConditionalWeakTable lives as long as its key, and a weak reference holds nothing, although the WeakReference objects themselves in an ever-growing static list are a leak too.

cards.q: The timer is created and not stored anywhere. What can happen?
options: After some garbage collection the timer may stop firing
The timer fires forever: the timer queue holds it
It does not compile: the result of new must be assigned
The timer fires once and stops
cards.explain: The queue holds the timer's internal object and the callback, but not the Timer itself. When the Timer is collected, the finalizer of its internal object stops the timer. The documentation explicitly says to keep a reference to the Timer for as long as you need it.

lessons.title: Final: object lifetime
lessons.sub: Finalization queues, weak references and leaks

cards.task: Owner has no finalizer and holds a small Handle that has one. Null out o and free both. Which of them dies first?

cards.q: Put the steps of a single collection in order
items: Mark everything reachable from the roots
Clear short weak references to unmarked objects
Move unmarked finalizable objects to the f-reachable queue
Mark everything reachable from the f-reachable queue
Clear long weak references to still unmarked objects
cards.explain: Short weak references go empty before finalizable objects are rescued, long ones after. That is why a long reference still sees an object waiting for its finalizer.

cards.q: An object has no finalizer. A short and a long weak reference point to it, no strong references. What after a collection of its generation?
options: Both are empty
The short one is empty, the long one still returns the object
Both return the object until the finalizer is called
The long one holds the object until it is freed
cards.explain: Without a finalizer the object does not go to the f-reachable queue, nobody "rescues" it, and by the long-reference step it is still unmarked. Short and long differ only for finalizable objects.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: After GC.SuppressFinalize the finalization queue entry stays, but a collection skips it
A resurrected object is finalized again automatically when it dies next time
An object referenced by finalizable garbage survives the same collection and gets promoted
Critical finalizers are called before ordinary ones
cards.explain: For the finalizer to be called again you need GC.ReRegisterForFinalize. Critical finalizers run after ordinary ones among objects that died in the same collection, so a wrapper can still use its SafeHandle.

cards.q: Dispose is called on the sessions, yet memory keeps growing. Which line holds the closed sessions?
cards.explain: Dispose stops the timer, and the timer queue lets go of the callback. But the static All list is a root, and nobody removes sessions from it. Dispose should also do All.Remove(this).

cards.q: Match the leak source to the cure
pairs: A cache on a static Dictionary
Data attached to someone else's objects
A lambda captured an extra big array
Split the captures into different scopes

cards.q: Attach metadata to widgets so that it dies together with the widget
cards.code:
static readonly ___<Widget, Meta> _meta = new();

Meta MetaOf(Widget w) => _meta.___(w, _ => new Meta(w));
cards.explain: GetValue finds the value or creates it with the factory, atomically. The key is weak, and the value lives while the widget lives, even if Meta references it.

cards.q: A service moves from .NET Framework 4.8 to .NET 8. The logger flushed the tail of its buffer in its finalizer on exit. What changes?
options: The last entries start getting lost: finalizers are not called on exit
Nothing: finalizers work the same way
The tail is written twice: the finalizer runs both on exit and on collection
The process hangs on exit waiting for the finalizer thread
cards.explain: In .NET Core and later, finalizers do not run when the process terminates. The buffer must be flushed explicitly: Dispose, ProcessExit or ApplicationStopping.

cards.q: A Writer with an ordinary finalizer flushes its buffer through its own SafeFileHandle. Both became garbage in the same collection. Why is the handle still open at flush time?
options: SafeHandle is a CriticalFinalizerObject: among objects that died together, its finalizer runs after the ordinary ones
Writer references the SafeHandle, so the latter is finalized later
SafeHandle is never finalized, only Dispose closes it
The OS closes the handle on process exit
cards.explain: A reference between objects does not set the finalization order. Order comes only from the split into ordinary and critical finalizers, and only for objects that died in the same collection.

wrong.1: The reference graph does not affect order: both go to the f-reachable queue together.

units.blurb: Pinning and the pinned object heap, unsafe code, pointers and native memory, no-GC regions and the collector API, and what changes in memory under Native AOT without a JIT. The course final.

lessons.title: Pinning and the POH
lessons.sub: fixed, GCHandle, Memory.Pin and the pinned object heap

cards.title: Why stop the collector from moving an object
cards.body:
During compaction the collector slides surviving objects and rewrites every reference to them. Managed code never notices: references are updated and everything works.

But native code — an OS function, a C library, a network card driver — holds a raw address. The collector cannot see it and will not update it. If the object has moved, native code writes its data over someone else’s object.

So before handing an address out, you pin the object: you tell the collector "do not move this one". A pinned object stays put until the pin is released.
cards.deep: The P/Invoke marshaller pins blittable arrays and strings by itself for the duration of a synchronous call — you write nothing extra. The trouble starts when native code remembers the address for longer than one call: asynchronous I/O, callbacks, driver ring buffers. Then the lifetime of the pin is your job.

cards.title: fixed: a pin for the length of a block
cards.body:
The cheapest way is the fixed statement in unsafe code. It gives you a pointer to the data and pins the object until the end of the block.

The mechanism: the compiler puts the reference into a local variable marked pinned. There is no runtime call at all. Only if a collection happens during the block does the collector, walking the stack, see the mark and leave the object in place.

The cost is close to zero when no collection happened. The limitation: the pointer is valid only inside the block; after the } the object may move again.
cards.deep:
In IL this is a local like uint8& pinned: a managed pointer to the first element. The JIT records in the method’s GC info that the slot is pinned, and the collector learns it while walking frames. For string, Span<T> and your own types, fixed works through the GetPinnableReference() pattern (C# 7.3).

If the array is empty or null, fixed gives a null pointer rather than an exception.

cards.q: The method keeps the pointer it got from fixed. Which line writes to where the array may no longer be?
cards.explain: Copying the pointer inside the block is allowed, but after leaving fixed there is no pin. A compacting collection may move data, and the write through saved corrupts someone else’s memory. The compiler does not catch it: to the compiler a pointer is just a number.

cards.title: GCHandle: a pin without a scope
cards.body:
When you need the address for longer than one method, use GCHandle.Alloc(obj, GCHandleType.Pinned). The runtime creates an entry in the handle table: the collector walks it as roots and does not move pinned objects.

  • AddrOfPinnedObject() returns the address of the data;
  • the pin holds until you call Free(). Forget it and the object is pinned forever and never collected;
  • you can only pin an object without references inside: an array of primitives, a string, a class made of numbers. Otherwise — ArgumentException.
cards.deep:
The rule comes from marshalling: only blittable data, which looks the same in the native world, is handed out. References inside an object are useless to native code, and writing to them behind the write barrier’s back would break the collector’s bookkeeping. So the runtime checks the type when pinning.

.NET 10 added typed wrappers GCHandle<T>, PinnedGCHandle<T> and WeakGCHandle<T> with Dispose instead of Free — handy to keep in a using.

cards.q: What does this code do?
cards.code:
var list = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };
var h = GCHandle.Alloc(list, GCHandleType.Pinned);
options: Throws ArgumentException
Pins the list and its inner array
Pins only the List<int> object
Does not compile
cards.explain: List<int> holds a reference to its _items array, and objects with references cannot be pinned. You can pin the int[] itself — but the list will replace it with a new one when it grows.

wrong.1: Pinning does not follow references: each object is pinned on its own.
wrong.3: The signature takes object; the compiler does not check whether it can be pinned — the runtime does.

cards.title: Memory<T>.Pin: pinning for async
cards.body:
Span<T> lives only on the stack and cannot cross an await. In async code a buffer travels as Memory<T>, and you get its address through Pin().

Pin() returns a MemoryHandle with a Pointer field. Until the handle is released with Dispose(), the data does not move. Under the hood, for an ordinary array it is the same GCHandle; for native memory there is nothing to pin, and Pin is almost free.
cards.deep: If the array already lives in the POH, an extra GCHandle is not needed: MemoryMarshal.CreateFromPinnedArray creates a Memory<T> flagged as "already pinned", and Pin() then just computes the address. For your own MemoryManager<T> you define what Pin does.

cards.q: Match the task with the way to pin
pairs: A pointer loop over an array inside one method
A native library keeps a buffer address between calls
A buffer for the whole lifetime of the process
A synchronous P/Invoke call with a byte[] array

cards.title: The cost: holes in the heap
cards.body:
Compaction slides survivors to the start, freeing one contiguous area. A pinned object stands like a rock: it cannot be moved, and a gap is left in front of it. Many such gaps add up to fragmentation.

  • free memory exists, but in pieces: new objects and allocation chunks do not always fit;
  • the heap takes more than the live data;
  • worst of all are many small pins scattered across generation 0: that is the generation the collector most wants to compact cleanly.

A short pin during which no collection happened costs nothing. Long pins on fresh objects are what hurts.
cards.deep: The collector fights back: gaps in front of pinned objects become free blocks used for new chunks, and pinned objects from a young generation may stay in it (demotion) instead of being dragged into gen 2. But that is a workaround. You can see the problem in GC.GetGCMemoryInfo(): the PinnedObjectsCount and FragmentedBytes fields, and in a dump with the SOS command !gchandles.

cards.q: A server creates a byte[8192] per connection and keeps it pinned while the connection is open (minutes). What is wrong with that?
options: Thousands of fresh pinned arrays riddle the young generations, and compaction cannot remove the holes
Pinned arrays are not freed even after Free
Every pin suspends all threads
Nothing: 8 KB is a small object
cards.explain: The buffers are born in generation 0 among other objects and stay pinned for a long time. Each one has a gap around it that compaction cannot close. The cure is a pool of buffers allocated up front, ideally in the POH.

wrong.2: Pinning itself is cheap: fixed is a mark on the stack, GCHandle is an entry in a table. Threads are suspended by a collection, not by a pin.

cards.title: The POH: a heap where nothing moves
cards.body:
Since .NET 5 the collector has a pinned object heap (POH). Objects in it never move, so they need no pinning and leave no holes in the SOH.

  • allocate an array with GC.AllocateArray<T>(length, pinned: true) or GC.AllocateUninitializedArray<T>(length, pinned: true) — without zeroing;
  • the POH is collected together with generation 2, that is, rarely;
  • allocating there is slower than usual: a free list instead of a pointer bump.

Takeaway: the POH is for long-lived buffers allocated once, such as a pool for sockets. Putting temporary arrays there is a bad idea.
cards.deep: Only arrays go to the POH. In .NET 5–7 the element type could not contain references (ArgumentException); .NET 8 lifted that restriction. Before the POH, pools of pinned buffers were made large (≥ 85,000 bytes) so they landed in the LOH, which is not compacted by default. Kestrel in ASP.NET Core keeps its memory blocks in the POH.

cards.q: Allocate the array straight in the pinned object heap
cards.code: byte[] ring = GC.___<byte>(1 << 20, pinned: ___);
cards.explain: GC.AllocateArray with pinned: true puts the array in the POH. With pinned: false it is an ordinary array in the SOH or LOH — like new byte[n].

cards.q: What is true about the POH? Select all.
options: The collector never moves objects in the POH
The POH is collected together with generation 2
Any object can go into the POH, not just arrays
Allocating in the POH is cheaper than in generation 0
The POH removes the SOH fragmentation that long pins would cause
cards.explain: The POH accepts only arrays via GC.AllocateArray and GC.AllocateUninitializedArray. Allocation there goes through a free list and costs more than a pointer bump, so the POH is for rare, long-lived buffers.

lessons.title: unsafe and pointers
lessons.sub: Pointers, native memory, Unsafe and MemoryMarshal

cards.title: What unsafe unlocks
cards.body:
The unsafe keyword unlocks pointers: T*, taking an address with &, dereferencing with *, -> and arithmetic. The project has to allow it explicitly: <AllowUnsafeBlocks>true</AllowUnsafeBlocks>.

A pointer can only point to an unmanaged type: numbers, bool, char, enums, other pointers and structs made of them. You cannot take a pointer to a class or a string.

What goes away: bounds checks, type checks and — most importantly — the collector’s involvement. To the GC a pointer is just a number.
cards.deep: unsafe does not change the IL much: pointer arithmetic is plain add and ldind/stind. What changes is that the code becomes unverifiable: memory safety is now your guarantee. In .NET Framework this mattered for partial trust (CAS); .NET Core has no partial trust, and unsafe is just a compiler flag.

cards.title: The collector sees ref, not pointers
cards.body:
.NET has two kinds of "address":

  • A managed pointer — ref T, and what sits inside a Span<T>. The JIT tells the collector where such references live. If the object moves, the collector updates even a reference into its middle. No pinning needed.
  • An unmanaged pointer — T*, nint, IntPtr. The collector knows nothing about it. You may hold one to a heap object only while the object is pinned.

Hence the rule: for managed memory use ref and Span. Pointers are for memory the collector does not move: the stack, stackalloc, native memory, the POH.
cards.deep: A pointer to an unpinned heap object is the classic "GC hole". The code works thousands of times until a compacting collection lands exactly between taking the address and writing through it. Such bugs barely reproduce under a debugger. To hunt them the runtime has a debug mode, GC Stress, which triggers a collection at every point where one is possible. It is used mostly by the CLR developers themselves.

cards.q: You need a local "address" of the fifth element of a heap array and to write through it. What is safe without pinning?
options: ref int
int*
IntPtr
nint
cards.explain: ref int is a managed pointer: the collector knows about it and moves it along with the array during compaction. int*, IntPtr and nint are just numbers; once the array moves they point to nowhere.

cards.title: NativeMemory: memory the collector never sees
cards.body:
Since .NET 6 native memory comes from NativeMemory: Alloc, AllocZeroed, Realloc, Free, and the aligned AlignedAlloc and AlignedFree. It is a thin wrapper over the C library’s malloc/free.

What matters:

  • the collector does not see this memory: it is not part of the heap size, and the GC will not free it;
  • forget Free and you have a leak that only private bytes reveals (as in the "How to measure" unit);
  • free it in a finally, or via a SafeHandle if the memory lives as long as an object.
cards.deep: Before .NET 6 people used Marshal.AllocHGlobal: LocalAlloc on Windows, malloc on Unix. .NET 7 added NativeMemory.Clear, Copy and Fill. When memory runs out, Alloc throws OutOfMemoryException rather than returning null. The most convenient way to work with such memory is through Span<T>: it puts bounds checks on top of the raw pointer.

cards.q: Take a native buffer and make sure it is returned
cards.explain: Alloc allocates, Free returns the memory to the C library heap. Clear only zeroes the bytes, Realloc resizes, and NativeMemory has no Release method.

cards.title: Unsafe: unsafe without the unsafe keyword
cards.body:
The System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe class does what pointers do, but through ref — and needs no unsafe in your code. The collector sees the references, but types and bounds are on you.

  • Unsafe.As<T>(object) — treat a reference as a reference to T without a type check;
  • Unsafe.Add(ref x, n) — move a ref by n elements without a bounds check;
  • Unsafe.SizeOf<T>(), ReadUnaligned, SkipInit;
  • Unsafe.BitCast<TFrom, TTo> (.NET 8) — reinterpret the bits of a value.
cards.deep: Unsafe methods are JIT intrinsics: most compile to one or two instructions or vanish entirely. In the CoreLib sources many of them have a stub body with the IL in a comment, and the JIT substitutes the real implementation. The .NET libraries use them heavily in the inner loops of Span, strings and collections.

cards.title: MemoryMarshal: Span without ceremony
cards.body:
System.Runtime.InteropServices.MemoryMarshal lifts the restrictions on Span:

  • GetReference(span) and GetArrayDataReference(array) — a ref to the first element with no bounds check;
  • Cast<TFrom, TTo>(span) — see bytes as ints or structs without copying;
  • AsBytes, Read<T>, Write<T> — read and write structs in a byte buffer;
  • CreateSpan(ref x, length) — make a Span from a single ref.

The typical case is parsing a binary format right in the buffer, with no copies and no allocations.
cards.deep: Cast and Read work only with types without references — otherwise ArgumentException: turning bytes into a reference would mean forging an object address. Byte order is the machine’s (little-endian on x64 and ARM64); for portable formats use BinaryPrimitives.ReadInt32LittleEndian. Unaligned reads work on x64 and ARM64.

cards.q: Match the API with what it does
pairs: A reference to another type, unchecked
Moves a ref without a bounds check
The same bytes as another type
Memory the collector does not see
A ref to the first array element

cards.title: How it ends
cards.body:
A bug in unsafe code rarely crashes right away. The typical story:

  • a write past the end of an array overwrites the header or type pointer of the neighbouring object;
  • the program keeps running — until the next collection;
  • during marking the collector follows the corrupted type pointer and crashes. The process dies with an internal CLR error, and the stack shows the GC, not your code.

So the rules are simple: unsafe code only in hot spots, after measuring; small isolated methods; tests at the boundaries; and Span with its checks wherever you can.
cards.deep: In a dump you hunt such corruption with the SOS command !verifyheap: it walks the heap and reports the first corrupted object. The neighbour right before it is the first suspect. Unsafe.As with the wrong type does the same more subtly: a virtual call through the "wrong" type pointer jumps through someone else’s method table.

cards.q: Which line holds the bug that makes the code write past the end of the array?
cards.explain: The condition i <= a.Length gives five iterations for four elements. Ordinary indexing would throw IndexOutOfRangeException, but Unsafe.Add silently writes the number into the memory after the array — most likely into the next object’s header.

cards.q: A loop was rewritten from a[i] to Unsafe.Add to remove bounds checks. The benchmark showed no difference. Why?
cards.code:
for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++)
    sum += a[i];
options: The JIT already removes the bounds check in a loop from 0 to a.Length
Unsafe.Add checks bounds too
Bounds checks only run in Debug
Adding to a long is slower than any check
cards.explain: The JIT proves that i is always within the array and emits no check (bounds check elimination). So a simple loop over an array or Span is already fast. Unsafe pays off where the JIT cannot prove it: strided walks, indices taken from another array.

wrong.2: Bounds checks exist in Release too: they are part of memory safety, not a debugging feature.

cards.q: When is unsafe code justified? Select all.
options: A hot loop where measurement showed that bounds checks cost noticeably
A buffer for a native library that the collector must not see
Parsing a binary protocol in a buffer without copying
To speed up any code "just in case"
To get around an InvalidCastException
cards.explain: Unsafe code is a tool for bottlenecks and for talking to the native world. Without a measurement it only adds risk, and Unsafe.As in place of an honest cast turns a clear exception into memory corruption.

lessons.title: The collector API
lessons.sub: GC, GCSettings, no-GC regions and memory pressure

cards.title: What you can ask and what you can request
cards.body:
The GC class is the collector’s control panel. Its methods fall into two groups.

Ask: CollectionCount(gen) — how many collections ran; GetGeneration(obj) — which generation an object is in; GetTotalAllocatedBytes() — how much was allocated in total; GetTotalPauseDuration() (.NET 7) — total pause time; GetGCMemoryInfo() — a snapshot of the last collection (as in the "How to measure" unit).

Request: Collect, AddMemoryPressure, TryStartNoGCRegion, RefreshMemoryLimit. You rarely need anything from this group: the collector tunes generation budgets to the load by itself, and interfering usually gets in the way.
cards.deep: CollectionCount(0) also counts collections of older generations: a gen 2 collection collects 0 and 1 too. So the number of "pure" gen 0 collections is CollectionCount(0) - CollectionCount(1). GetGeneration reports objects in the LOH and POH as generation 2, and objects outside the GC heap (such as string literals since .NET 8) as int.MaxValue.

cards.title: GC.Collect: why it almost always hurts
cards.body:
GC.Collect() with no arguments is a full blocking collection of all generations. What it does to the program:

  • a pause over the whole heap rather than the small generation 0;
  • young live objects get promoted to older generations too early and then linger there;
  • the statistics the collector uses to pick budgets get thrown off.

Where a call is justified: tests and benchmarks (to level the start), and once after loading big data at startup — then together with LOH compaction.
cards.deep: GCCollectionMode.Optimized leaves the decision to the collector: it may skip the collection if it deems it pointless. GCCollectionMode.Aggressive (.NET 7) is a collection that also returns as much memory as possible to the OS; it is meant for when the process goes into the background for a long time. CompactOnce resets to Default after the very first full blocking collection.

cards.q: An HTTP request handler calls GC.Collect() at the end "so garbage does not pile up". What happens under load?
options: A full blocking collection per request: pauses and latency go up
Memory shrinks with no side effects
Nothing: under Server GC GC.Collect is ignored
The collector collects only this request’s garbage
cards.explain: Each call is a full collection of the whole heap with threads suspended. At hundreds of requests per second the process will mostly be collecting garbage. The request’s garbage would go away in a cheap gen 0 collection anyway.

wrong.2: Collect works in any mode. Only GCCollectionMode.Optimized may ignore the request.
wrong.3: The collector does not know which object belonged to which request: it collects generations, not requests.

cards.title: GCSettings: the mode at run time
cards.body:
System.Runtime.GCSettings has three properties:

  • IsServerGC — read-only: which mode is actually running;
  • LatencyMode — the latency mode, changeable on the fly: Batch, Interactive, LowLatency, SustainedLowLatency. The NoGCRegion value is read-only — it reports a no-GC region;
  • LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode — compact the LOH on the next full collection.

What each latency mode means and when to pick which is covered in the "GC modes" unit. What matters here: these are process-wide settings; you change them for a short stretch and put them back.
cards.deep: LowLatency is available only with Workstation GC and suppresses gen 2 collections — for short stretches. SustainedLowLatency also works with Server GC but requires background GC: without it the mode does not take effect. When memory runs low, or on an explicit GC.Collect(2), the collector still does a full collection.

cards.title: A region with no collections
cards.body:
GC.TryStartNoGCRegion(totalSize) asks: "until I allocate totalSize bytes, do not collect". The mechanism:

  • the collector commits the needed memory up front, and if there is not enough, first runs a full blocking collection;
  • it returns true — the region has started, GCSettings.LatencyMode is NoGCRegion;
  • while allocations fit in the budget there are no collections at all;
  • GC.EndNoGCRegion() restores normal mode.

Overrunning the budget or an explicit GC.Collect silently ends the region with a collection. Then EndNoGCRegion throws InvalidOperationException.
cards.deep: The one-argument version reserves totalSize for both the SOH and the LOH — effectively twice as much. The (totalSize, lohSize) overload splits the budget explicitly. Too large a size gives ArgumentOutOfRangeException; before .NET 7, with segments, the SOH limit was the ephemeral segment size, and with regions it is much higher. Regions cannot nest: a second call throws InvalidOperationException. The budget covers the runtime’s own allocations and those of every thread in the process, not just yours.

cards.q: Put the life of a no-GC region in order
items: TryStartNoGCRegion: the collector checks whether there is enough memory
If not — a full blocking collection
Memory for the budget is committed, the method returns true
Critical code allocates without any collections
EndNoGCRegion: normal mode is back
cards.explain: The collection, if needed, happens before the region starts — that is the point: pay the pause up front, not in the middle of the critical section. If there still were not enough memory at step two, the method would return false.

cards.title: A callback and opting out of the full collection
cards.body:
Two add-ons for regions.

disallowFullBlockingGC: true — do not run a full collection on entry. If memory is short, the method returns false right away. The scenario: a node behind a load balancer answers "not ready", requests go to its neighbours, and the node collects on its own when there is no load.

GC.RegisterNoGCRegionCallback(totalSize, callback) (.NET 8) — invoke a delegate once totalSize bytes have been allocated in the region. It is a "budget running low" warning, not a way to extend the region. One callback per region; outside a region the call throws InvalidOperationException.
cards.deep: The callback does not run on the thread that crossed the threshold, nor at the moment it crosses: the runtime runs it later on one of its own threads (in CoreCLR, the finalizer thread). So it must not wait on anything and is no good for precise accounting. If totalSize exceeds the region’s budget, registration throws InvalidOperationException.

cards.q: Which line throws an exception?
cards.explain: GC.Collect inside a region does not throw: it runs a collection and thereby ends the region. The InvalidOperationException comes from EndNoGCRegion — the region already ended because of the induced collection. Checking GCSettings.LatencyMode before EndNoGCRegion would have prevented it.

cards.title: AddMemoryPressure: a small object, a lot of memory
cards.body:
A wrapper around a native resource weighs tens of bytes on the heap but holds megabytes — an image, a codec buffer. The collector sees only the tens of bytes and is in no hurry. The wrappers pile up in generation 2, their native memory is never freed, and the process grows.

GC.AddMemoryPressure(bytes) says: "this much native memory stands behind it". The collector takes it into account and may start a gen 2 collection sooner. Once the memory is freed — GC.RemoveMemoryPressure with the same number.
cards.deep: It is a hint, not accounting: the collector compares the added pressure with the size of the managed heap and, if the imbalance is large, triggers a collection itself. Calls must come in pairs — a forgotten Remove makes the collector collect more often than needed. If the resource is counted in units rather than bytes (OS handles), there is HandleCollector in System.Runtime.InteropServices.

cards.q: Tell the collector about a native buffer and remove the note when it is freed
cards.explain: An Add/Remove pair with the same number. Collect is not needed here: knowing about the native memory, the collector decides for itself when to collect.

cards.title: Configuration is read once at startup
cards.body:
The mode, the number of heaps and the hard heap limit are set in the project (<ServerGarbageCollection>), in runtimeconfig.json (System.GC.Server) or in an environment variable (DOTNET_gcServer). The collector reads them once, at initialization.

  • AppContext.GetData("System.GC.Server") shows what is written in runtimeconfig.json;
  • GC.GetConfigurationVariables() (.NET 7) — what the collector actually accepted;
  • changing an environment variable of a running process does nothing.

The exception is memory limits: since .NET 8 GC.RefreshMemoryLimit() re-reads the container limit and values such as GCHeapHardLimit set via AppContext.SetData.
cards.deep: An environment variable wins over the runtimeconfig.json value: the runtime checks it first. Numbers in environment variables are hexadecimal, in runtimeconfig.json decimal. RefreshMemoryLimit throws InvalidOperationException if the new limit is below the memory already committed.

cards.q: Match the question with the API
pairs: How long have GC pauses lasted in total?
Which collector mode is actually running?
Which settings did the collector accept at startup?
How much fragmentation after the last collection?
Which generation is this object in?

cards.q: The orchestrator raised the container memory limit from 1 to 2 GB; the process was not restarted. What makes the collector take it into account?
options: Call GC.RefreshMemoryLimit()
Change the DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit variable
Call GC.Collect(2)
Nothing helps without a restart
cards.explain: Since .NET 8 RefreshMemoryLimit re-detects the limits: both the container’s and those set via AppContext. The runtime does not read environment variables after startup.

wrong.3: That was true before .NET 8. Now there is RefreshMemoryLimit.

lessons.title: Native AOT and memory
lessons.sub: The same collector, no JIT, data in the image

cards.title: What Native AOT is
cards.body:
A regular .NET app ships as IL, and the JIT turns methods into machine code while it runs. Native AOT (ahead-of-time) does that at publish time: the ILC compiler takes the IL of the whole app along with its libraries and produces a single native executable.

The runtime does not go away. A compact runtime is baked into the file: the garbage collector, exceptions, threads, type handling. What is missing is the JIT and everything needed to load and compile IL.

Native AOT is available for console apps since .NET 7 and for ASP.NET Core (minimal APIs, gRPC) since .NET 8.
cards.code:
<!-- in the .csproj -->
<PropertyGroup>
    <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
</PropertyGroup>

# publish for a specific platform
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64
cards.deep: Native AOT descends from the CoreRT and .NET Native (UWP) projects. Its runtime lives in dotnet/runtime under src/coreclr/nativeaot. Before it there was ReadyToRun (crossgen): it also compiles ahead of time, but keeps the IL and the JIT — for recompilation and for whatever could not be precompiled. Native AOT goes all the way: there is no IL in the output.

cards.title: The collector is the very same
cards.body:
The key point for this course: Native AOT runs the same collector, built from the same sources as in regular CoreCLR. So everything from the previous units still holds:

  • generations 0, 1, 2, the LOH and the POH;
  • the fast allocation path through the thread’s context and the slow path;
  • Workstation and Server, background GC, latency modes;
  • pinning, finalization, weak references.

Settings work the same way too: project properties (ServerGarbageCollection, ConcurrentGarbageCollection) and DOTNET_* environment variables. There is just no separate runtimeconfig.json next to the app — the project values go into the executable itself at publish time.
cards.deep: An allocation costs the same in AOT: new is the same pointer bump in the thread’s context. The differences are in the details around it: for example, AOT has no tiered compilation, and so no Dynamic PGO — in the regular runtime the JIT sometimes removes allocations using profile data (devirtualization, stack allocation), while AOT code is compiled once and without a profile.

cards.q: A service was moved to Native AOT. The load and the set of objects are the same. What happens to GC pauses?
options: Roughly the same: the collector and the heap work the same way
They disappear: Native AOT has no garbage collector
They grow: AOT code allocates twice as much
Gen 2 collections disappear: the heap does not age in AOT
cards.explain: Native AOT removes the JIT, not the collector. A pause depends on live objects, roots and the GC mode — none of that changed. Want fewer pauses — fewer allocations and live objects, same as without AOT.

cards.title: Where the savings come from
cards.body:
Native AOT saves not on the heap but on everything around it in a regular process:

  • no JIT — the compiler itself is not loaded, and neither is its working memory;
  • no code heap — in the regular runtime generated machine code sits in memory allocated by the process, often in two versions (tier 0 and tier 1);
  • no loading of IL and metadata — type structures are already built by the compiler and stored in the file;
  • fast startup — nothing to compile, the first request does not wait for the JIT.

Code and type data are mapped from the file as image pages (as in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit): they are read-only and shared between processes of the same file.
cards.deep: How much smaller depends on the app: for small services the working set difference can be several-fold, for services with gigabyte heaps it is within noise, because data takes most of the memory there. The flip side is file size: it contains all the library code that is used. That is why ILC aggressively trims everything unreachable.

cards.q: Which memory disappears or shrinks noticeably under Native AOT? Select all.
options: The memory of the JIT compiler itself
Code generated by the JIT at run time
The managed heap with your objects
Thread stacks
Type structures the runtime builds while loading IL
cards.explain: The heap and stacks work the same: there are as many objects and threads as the program creates. What goes away is everything tied to compiling and loading IL at run time.

cards.title: Frozen objects: data right in the image
cards.body:
Some objects in Native AOT are never created at run time at all. The compiler lays them out in the file ready-made, with a header and a type pointer — these are frozen objects:

  • string literals — every string from the code already sits in the image;
  • precomputed static data — if a static constructor is simple, ILC runs it at build time and writes the result into the file.

The collector neither moves nor collects such objects: they are not in its heap. You can reference them like any other object.
cards.deep: Regular CoreCLR has something similar since .NET 8: string literals, RuntimeType objects for typeof and Array.Empty<T>() are placed in a separate non-GC heap (NonGC heap). The JIT bakes their address straight into machine code, and GC.GetGeneration returns int.MaxValue for them. More on frozen segments in the "Inside the heap" unit.

cards.q: Native AOT. Where does each thing end up?
pairs: A frozen object in the executable

cards.title: What AOT does not have
cards.body:
No JIT means nothing that generates code at run time:

  • System.Reflection.Emit and dynamic assemblies — PlatformNotSupportedException;
  • loading assemblies from files at run time;
  • Expression.Compile() and RegexOptions.Compiled work, but through an interpreter;
  • reflection sees only what survived trimming: the compiler flags risky spots with IL2xxx and IL3xxx warnings.

For memory this means: serializers and DI containers that used to generate code on the fly switch to source generators under AOT. The code is produced at compile time, and no run-time memory goes into building and caching generated methods.
cards.deep: Another consequence: generics. Each List<T> with a value-type T needs its own machine code, and ILC has to see all such instantiations at build time. A MakeGenericType(typeof(MyStruct)) the compiler did not foresee fails at run time. For reference-type T the code is shared (as in the "Generics" unit of the "Deeper C#" course), so there are fewer problems with them.

cards.q: The app is published with PublishAot. Which line throws PlatformNotSupportedException?
cards.explain: Creating a dynamic assembly means generating IL at run time, and under AOT there is nobody to run it: there is no JIT. The compiler warns about this spot in advance (IL3050). The other lines are ordinary code known at build time.

cards.title: How to compare fairly
cards.body:
Before switching to AOT, measure both versions under the same load:

  • time to first response — AOT almost always wins here;
  • peak RSS / working set — at startup and under load;
  • steady-state throughput — here the JIT with Dynamic PGO may turn out faster;
  • GC counters — the number of collections and pauses should nearly match.

Where AOT pays off: short-lived processes (CLIs, serverless), dense container packing, cold start. Where the gain is small: a long-running service with a big heap.
cards.code:
# Linux: peak RSS over the whole process lifetime
/usr/bin/time -v ./app 2>&1 | grep "Maximum resident"

# GC counters of a live process
dotnet-counters monitor -n app --counters System.Runtime
cards.deep: Diagnostics support in AOT is narrower than in the regular runtime and depends on the version. EventPipe (which dotnet-counters and dotnet-trace rely on) has to be enabled in an AOT app at build time with the EventSourceSupport property, and analyzing dumps with SOS is not supported for AOT processes. Before switching, check which tools from the "How to measure" unit you are going to use.

cards.q: Put in order the path from sources to a running AOT process
items: Roslyn compiles C# to IL
ILC builds the graph of reachable code and trims the rest
ILC compiles methods to machine code and lays out frozen data
The linker combines the code and the runtime with its collector into one file
At startup the collector creates the heap; no JIT is loaded
cards.explain: First a regular compilation to IL, then ILC: trimming, generating code and data. The system linker binds everything with the runtime. At startup the heap is created as usual — via reserve and commit, as in the "Memory through the OS’s eyes" unit.

cards.q: For which app will Native AOT save the most memory?
options: A CLI tool that is run hundreds of times a day for seconds
A service with a 20 GB cache that runs for weeks
An app that builds proxies with Reflection.Emit
A batch job that holds big arrays in the LOH for a month
cards.explain: For a short process the main cost is startup and the runtime’s fixed overhead: the JIT, code, metadata. AOT removes exactly those. In the 20 GB cache service and the batch job data takes the memory, and Reflection.Emit does not work under AOT at all.

lessons.title: Course final: memory in .NET
lessons.sub: From OS pages to pinning and Native AOT

cards.q: What is true about a process’s memory numbers? Select all.
options: Virtual size includes reserved but uncommitted addresses
Private bytes grow on commit, even if the pages were never touched
The managed heap size includes memory from NativeMemory.Alloc
Working set is the process’s pages currently in physical memory
GC.GetTotalMemory shows the process’s private bytes
cards.explain: The numbers nest: virtual size ⊇ private bytes ⊇ what the GC heap occupies. The collector does not see native memory and does not count it in the heap size, and GC.GetTotalMemory counts only managed objects.

cards.q: A thread allocates an object and there is no room. Put what happens next in order
items: The thread’s allocation chunk is used up — the slow path
The gen 0 budget is exhausted — a collection is needed
Threads stop at safepoints
Marking: walk from the roots and through the card table
Planning: compact or sweep
Compaction: survivors slide, references are updated
Threads resume
cards.explain: A collection is triggered by an allocation, not a timer. The card table lets a young-generation collection find references into it from old objects without walking the whole heap. Pinned objects stay put during compaction.

cards.q: Where does the memory end up?
pairs: The C library heap, outside the GC

cards.q: A Server GC service runs on a 32-core machine with a 1 GB memory limit. Load is light, yet the heap takes far more than the live data. What helps?
options: DATAS (on by default for Server GC in .NET 9) or capping the heap count with GCHeapCount
Calling GC.Collect() once a second
Switching to SustainedLowLatency mode
Calling GC.AddMemoryPressure with the heap size
cards.explain: Server GC keeps a heap and a gen 0 budget per core: 32 heaps is a lot of memory even under light load. DATAS adapts the number of heaps to the load, GCHeapCount caps it explicitly. Workstation GC is an option too.

wrong.1: Full blocking collections every second add pauses, and the budgets for 32 heaps stay where they are.
wrong.2: SustainedLowLatency suppresses blocking full collections — the heap only gets bigger.

cards.q: Windows get closed and forgotten, but the collector never collects them. Which line keeps them alive?
cards.explain: The Redraw delegate holds a reference to the window (Target), and a static event is a root that lives for the whole process. Until the window unsubscribes, it is reachable. The cure is unsubscribing on close or weak subscriptions.

cards.q: What does this method allocate on the heap on every call, in any .NET version?
options: A closure object with a limit field, and a delegate
Nothing: the lambda becomes a static method
Only a delegate
An array for a params argument
cards.explain: The lambda captures limit, so the compiler creates a closure class, an instance of it and a delegate to its method — on every call. A lambda with no captures would be cached by the compiler in a static field. Depending on the version, a boxed enumerator inside Count may come on top.

wrong.2: A delegate without captures is indeed cached, but this one points to the closure object, and that is new on every call.

cards.q: A native library remembers a buffer’s address while the connection is open. There are a thousand buffers, needed for the whole run. What do you pick?
options: A pool of arrays from GC.AllocateArray(..., pinned: true)
A new byte[] per connection plus GCHandle.Alloc(..., Pinned)
fixed in the method that hands the address to the library
stackalloc in the connect method
cards.explain: Buffers in the POH never move and leave no holes in the young generations. A thousand fresh arrays with long pins is exactly the case that fragments the heap.

wrong.2: A fixed pin ends with its block, while the library keeps writing to the address.
wrong.3: stackalloc memory vanishes when the method returns — the library would write into someone else’s stack frame.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: TryStartNoGCRegion may run a full collection before the region starts
The collector updates a ref T during compaction, but not a T* pointer
Native AOT has no garbage collector
GC.AddMemoryPressure frees native memory
Memory from NativeMemory.Alloc has to be freed by you
cards.explain: Native AOT uses the same collector as CoreCLR. AddMemoryPressure only hints to the collector that native memory stands behind objects — freeing it is still your job.

cards.q: n comes from outside. Put a small buffer on the stack and a large one on the heap
cards.explain: A thread’s stack is limited (usually 1 to 8 MB), and stackalloc sized by input can overflow it — which ends the process. So only a small buffer of known size goes on the stack; a large one goes on the heap or comes from ArrayPool.
